In prolonged labor, before complete cervical dilatation, the portion of the fetal scalp immediately over the cervical os becomes edematous. A swelling is formed is due to the stagnation of fluid in the layers of the scalp beneath the girdle of contact. This is known as caput succedaneum.

The swelling is diffuse, boggy, and not limited by the suture lines. It resolves spontaneously within 2-3 days after birth. It is a result of the static position of the head for a long period of time.

Chignon is a type of artificial caput succedaneum, which is a swelling produced on the fetal head because of the scalp getting sucked into the cup during vacuum extraction.

A placental cotyledon is comprised of portions of the basal plate divided by clefts. It is the functional unit of the placenta.

A placental cotyledon or placental lobule constitutes one truncal or main stem villi and its ramifications (rami). Each lobule is supplied by a single truncal branch of the chorionic artery. Each lobule also has a single vein. The lobules constitute functional units of placental architecture.

The fetal surface is the chorionic plate. The umbilical cord inserts in the center of the chorionic plate.

Maternal leucopenia is not seen in pregnancy, instead leucocytosis is seen. This plays no part in the prevention of rejection of fetus.

The fetus is a semiallogenic graft inside the maternal body as half of its genes are from the father. Uterine transplantation immunity contributes to the survival of the fetus in spite of it being semiallogenic. This occurs due to the following factors:

  • Decidual natural killer cells are inefficient, and therefore are unable to attack the 'foreign' fetal cells.
  • Decidual stromal cells work with natural killer cells to allow trophoblastic invasion.
  • Villous trophoblastic cells don't express HLA antigens and therefore, they are non-immunogenic.

explanationHtml:
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) does not cause involution of the corpus luteum, but it maintains corpus luteum function.

hCG is produced by the syncitiotrophoblasts of the placenta. It is a glycoprotein hormone with two subunits. The alpha-subunit is similar to LH, FSH and TSH. The beta-subunit is specific and is measured by pregnancy tests.

hCG can be detected in maternal blood 8 days after fertilisation. Thus, it can help in diagnosis of pregnancy even before the period is missed. Its levels nearly doubles every 48 hours in early pregnancy reaching a maximum of 50000 - 100000 IU/L by 60-70 days of gestation. Then the level starts falling reaching a minimum at 16 weeks, which continues throughout pregnancy.

  • Circummarginate placenta - In this type, the space between the fetal membranes and the basal plate is filled up by fibrin and old hemorrhage.
  • Circumvallate placenta - In this type, the peripheral chorion is thickened into a ridge composed of a double fold of chorion and amnion. Complications associated with circumvallate placenta are:

Morbidly adherent placenta occurs due to the partial or total absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the fibrinoid or Nitabuch layer. It is of three types:

  • Placenta Accreta: placental villi adhere to the myometrium without invasion.
  • Placenta Increta: villi invade into the myometrium.
  • Placenta Percreta: villi penetrate through the myometrium, sometimes reaching or breaching the serosa.

Based on the adherence of placental lobules, all three types of morbidly adherent placenta can be:

  • Total - involving all lobules of the placenta
  • Focal - involving a single lobule or part of a lobule of the placenta

A morbidly adherent placenta can lead to torrential post-partum hemorrhage. It is managed via C-section and peripartum hysterectomy.

explanationHtml:
Ultrafiltrate of maternal plasma contributes to the formation of amniotic fluid during early pregnancy.

Amniotic fluid is formed by:

  • Early pregnancy - ultrafiltrate of maternal plasma.
  • Second trimester - the extracellular fluid that diffuses through the fetal skin and thus reflects the composition of fetal plasma.
  • After 20 weeks - keratinization of fetal skin prevents diffusion across the skin. Hence, fetal urine forms amniotic fluid.

Note: Fetal kidneys start producing urine at 12 weeks (8–11 weeks), and by 18 weeks, they produce 7 to 14 mL per day.
question: What contributes to the formation of amniotic fluid during early pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
The amniotic fluid index (AFI) is a measure of the amniotic volume which is maximum at 34 weeks of gestation.

The volume of amniotic fluid at each week is variable. The volume gradually increases till 32-34 weeks of gestation. At 34 weeks, it is maximum and thereafter there is a gradual reduction till term.

Amniotic fluid volume is a passive reflector of the fetal condition. Its volume is determined by the following:

Pathway Volume in ml
Fetal urination +1000
Fetal swallowing -750
Fetal lung fluid secretion +350
Intramembranous flow across fetal vessels on the placental surface -350

Any alteration in fetal homeostasis, caused by fetal and maternal conditions, affects the amniotic fluid volume. Thus, AFI is measured as a part of the biophysical score.
question: While performing the USG assessment of a woman at 28 weeks of gestation, you note her amniotic fluid index to be 12.8. When does this parameter reach its maximum value in a normal pregnancy?

correctAnswer: C. Provide nutrition in the form of fat and protein
explanationHtml:
The nutritive value of amniotic fluid is negligible because amniotic fluid is predominantly water. It contains the following:

  • Water (98–99%)
  • Solid components (1-2%) - Organic, inorganic, suspended particles

Functions of amniotic fluid during pregnancy:

  • It acts as a shock absorber and prevents trauma to the fetus
  • Temperature regulation of the uterine environment
  • It distends the amniotic sac and thereby allows for growth and free movement of the fetus.
  • It has no nutritive function, as it is mostly formed by water.
  • Bacteriostatic property

Functions of amniotic fluid during labor:

  • The amnion and chorion are combined to form a hydrostatic wedge which helps in dilatation of the cervix.
  • During uterine contraction, it prevents any interference in placental circulation so long as the membranes remain intact.
  • It protects the umbilical cord by providing a cushion between the fetus and the umbilical cord during contraction
  • It flushes the birth canal at the end of the first stage of labor and by its aseptic action protects the fetus and prevents ascending infection to the uterine cavity.

options.text: Provide nutrition in the form of fat and protein
Prevent ascending infection to uterine cavity during labor

explanationHtml:
The composition of amniotic fluid is not the same throughout pregnancy but changes later in pregnancy due to contamination by fetal urinary metabolites.

In early pregnancy, it is identical to plasma in composition as it is mainly composed of a transudate of plasma. In late pregnancy, as amniotic fluid is primarily formed by fetal urination, the composition is altered. Disorders of the fetal kidney can lead to oligohydramnios.

Fetal swallowing is the primary method of resorption of amniotic fluid. Disorders of swallowing in the fetus can cause polyhydramnios.

Amniotic fluid is alkaline in nature and this helps in differentiating it from vaginal secretions which are acidic. This forms the basis of the nitrazine paper test used for the diagnosis of premature rupture of membranes.

Option D: Artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is avoided as:

  • Once ARM is done, delivery needs to be performed. In this case, preterm delivery would occur, hence ARM is avoided.

question: A 28-year-old G2P1L1 at 35 weeks of gestation is complaining of difficulty in breathing. On examination, flanks are full, and abdominal girth is 160cm. Ultrasound determined that the  SDP is 10cm. What is the next step in management?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of fetal compromise. The management in this patient is immediate termination of pregnancy. Since this pregnancy has crossed 34 weeks, it can be terminated by cesarean section.

Abnormal flow patterns in the umbilical artery:

  • Reduced end-diastolic flow indicates uteroplacental insufficiency (S/D ratio increases)

question: A female presents with 35 weeks and 3 days of gestation, AFI = 5 and there is no end-diastolic blood flow. What is the management?

correctAnswer: A. It has one artery and two veins
explanationHtml:
The umbilical cord normally has two arteries and one vein. The presence of a single umbilical artery is the most common vascular anomaly of the cord. It is associated with congenital anomalies such as genitourinary and cardiac anomalies.

The umbilical cord is a tube that connects the fetus to the placenta. It contains umbilical vessels and an obliterated allantois duct, all surrounded by Wharton's jelly and contained within an outer layer of amnion. Maternal blood enters the intervillous space, and after exchange across the placental barrier, oxygenated blood reaches the fetus through the umbilical vein, while blood exits the fetus via the two umbilical arteries. Wharton's jelly is a gelatinous mucopolysaccharide that protects the umbilical vessels. Local collections of Wharton's jelly produce false knots in the cord.

The average length of the umbilical cord is between 40-70 cm at term. A long cord can form a loop around the fetus's neck and can cause asphyxia. A short cord can result in cord rupture during labor.

  • Epilepsy
  • Oligohydramnios
  • Polyhydramnios
  • Preeclampsia
  • Antepartum hemorrhage

It is frequently associated with congenital malformations of the fetus (20–25%) such as:

  • Cardiovascular anomalies
  • Genitourinary anomalies
  • Trisomy 18

It increases the risks of adverse obstetric outcomes like:

  • Abortion
  • Fetal aneuploidy
  • Prematurity
  • Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
  • Perinatal mortality

In a hysterosalpingogram, the uterine anomaly cannot be determined as the external contour of the uterus cannot be seen.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) provides excellent information about the interior contour of the uterine cavity. However, it doesn't show the external contour, so it cannot distinguish between uterine anomalies such as didelphys, bicornuate, septate or arcuate uteruses.

Transvaginal 3-D ultrasonography (3D TV-US) is very accurate for the diagnosis and differentiation of uterine anomalies. It is the first and only mandatory step in the assessment of the uterine cavity in patients with a suspected uterine anomaly.

Pelvic MRI without contrast provides excellent delineation of both internal and external uterine contours. It should be reserved for patients in whom 3D TV-US is not possible.
question: Given below is the hysterosalpingogram of a woman who presented with infertility. Identify the uterine anomaly seen.

explanationHtml:
Ultrasonography (USG) is the preferred best next step of investigation for this clinical scenario of uterus didelphys.

Uterine didelphis is a congenital condition that occurs when the incomplete fusion of Mullerian ducts that form the uterus during embryonic development leads to the development of two separate uterine cavities and two cervices, each with its own set of endometrial lining.

It is commonly associated with renal anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis, severe renal hypoplasia, etc, and is often associated with recurrent pregnancy loss, preterm labour, malpresentation, and prematurity.

3D ultrasound, a non-invasive test, visualizes both the external (serosal) and internal (endometrial) uterine contours, effectively identifying anomalies. Hysterosalpingography (Option C) shows only the internal contour, making it unable to distinguish between conditions like didelphys, bicornuate, septate, or arcuate uterus.

The USG findings in didelphys uterus are two widely separated uterine horns and a deep fundal indentation.

Laparoscopy and hysteroscopy, being invasive diagnostic procedures, should be reserved for cases where simultaneous surgical treatment is planned following a comprehensive non-invasive assessment of a Mullerian anomaly. (Option A)

Intravenous pyelography is used to diagnose congenital renal anomalies. (Option B)

Metroplasty is the surgical resection of the intrauterine septum. This is done by approaching the uterus transabdominally via 3 methods:

The sequence of pubertal changes in girls is thelarche → pubarche → menarche.

Puberty marks the normal physiologic transition from childhood to sexual and reproductive maturity. The order of changes in puberty are:

  1. Thelarche - It refers to breast budding, and is the first visible sign. It indicates the competency of the hypothalamo-pituitary-ovarian axis. It appears between the age of 9-11 years, and is described using Tanner staging.
  2. Adrenarche - It refers to the generation of androgens (estrogen and testosterone) from the adrenal gland.
  3. Pubarche - It refers to the development of pubic hair, and occurs usually 6 months after thelarche. It is also described using Tanner staging.
  4. Menarche - It refers to the first occurrence of menstruation.

Growth spurt usually occurs between ages 10.5 to 13.5 years.
question: What is the sequence of pubertal changes in girls?

explanationHtml:
Pubarche or the development of axillary and pubic hair is not mediated by estrogen. It occurs due to testosterone in both sexes. Around 25% of testosterone comes from the ovaries and 25% from the adrenal gland. The remaining 50% is produced by peripheral conversion of testosterone.

Puberty in girls involves breast development (thelarche), an increase in adrenal androgen secretion (adrenarche), and the beginning of menstrual cycles (menarche).

Estrogen has the following actions during puberty:

  • Breast development
  • Development of the reproductive tract
  • Starting of menstruation (option D)

  • Regulation of pubertal growth spurt
  • Vaginal cornification (option C)
  • Cervical mucus production (option B)
  • Epiphyseal closure

The scenario of a 16-year-old girl with absent secondary sexual characters, normal stature, with XX karyotype and high FSH and LH is suggestive of pure gonadal dysgenesis.

46 XX and 46 XY gonadal dysgenesis without the phenotype of Turner's syndrome (short stature, webbed neck) is described as pure gonadal dysgenesis. It is characterized by the presence of primary amenorrhea with or without normal secondary sexual characteristics.

Option A: Testicular feminizing syndrome occurs in karyotype XY. Secondary sexual characters are present and the uterus is absent.

Option C: Kallmann syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. GnRH synthesis is reduced, therefore FSH and LH are low, and secondary sexual characters are absent.

question: A 16-year-old girl has come to your clinic with primary amenorrhea. On evaluation, height and secondary sexual characteristics are normal for her age. Ultrasound showed ovaries but no uterus was seen. Her karyotype is 46XX. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of an imperforate hymen, which has led to cryptomenorrhoea. This is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract.

The menstrual fluid gets collected in the reproductive tract. When this collection occurs in the vagina, it is known as hematocolpos. If the collection extends to the uterus, it is known as hematometra. The collection of blood in the fallopian tubes is called hematosalpinx.

The most common causes of cryptomenorrhea are:

  • Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen.
  • Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen

Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis.

Management:

Imperforate hymen - A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function.

Transverse vaginal septum - Extensive dissection and vaginoplasty is required.

Option A: Bartholin's cyst appears as a swelling on the inner side of the labia majora. Larger cysts can bulge across the introitus. Small cysts can remain asymptomatic.

Option D: Endometriomas are endometriotic lesions seen on the ovary. They present as adnexal masses. Endometriosis is a complication in cryptomenorrhea, due to retrograde menstruation.
question: A 14-year-old girl presented with cyclical abdominal pain and a midline hypogastric lump. She has not achieved menarche yet. On examination, a bluish bulge is noted on parting the labia. What is the likely cause of her condition?

correctAnswer: B. LH and FSH levels will be low
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of gonadal dysgenesis. Hence, the patient will have high LH and FSH levels as it is a condition of hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.

Gonadal dysgenesis is the most frequent cause of premature ovarian failure. In this disorder, a normal complement of germ cells is present in the early fetal ovary. However, oocytes undergo accelerated atresia, and the ovary is replaced by a fibrous streak. This is called a streak gonad.

There are two types of gonadal dysgenesis:

1. Pure gonadal dysgenesis:

  • Karyotypes seen:
    • 46 XX is seen in pure gonadal dysgenesis due to FSH gene mutation.
    • 46 XY - Swyer syndrome
  • Associated with primary amenorrhoea
  • They are phenotypically female due to:
    • Absence of testosterone
    • Absence of Anti-Mullerian hormone secretion by testes
  • The underdeveloped gonad ultimately fails, which is indicated by elevated gonadotropin (LH, FSH) levels
  • The presence of a Y chromosome can result in a germ cell tumor in the dysgenetic gonad
  • Treatment:
    • Hormone replacement therapy - with estrogen and progesterone
    • Infertility - Pregnancy can occur with a donated ovum

2. Mixed gonadal dysgenesis:

  • Karyotypes seen:
    • 45 X0 - e.g. Turner's syndrome
    • 46 XX
    • 46 XY
    • Mosaicism
  • Dysgenetic gonad can develop into a germ cell tumor.

explanationHtml:
Among the given features, hypothyroidism is not a major physiological change in pregnancy.

The α-subunits of hCG and TSH are identical. An increase in hCG during pregnancy stimulates the thyroid and leads to a decrease in TSH levels. The thyroid undergoes enlargement and boosts the production of hormones. This is accompanied by an increased production of thyroid-binding globulin (TBG). All these changes increase total T4 and T3 in the first trimester. But the physiologically important free T4 and T3 levels remain unchanged. Hence, physiologically pregnant women remain euthyroid.

Option A: Normal pregnancy is characterized by insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia. Human placental lactogen (hPL), secreted during pregnancy, helps in adapting to fetal energy requirements. Insulin resistance causes prolonged hyperglycemia and glucose flow to the fetus. It also favours protein synthesis. To counterbalance the increased insulin resistance and prevent maternal hyperglycemia, maternal insulin levels are increased.

Option B: By the 3rd trimester, there is an increase in the maternal basal metabolic rate by 10 to 20% in comparison to a nonpregnant woman.

Option D: During a typical pregnancy, mean arterial pressure and vascular resistance fall, while blood volume and cardiac output increase. These changes support the metabolic needs of the expanding uterus, deliver nutrients to the rapidly developing placenta and fetus, and protect the mother from blood loss during childbirth.
question: Which among the given features is not a major physiological change in pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
hCG is not implicated in insulin resistance during pregnancy.

As the fetus is dependant on maternal glucose for sustenance, the blood glucose levels are maintained at a high level in the mother. In response to this, the insulin level in the mother increases, which reduces the maternal blood glucose. To counteract this, the placenta secretes certain hormones which increase insulin resistance in the mother. This resistance is maximal between 24 to 28 weeks.

Hormones increasing insulin resistance include:

  • Human placental lactogen - Increases lipolysis and liberation of free fatty acids
  • Progesterone and estrogen
  • Placental growth hormone - Major determinant of maternal insulin resistance after mid-pregnancy
  • Cortisol
  • Prolactin

Serum creatinine levels decrease during normal pregnancy from a mean of 0.7 mg/dL to 0.5 mg/dL.

Physiological changes in the renal system during pregnancy include:

  • Increase in:
    • Renal blood flow(+80%)
    • GFR(+50%)
    • Creatinine clearance
    • Glucosuria
  • Decrease in:
    • Plasma osmolality
    • Creatinine
    • Uric acid
    • Na/K/Cl

Anatomical changes in the renal system during pregnancy include:

  • Both kidneys enlarge by 1 cm
  • Hydroureter and hydronephrosis - More common on the right side due to dextrorotation of the uterus
  • Congestion of the bladder causing decreased bladder capacity
  • Increased bladder pressure and intraurethral pressure
question: Which of the following changes are not seen in the renal system during pregnancy?

correctAnswer: C. Total oxygen carrying capacity of blood
explanationHtml:
The total oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood increases during pregnancy.

During pregnancy, there is an increase in total haemoglobin (Hb) resulting in increased total oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. However, there is a relative decrease in Hb concentration (hematocrit) due to a greater increase in plasma volume. This decreases oxygen-carrying capacity per unit volume of blood.

Maternal iron stores are not sufficient to meet the increased demand during pregnancy and hence the serum iron and ferritin concentration falls.

The plasma volume expansion also lowers serum potassium.

options.text: Total oxygen carrying capacity of blood

question: Which of the following is increased during pregnancy?

correctAnswer: D. Increase in peripheral vascular resistance
explanationHtml:
Decrease in peripheral vascular resistance is a physiological change seen in pregnancy.

Cardiovascular parameters that increase in pregnancy are:

  • Cardiac output
  • Stroke volume
  • Heart rate

Cardiovascular parameters that decrease in pregnancy are:

  • Peripheral vascular resistance (due to smooth muscle relaxation by progesterone)
  • Both diastolic BP and systolic BP (decrease in DBP > SBP)
  • Mean arterial BP
  • Artery venous O2 gradient
question: Which of the following is not a physiological change seen in pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of physiological edema during pregnancy for which the most appropriate treatment is bed rest.

It occurs due to increased venous pressure of the inferior extremities by the gravid uterus pressing on the common iliac veins.

Features of physiological edema in pregnancy are:

  • Slight degree of ankle edema
  • Usually confined to one leg, more commonly the right leg
  • Not associated with any other features of preeclampsia (like BP>140/90mm Hg, proteinuria)
  • Disappears with rest
  • Other cardiac, renal and hematological pathologies are absent
question: A primigravida presents in the 2nd trimester complaining that her slippers do not fit anymore. On examination, her pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 130/84mm Hg. You note bilateral pitting edema up to the level of ankles. What would you advise her?

correctAnswer: B. Blood flow to the skin decreases to 300 mL/min
explanationHtml:
The blood flow to the skin and mucous membranes increases during pregnancy to a maximum of 500 mL/min by the 36th week. Symptoms experienced during pregnancy such as increased heat sensation, sweating or having a stuffy nose can be explained by the increased blood flow.

Regional distribution of blood flow during pregnancy:

  • Uterine blood flow - increased from 50 mL/min in the non-pregnant state to about 750 mL near term.
  • Pulmonary blood flow - increased by 2,500 mL/min.
  • Renal blood flow - increases by 400 mL/min at 16th week and remains at this level till term.

question: Which of the following is not a physiological change seen during pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
S3 is normally heard during pregnancy.

The third heart sound (S3) occurs due to rapid diastolic filling in hypervolemic states such as pregnancy, anemia or thyrotoxicosis. Hypervolemia is a normal physiological change during pregnancy.

The auscultation of a fixed split S2, fourth heart sound (S4) or a pericardial knock are suggestive of cardiac pathology.
question: A 23-year-old primigravida presents to the antenatal clinic at 30 weeks of gestation. During examination, which of the following cardiovascular findings would not be a cause for alarm?

explanationHtml:
All clotting factors increase in pregnancy except factors XI and XIII.

Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with physiological changes such as:

  • All clotting factors are increased (except factors XI and XIII)
  • Fibrinogen levels are also increased
  • The viscosity of blood decreases due to hemodilution
  • Clotting time and bleeding time is unaffected

The most common cause of decreased platelet count in pregnancy is benign gestational thrombocytopenia. This is due to hemodilution and increased platelet consumption and the women are generally asymptomatic.

The clinical features are suggestive of supine hypotension syndrome due to inferior vena caval compression.

During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus produces a compression effect on the inferior vena cava (IVC) when the patient is in the supine position. To compensate, there will be an opening up of the collaterals of paravertebral and azygous veins.

When collaterals fail to open, venous return of the heart is reduced leading to hypotension, tachycardia, and syncope. The normal blood pressure is quickly restored by turning the patient to lateral position.
question: A 24-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks of gestation presents to the antenatal clinic with complaints of dizziness on lying down for the past one week.  She feels better on sitting up or turning to the side.  What is the cause of this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Enhanced by estrogen and inhibited by progesterone
explanationHtml:
The sensitivity of uterine musculature is enhanced by estrogen and inhibited by progesterone.

Estrogen stimulates the synthesis of myometrial contractile proteins through cAMP. This increases the excitability of uterine muscles and the frequency of action potentials.

Progesterone decreases the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions. This helps to prevent the expulsion of the implanted ovum. However, it increases the amplitude of contraction.

correctAnswer: A. Extend knee and dorsiflex foot
explanationHtml:
Extension at the knee joint and dorsiflexion at the ankle joint helps in stretching the calf muscles which relieves the pain.

Leg cramps are minor ailments during pregnancy mostly due to a deficiency of diffusible serum calcium or elevation of serum phosphorus. Management includes massaging the leg, stretching exercises, application of local heat, and supplementation of vitamin B1 and calcium.

Theca lutein cysts are not seen in hyperprolactinemia.

Theca-lutein cysts are benign ovarian lesions resulting from exaggerated physiological follicle stimulation. They are usually associated with markedly elevated serum levels of hCG.

Theca lutein cysts are found in association with:

  • Large placenta
    • Diabetes
    • Anti-D alloimmunization
    • Multifetal gestations
    • Fetal hydrops

They may also be found in normal pregnancy due to an exaggerated response of the ovaries to normal circulating levels of hCG.

explanationHtml:
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) occurs most commonly in the third trimester or early postpartum period.

Risk factors include Pre-eclampsia/HELLP syndrome, male fetus, previous history of AFLP, and multiple gestations.

AFLP (acute yellow liver or acute fatty metamorphosis) is the most common cause of acute liver failure in pregnancy. It usually occurs in the later stages of pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester. It occurs due to fetal deficiency of long-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (LCHAD) or poor placental mitochondrial function.

The patients present with persistent nausea and vomiting, progressive jaundice, and epigastric pain. Features like acute hemolysis, hypoglycemia, hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and edema can also be present. Symptoms may progress to fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death.

Liver function tests, such as AST, ALT, and serum bilirubin levels, are raised. Hypofibrinogenemia, hypocholesterolemia, and prolonged clotting time can be seen. An elevated d-dimer is seen. Microscopy reveals a characteristic microvesicular fatty infiltration.

The condition worsens till delivery, after which the hepatic dysfunction resolves. A trial of labor by induction or delivery by Cesarean is done. Intensive supportive measures, including blood transfusion, should be provided.

The ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

The total number of antenatal visits should ideally be 12-15 which are distributed throughout pregnancy as follows:

  • One a month up to 28 weeks
  • Once every two weeks from 28 to 36 weeks
  • Once a week from 36 weeks onwards

The WHO increased the minimum number of antenatal visits from 4 to 8 visits to reduce perinatal mortality.

In the Indian scenario, the earlier minimum of 4 visits were implemented as follows:

  • 1st visit: within 12 weeks (preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected)
  • 2nd visit: between 14-26 weeks
  • 3rd visit: between 28-34 weeks
  • 4th visit: between 36 weeks and term

A booked case is one that has at least 3 antenatal visits with two visits in the third trimester.

explanationHtml:
If a female has stillbirth, her parity does not decrease.

Parity is determined by the number of previous pregnancies reaching a period of viability, which is 28 weeks in India.

Multifetal pregnancies, such as twins or triplets, count as one for the purpose of this notation. The current pregnancy is not included in this count.

Multipara refers to a woman who has completed two or more pregnancies past the period of viability. When the pregnancy is preceded by five or more previous viable pregnancies, the woman is called a grand multipara.

Note: Gravida indicates the number of times the mother has been pregnant, regardless of whether these pregnancies were carried to term. The current pregnancy is included in this count.

explanationHtml:
The obstetric score is G4 P1 A2 L1.

The obstetric score is used to summarise the past obstetric history as follows:

  • G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one
  • P - Parity, denoting the total number of pregnancies crossing the period of viability
    • This includes both live births and stillbirths
    • The current pregnancy is not included
  • A - Abortus or the number of pregnancies that were lost for any reason, including induced abortions or miscarriages.
  • L - Living children

Multifetal pregnancies count as one for both gravida and para. A pregnant woman who delivers twins will be expressed as primipara.

The GTPAL system includes the following:

  • Preterm (20w - 36w 6d)

question: A 30-year-old woman came to the OPD with a twin pregnancy at 10 weeks of gestation. She has a 3-year-old female child who was born at term and had 2 first trimester abortions previously. Which of the following is the correct representation of her obstetric score.

The first pregnancy resulted in delivery at term (crossed viable period), hence her para score is 1 (parity doesn't include current pregnancy). Hence, her obstetric score would be G2P1 (Gravida - 2, Para - 1).

explanationHtml:
As per Naegele’s rule, the EDD (expected date of delivery) of this woman is October 16, 2017.

Naegele’s rule states that EDD is obtained by adding 7 days and subtracting 3 months from the LMP (the 1st day of the last menstrual period). Another method is adding 9 months and 7 days to LMP. Less than 5% of births follow Naegele's rule.

It is based on a 28-day regular cycle. If the cycle is shorter/longer than 28 days, corrected EDD is calculated as follows:

  • For a 35-day cycle, add another 7 (35-28=7) days to the calculated EDD to get the corrected EDD.
  • For a 25-day cycle, subtract 3 (28-25=3) days from the calculated EDD to get the corrected EDD.

Naegele’s rule cannot be followed in IVF pregnancies. Considering the human embryo takes 266 days to develop, EDD is calculated in IVF pregnancies by the following method:

  • Same day as fertilization (day 0): EDD = date of transfer + 266 days
  • Day 3 frozen embryo transfer: EDD = date of transfer + 263 days
  • Day 5 frozen embryo transfer: EDD = date of transfer + 261 days

question: The recommended calorie intake for a pregnant woman in the second trimester, who is a sedentary worker would increase by _______.

explanationHtml:
The pregnant lady can continue the same diet since there are no additional calorie requirements in the first trimester.

Pregnancy requires an additional 80,000 kcal, mostly during the last 20 weeks. To meet this demand, a caloric increase of 100 to 300 kcal/d is recommended during pregnancy. This greater intake, however, should not be divided equally during the course of pregnancy. The Institute of Medicine (2006) recommends adding 0, 340, and 452 kcal/d to the estimated nonpregnant energy requirements in the first, second, and third trimesters respectively.

Whenever caloric intake is inadequate, protein is metabolized rather than being spared for its vital role in fetal growth and development.

In the given clinical case, the patient should be advised to continue the pregnancy.

The radiation dose to the fetus during the declared term of pregnancy should be less than 1 mSv. In chest X-ray PA view, the absorbed dose of radiation by the fetus is less than 0.1 mSv. Hence, pregnancy can be continued.

An X-ray has a very limited role in obstetric imaging. There are very few indications where an X-ray will be useful:

  • Fetal: congenital malformation of the fetus and neonates, skeletal malformations, birth injuries like fractures or dislocations.
  • Maternal: Patients having cardiopulmonary disease may require an X-ray chest during pregnancy and that should be done beyond 12 weeks.

Radiation can cause fetal morbidity (FGR, genetic mutations, neurologic abnormalities, mental retardation, childhood leukemia) and mortality. The risks are high with radiation after the first 2 weeks postconception and within the first trimester (period of organogenesis).

Radiation during pregnancy can damage the early phase of the embryo but the risk can be minimized by using the ‘10-day rule’. This rule states that no woman should be exposed to an X-ray for a nonurgent indication outside 10 days from her last period during the reproductive period unless the pregnancy is excluded.

explanationHtml:
Fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of fetal head are assessed by Leopold's manoeuvres:

  1. Fundal grip (first Leopold):
    • Assesses the uterine fundus.
    • Helps in identification of fetal lie and determination of fetal pole at the fundus.
    • The breech gives the sensation of a large, irregular mass.
    • The head feels hard and round and is more mobile.

  2. Lateral grip (second Leopold):
    • Assesses the fetal orientation.
    • The palms are placed on either side of the maternal abdomen, and gentle but deep pressure is exerted.
    • The back is felt on one side as a hard, resistant structure.
    • The fetal extremities are felt on the other side as numerous small, irregular, mobile parts are felt.
    • Fetal orientation can be determined by noting whether the back is directed anteriorly, transversely, or posteriorly.
    • The position of the anterior shoulder is mainly assessed by this grip.

  3. Pawlik's grip / 1st pelvic grip (third Leopold):
    • Assesses the presenting part in respect to the true pelvis.
    • The thumb and fingers of one hand grasp the lower portion of the maternal abdomen just above the symphysis pubis.
    • If the presenting part is not engaged, a movable mass will be felt, usually the head.

  4. Deep pelvic grip / 2nd pelvic grip (fourth Leopold):
    • Assesses the engagement, attitude of the fetal head and determine the degree of descent.
    • The examiner faces the mother's feet, and the fingertips of both hands are positioned on either side of the presenting part.
    • They exert inward pressure and then slide along the axis of the pelvic inlet.
    • If the head has already descended into the pelvis, the anterior shoulder or the space created by the neck may be differentiated readily from the head.
    • It is the only grip performed facing the feet.

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is detectable in the plasma of pregnant women as early as 7-8 days after conception by radioimmunoassay. It doubles every 2 days and reaches a maximum level at 9 weeks. Thereafter, it declines to reach the lower level at 20 weeks and disappears from circulation 2 weeks postpartum.

Increased levels of beta-hCG are found in:

  • Multiple preganancies
  • Rh isoimmunization
  • Down's syndrome
  • Choriocarcinoma
  • Hydatidiform mole

Decreased levels of beta-hCG are found in:

question: Which of the following is not considered as a factor for a high-risk pregnancy?

correctAnswer: B. It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
explanationHtml:
Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome. It is not a diagnostic test.

It is a novel genetic test that uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum for screening of chromosomal anomalies.

DNA from the fetus is found circulating in the maternal blood in two forms - either inside the intact fetal cells or as cell-free DNA from the breakdown of placental fetal cells. In NIPT, the cell-free chromosome fragments are measured and the quantitative differences from normal fetuses are noted.

NIPT can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation and is recommended after the routine first-trimester ultrasound assessment in high-risk pregnancies or if either 1st or 2nd-trimester screening becomes positive. Its disadvantage is that it is very expensive and it can be used for screening of only a few chromosomal anomalies such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21 and it doesn't analyse the entire karyotype.

It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation
It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment

Second-trimester screening (quad screening) at 15–18 weeks: (↓) MSAFP, (↓) uE3, (↑) inhibin A and (↑) hCG can detect trisomy 21 in 85% of cases with a false-positive rate of 0.9%. When it is combined with first-trimester screening, the detection rate is increased to 95%.

question: In which of the following conditions is an increased level of alpha fetoprotein seen?

explanationHtml:
The next best step is targeted sonography. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) levels are only used as a screening test and must be followed by a diagnostic test.

Amniocentesis is a diagnostic test for amniotic fluid AFP measurement. It was once considered the standard for the diagnosis of open neural tube disorders but has been replaced in most centers by targeted sonography.

Defects in fetal integuments, such as ventral wall and neural tube defects, permit fetal AFP to leak into the amnionic fluid. This results in increased MSAFP levels. This is detected on screening performed from 15 to 20 weeks of gestation.

Conditions with elevated MSAFP:

  • Neural tube defects
  • Multiple pregnancies

Conditions with decreased MSAFP:

Deceleration is a decrease in fetal heart rate below the baseline by 15 bpm for more than 15 seconds. Absent variability of FHR with late decelerations is an indication for immediate Cesarean section.
question: A 35-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks of gestation came to the labor room with complaints of decreased fetal movements. Non-stress test was done and late decelerations were noted. What does this indicate?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the NST showing a sinusoidal pattern point towards a diagnosis of vasa previa.

Vasa previa is a condition where fetal vessels travel within the membranes and overlie the cervical os. Hence, there can be bleeding during cervical dilatation or membrane rupture.

Fetal mortality is high due to fetal exsanguination. When bleeding is present in vasa previa, an emergency cesarean section is indicated.

Causes of sinusoidal pattern on NST include:

  • Severe fetal anemia - Rh isoimmunisation, vasa previa, fetomaternal hemorrhage, or twin to twin transfusion
  • Opioids - meperidine, morphine, alphaprodine, butorphanol
  • Amnionitis
  • Fetal distress
  • Umbilical cord occlusion.

explanationHtml:
Nuchal translucency evaluation, a component of first-trimester aneuploidy screening, is done between 11-14 weeks.

It represents the maximum thickness of the subcutaneous translucent area between the skin and soft tissue, overlying the fetal spine, at the back of the neck. Risk of fetal aneuploidy and structural anomalies like heart defects increases with the increase in nuchal translucency.

First trimester aneuploidy screening (done between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation) is a combination of serum analysis and sonographic measurement. The components of maternal serum analysis includes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) while the nuchal translucency (NT) is checked through sonography.

In cases of fetal Down syndrome, the first-trimester serum-free β-hCG level is higher and the PAPP-A level is lower. With trisomy 18 and trisomy 13, levels of both analytes are lower.

Note: Nuchal fold is a normal fold of skin seen at the back of the fetal neck during the second trimester of pregnancy. Increased nuchal fold thickness is associated with fetal aneuploidy.

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation. Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.

  • Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies.

question: Which of the following is false regarding sonography in pregnancy?

Absent end diastolic flow indicates fetal compromise in Doppler.

Umbilical artery vessels:

  • They are characterized by forward low-resistance flow.
  • As gestation increases, there is a gradual fall in all the resistance indices so the amount of forward diastolic flow increases.
  • S/D ratio decreases as the period of gestation increases.

Abnormal flow patterns in umbilical artery:

  • Absent end-diastolic flow - Fetal compromise (hence pregnancy is terminated by cesarean section if >34 weeks)
  • Reverse end-diastolic flow - Impending death (pregnancy is terminated at 30-32 weeks)

Fetal ejection reflex or Ferguson reflex is a phenomenon in which mechanical stretching of the internal cervix enhances uterine activity. Release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary has been suggested but not proven.

It is seen in stripping/sweeping and artificial rupture of membranes. Both of these are methods of induction of labor. It is associated with an increase in blood levels of prostaglandin F2α metabolite, also known as dinoprost/carboprost.

Comparison between two types of placental separation methods:

Schultze method Duncan method

Blood does not escape externally, as the blood pours into the membrane sac. Blood escapes from the vagina as the blood collects between the membranes and the uterine wall.

Brandt Andrew's method or controlled cord traction is a manoeuvre of expressing the placenta from the uterus in the third stage of labour.

One hand grasps the umbilical cord while the other is placed on the mother's abdomen with the fingers over the anterior surface of the uterus. While the hand on the abdomen is pressed backwards and slightly upward, the other applies gentle traction on the cord.

explanationHtml:
The practice of guarding the perineum during delivery of the fetal head is part of the WHO management guidelines for the second stage of labor.

The fingers of one hand support the perineum, while the second hand applies pressure to the fetal head to control the speed of crowning. The advantage of this is to prevent perineal tears.

The second stage of labor begins with full dilatation of the cervix and ends with the delivery of the fetus.

The main events include the descent of the fetus (bearing down by the mother, uterine contractions), cardinal movements of labor, and delivery of the fetus.

Second stage Nulliparous Multiparous
Mean/average duration 50 minutes 30 minutes
Maximum duration 2 hours (+1 with epidural) 1 hour (+1 with epidural)
WHO maximum duration of 2nd stage/diagnosis of arrest 3 hours 2 hours

Management of the second stage of labor:

  • The most common position used is the dorsal position with the hips flexed, knees flexed and abduction of the thighs. WHO recommends any position of choice including the upright position.
  • WHO recommendations for the prevention of perineal tears include warm compresses to the perineum, perineal massage, guarding the perineum, and modified Ritgen's maneuver.
  • Modified Ritgen's maneuver: A sterile towel or pad is held in one hand and placed over the perineum; the other hand applies gentle downward pressure on the occiput to promote flexion and controlled delivery of the head (ensuring the smallest diameter of the head passes through the outlet). Once the occiput is born–with gentle pressure, the head is extended–forehead, nose, and mouth are then delivered.
  • WHO doesn't recommend fundal pressure and routine episiotomy.

Other options:

Option A: A liberal or routine episiotomy is discouraged. Episiotomy is indicated in cases of:

  • Shoulder dystocia
  • Breech delivery
  • Fetal macrosomia
  • Operative vaginal deliveries
  • Persistent occiput posterior positions

Option C: Manual techniques, such as massage or application of warm compresses, are recommended for healthy pregnant women requesting pain relief during labor.

Option D: The position that is most comfortable to the mother i.e. upright/squatting position is encouraged. This position gives:

  • less discomfort and difficulty in bearing down
  • less labor pain
  • less perineal/vaginal trauma and wound infections

True labor pain is not relieved by enema and sedatives.

It is characterized by the following:

  • Painful uterine contractions at regular intervals
  • The frequency of contractions increases gradually
  • The intensity and duration of contractions increase progressively
  • Associated with 'show'- extrusion of the mucus plug that had previously filled the cervical canal during pregnancy
  • Progressive effacement and dilatation of the cervix

  • Formation of the 'bag of forewaters' i.e., bulging fluid-filled amniotic membrane presenting in front of the fetal head

False labour pain is seen more in primigravidae than in parous women. It usually appears prior to the onset of true labor pain by 1 or 2 weeks in primigravidae and by a few days in multiparae.

Such pains are probably due to stretching of the cervix and lower uterine segment with consequent irritation of the neighboring ganglia.

  • Episiotomy repair
  • Pelvic floor relaxation for outlet instrument delivery

question: You notice the gynecology resident administer the nerve block seen in the image before performing an episiotomy. Which nerve roots are blocked?

Pain from the lower third of the vagina is relieved by pudendal block, not paracervical block.

Paracervical block is used to relieve pain during the first stage of labour which constitutes uterine contractions and cervical dilatation. It also relieves pain from upper third of the vagina. It is not useful at the time of episiotomy as the lower part of the vagina is not anesthetized.

Note: Paracervical block causes fetal bradycardia and is no longer considered safe. Epidural analgesia is preferred when complete relief of pain is needed throughout labour.
question: Paracervical block relieves pain from all except:

Postdated pregnancy is not an indication for early cord clamping.

Early cord clamping is indicated in:

  • Birth asphyxia
  • Rh isoimmunization
  • Conditions in which placental circulation is not intact such as placental abruption

The benefits of delayed cord clamping for up to 60 seconds is an increase in total body iron stores, expand blood volume and a decrease in anemia incidence in the neonate.

On the other hand, delayed cord clamping can lead to a higher hemoglobin concentration, which increases risks for hyperbilirubinemia and extended hospitalization for neonatal phototherapy. Delayed cord clamping can also hinder timely neonatal resuscitation.

According to AIIMS Protocols in Neonatology, in uncomplicated preterm birth, delayed cord clamping should be attempted. This is done for a minimum time of 60 seconds after delivery for preterm infants not requiring immediate resuscitation after birth. It states that DCC must be done even if the mother has an HIV infection. And as per the NACO guidelines, delayed cord clamping is advised.

Signs of placental separation:

  • Slight suprapubic bulging due to separated placenta distending the lower segment.

The instrument given in the picture is episiotomy scissors. The angulation in the scissor is to prevent the extension of pelvic tears into the anal margins and obstetric anal sphincter injuries / complete perineal tears.

Complications of episiotomy:

They can be immediate or remote.

Immediate complications include an extension of the incision into the rectum, vulval hematoma, wound dehiscence and injury to anal sphincter.

Remote complications include dyspareunia, chances of perineal lacerations in subsequent labor and scar endometriosis (rare).

Mayo scissors are long and stout scissors. They can be blunt-tipped/pointed tip/straight or curved. Straight mayo scissors are designed for cutting body tissues near the surface of a wound. They are also used to cut sutures and are also known as suture-cutting scissors.

Curved mayo scissors allow much deeper penetration into the wound and are used to cut thick tissues such as those found in the uterus, muscles, breast, and foot. Mayo scissors used for dissection are placed in tissue with the tips closed. The scissors are then opened so that the tips open and spread out the tissue during the dissection process.

The WHO Labour Care Guide begins the documentation of labour progression at 5 cm of cervical dilatation.

The WHO Labour Care Guide is a tool designed to help health personnel involved in labour care. It aims to

  • Guide the monitoring and help in the documentation of the progress of labour.
  • Guide the health professionals to offer supportive care throughout labour.
  • Assist doctors in promptly identifying and addressing emerging labour complications.
  • Prevent the use of unnecessary interventions in labour.
  • Support audits and quality improvement.

The differences between the WHO-modified partograph and the latest WHO Labour Care Guide are tabulated below:

WHO modified partograph WHO Labour Care Guide
Documentation of labour progression begins at 4 cm of cervical dilatation. Documentation of labour progression begins at 5 cm of cervical dilatation.
Fixed 1 cm/hour ‘alert’ and ‘action’ lines Time-based cut-offs for each centimetre of cervical dilatation to guide the obstetrician to take action. For example, at 5 cm of cervical dilatation, if there is no progress >6 hours, action needs to be taken.
Monitoring of labour is restricted to the first stage only. Monitoring of the second stage of labour is included
No section on supportive care interventions Addition of a section on supportive care of the mother- labour companionship, pain relief, oral fluid intake and posture

explanationHtml:
Perineal injury cannot be prevented in normal labor by routine timely episiotomy. Routine episiotomy is associated with an increased incidence of disruption of anal sphincters and rectal tears.

Indications of episiotomy:

  • Shoulder dystocia
  • Breech delivery
  • Fetal macrosomia
  • Operative vaginal deliveries
  • Persistent occiput posterior positions

Methods of prevention of perineal laceration:

  • Avoid delivery by early extension
  • Deliver head in between contractions
  • Perform timely episiotomy when indicated (not routine).

The most common cause of true cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) in India is rickets.

The most common cause of true CPD in developing countries is vitamin D deficiency and rickets. In developed countries, it is trauma to the pelvis. It occurs due to pelvic dystocia (larger fetus and smaller pelvis).

Relative CPD is the most common type of CPD. It is caused due to fetal malposition (occipitoposterior position/brow presentation).

The given clinical finding is suggestive of uterine tachysystole. Oxytocin administration is not beneficial here as it leads to hyperstimulation of the uterus.

Tachysystole (hypertonic uterine dysfunction):

  • The uterine contractions are uncoordinated and increased in frequency (>5 contractions in 10 minutes)
  • Contractions occur with an increase in the baseline tone without rest in between them
  • It is associated with late active phase dysfunction i.e., when the cervix is almost 7 cm dilated
  • The most common cause is occipito-posterior position. Hence, a wait and watch policy is adopted
  • It is more common in nulliparous females
  • Oxytocin administration leads to hyperstimulation of the uterus and is not recommended.

Hypotonic uterine dysfunction:

  • Uterine contractions are inadequate
  • It is associated with early active phase

question: You are monitoring uterine contractions in a term primigravida in labor. You find that the contractions are uncoordinated and the frequency is about 8 contractions every 10 minutes. Which of the following is incorrect regarding your finding?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of either false labor pain or prolonged latent phase. The appropriate management is to sedate the patient and wait.

False labor can be differentiated from the latent phase of labor by therapeutic rest i.e., the patient is sedated with morphine.

Augmentation with oxytocin is done only in those patients who even after therapeutic rest continue to be in prolonged latent phase.

There is no indication of cesarean section unless cephalopelvic disproportion is present. Amniotomy is not useful and should be avoided in patients with prolonged latent phase.
question: A 37-week primigravida has mild labor pains for 20 hours and the cervix is persistently 1 cm dilated but non-effaced. What would be the appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of uterine rupture. Maternal tachycardia is seen in this condition.

Clinical features of uterine rupture:

  • Maternal tachycardia
  • Fetal bradycardia/absent fetal heart sounds
  • Hypotension
  • Abdominal tenderness
  • Palpable fetal parts on per abdomen examination
  • Bandl’s ring
  • Bleeding per vagina
  • Hematuria

question: A 34-year-old G3P2L2 woman presents to the ER with hypotension and severe abdominal pain. On examination, fetal parts are palpable over the abdomen. USG abdomen revealed a large uterine wall defect. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of intrauterine fetal death (IUFD). The best management for such cases at 36 weeks is waiting for spontaneous expulsion.

Forceps extraction is only necessary if spontaneous expulsion doesn't take place.

Artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is not done due to the risk of infections. Cesarean section is avoided as far as possible in case of fetal death.

Waiting till term is not recommended in cases of uterine infections, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and psychological upset.
question: A young primigravida at 36 weeks of gestation came with complaints of decreased perception of fetal movements for the past 2 days. NST is non-reactive and on ultrasound fetal cardiac activity is absent. What will be the best management in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The best time for elective delivery in patients with a history of previous stillbirth is 39 weeks, either by induction or cesarean section.

The recommendations for the management of subsequent pregnancy after stillbirth is as follows:

  • Ultrasonographic screening for fetal growth restriction after 28 weeks
  • Kick counts starting from 28 weeks of gestation
  • Antenatal fetal monitoring is started at 32 weeks of gestation or 1 to 2 weeks prior to the gestational age at which a previous stillbirth occurred.
  • Support and reassurance

Labor induction is suitable in such cases. Cesarean delivery is done for those with a contraindication to induction.
question: A G2P1L0 woman presents to OPD at 36 weeks of gestation for a routine visit. She mentions that she has a history of prior stillbirth at 37 weeks. What is the best time for delivery in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The best management in the given clinical scenario is cesarean section.

Obstructive labor management involves administering intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, providing antibiotics to prevent infection, and promptly performing a cesarean section to relieve the obstruction. If the fetus is alive, an immediate cesarean section is typically performed. Management of obstructed labor never involves a wait-and-watch approach or augmenting with oxytocin.

Clinical features of obstructed labor include maternal exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, tachypnea, genital sepsis, postpartum hemorrhage, and shock.
On P/A examination the upper uterine segment is tender and tonically contracted. The lower uterine segment is thin and stretched. A groove/depression is felt between the upper uterine segment and the lower uterine segment. This is called a Bandls ring.

Complications of obstructed labor include rupture of the uterus and vesicovaginal fistula.
question: A pregnant woman presents with obstructed labor and is grossly dehydrated. Investigations reveal fetal demise. What will be the management?

explanationHtml:
The above partogram shows a case of obstructed labour and management is caesarean section.

There is a secondary arrest of dilatation for >2 hours and arrest of descent for >1 hour. The patient has adequate uterine contractions as shown. The amniotic fluid is stained with meconium and there is fall in fetal heart rate which indicates that the baby is in distress.

There is no place for wait and watch and use of oxytocin to stimulate uterine contractions in obstructed labor.

Forceps can be applied only when the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low down.
question: The partogram of a 28 year old G2P1 is shown below. What is the next step in management?

explanationHtml:
External anal sphincter is the structure injured in an episiotomy extended posteriorly beyond the perineal body.

Perineal tear have been divided into four degrees:

  • First degree- laceration is restricted to the skin of the fourchette
  • Second degree- muscles of the perineal body are torn through
  • Third degree- the tear extends partially backward through the external sphincter of the anus
  • Fourth degree- the external anal sphincter is torn and anal mucosa is also involved

A central tear of the perineum is when the head penetrates first through the posterior vaginal wall, then through the perineal body and appears through the skin of the perineum. It usually occurs in patients with a contracted outlet.
question: After successful delivery of the baby, the obstetrician witnesses that the episiotomy performed has extended backwards beyond the perineal body. Which among the following structures is likely to be injured in this case?

correctAnswer: C. Put her in Trendelenberg position

Caesarean section is the recommended treatment of choice for cord prolapse. Prior to performing the procedure, several measures can be taken to alleviate cord compression. These measures involve:

  • Manually elevating the fetal presenting part using two fingers or the entire hand through the vagina
  • Positioning the patient in steep Trendelenburg, exaggerated Sim's position, or knee-chest position
  • Filling the bladder with 500–700 cc or more of saline (known as the Vagos method)

After the diagnosis of cord prolapse is made, it is crucial not to attempt cord replacement. Such attempts are not only ineffective but also result in the inevitable rupture of the membranes, leading to cord prolapse.

question: A midwife is examining a pregnant woman in labour when she noticed that the cord is prolapsed. What should be the next immediate step of management?

explanationHtml:
Bandl's ring refers to pathological retraction ring. It is formed in cases of obstructed labour.

The upper segment of the uterus contracts and retracts vigourously in an attempt to overcome the obstruction while the lower segment dilates.

With each contraction there is myometrial shortening so that the actively contracting upper segment becomes progressively thicker and shorter. The passive lower segment is progressively stretched and becomes thinner.

The junction between the two segments stands out prominently as a pathological retraction ring.

Schroeder's constriction ring is formed due to incordinate uterine action when there is localized spastic contraction of a ring of circular muscle fibres of the uterus. It is formed due to injudicious use of oxytocin and premature rupture of membranes (PROM).
question: Abdominal examination of a 28-year-old primigravida, who is in the second stage of labour, reveals retraction ring between the active upper segment and the distended lower segment. Which would best describe this ring?

The most common cause of non-engagement at term in a primigravida is deflexed head followed by cephalopelvic disproportion.

The problems of prolonged labour are that the woman is exposed to high risk of infection, ketosis and obstructed labour while the fetus faces the danger of asphyxia and infection.
question: A 26-year-old term primigravida presents to the clinic for a regular check-up. On examination, uterus corresponds to term and head of the fetus is non-engaged.  What is the most common cause for this finding?

explanationHtml:
Asynclitism is not a cardinal movement during labor.

Asynclitism refers to the position of a baby in the uterus such that the head of the baby is presenting first and is tilted to the shoulder. This causes the fetal head to no longer be in line with the birth canal.

Moderate degrees of asynclitism are the rule in normal labor. However, if severe, this condition is a common reason for cephalopelvic disproportion even with an otherwise normal sized pelvis.

Asynclitism can be of 2 types:

  • When the sagittal suture lies anteriorly, the posterior parietal bone becomes the leading presenting part and is called posterior asynclitism.
  • When the sagittal suture lies posteriorly, the anterior parietal bone becomes the leading presenting part and is called anterior asynclitism.
question: Which of the following  is not a cardinal movement occurring during labor?

Latent phase is said to be prolonged in a primigravida if it lasts for more than 20 hours.

  • 14 hours in a multipara

According to the WHO Labour Care Guidelines, documentation of labour progress begins at a cervical dilatation of 5cm.

WHO Labour Care Guidelines:

  • Time axis - examination findings are plotted every one hour
  • Alert column- has values which if reached indicates the need for urgent medical intervention
  • Active first stage - findings are plotted every hour upto 12 hours. If the first stage continues, a new sheet is used.
  • Second stage - plotted every hour upto 3 hours

1) Section 1: Preliminary information

Name, parity, labour onset, active labour diagnosis (date), ruptured membranes (date&time), risk factors

2) Section 2: Supportive care

  • Companionship
  • Pain relief
  • Oral fluid
  • Posture

3) Section 3: Baby

  • Baseline FHR
  • FHR deceleration
  • Amniotic fluid
  • Fetal position
  • Caput
  • Moulding

4) Section 4: Vitals

Pulse, SBP, DBP, temperature, and urine for proteins are recorded every 4 hours

5) Section 5: Labour progress

  • Count the number of uterine contractions over a 10-minute period.
  • Assess the duration of contractions
  • Cervical dilatation: starts at 5 cm and is plotted as X; it is assessed every hour. For example - if the cervical dilatation remains at 5cm for ≥ 6hrs, it indicates the need for urgent intervention. Similarly, the cut-offs for - 6cm is ≥ 5hrs; 7cm is ≥ 3hrs; 8cm is ≥ 2.5hrs; 9cm is ≥ 2 hrs
  • Descent - plotted as O

6) Section 6: Medication

  • Oxytocin
  • Medicine
  • IV fluids

7) Section 7: Shared decision making

  • Assessment
  • Plan

*Fetal position, vitals of the mother and cervical dilatation can be assessed at 4 hourly if the labour is progressing adequately

*If birth is not completed by 3 hours from the start of the active second stage in nulliparous and 2 hours in multiparous women, intervention is needed

question: A woman with gestational diabetes mellitus is admitted to the labour room. The delivery of the baby's shoulder is delayed after the delivery of the head. When is shoulder dystocia considered?

explanationHtml:
A patient with gestational diabetes and the presence of turtle sign is suggestive of shoulder dystocia. Mc Robert's manoeuvre, Wood's corkscrew manoeuvre, Gaskin's manoeuvre, and Rubin's manoeuvre are all used in its management.

Shoulder dystocia occurs when either the anterior or the posterior fetal shoulder gets impacted on the maternal pelvis. Turtle sign may be seen which refers to the recoil of the fetal head against the perineum.

Management of labour in case of shoulder dystocia:

  • 1st line of management - Mc Roberts manoeuvre (flexion and abduction of thigh)
  • 2nd line of management - Rubin's (rotation of the easily accessible shoulder by 30-45°), Woods corkscrew manoeuvre (rotate the posterior shoulder to 180o in a cork screw fashion) ; OR Gaskin (all four's position)
  • Last line of management - Zavanelli manoeuvre (head is rotated to its pre-restitution position and caesarian section is performed); OR procedures such as cleidotomy (fracture of the clavicle of the baby); symphysiotomy (divide pubic symphysis of mother)

In a case of bilateral shoulder dystocia, directly proceed to perform cesarean section after doing Zavanelli manoeuvre.

question: The first manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia consists of:

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of shoulder dystocia and the manoeuvre shown above is the McRoberts manoeuvre. This is the most effective intervention and should be the first manoeuvre to be performed in shoulder dystocia.

McRoberts manoeuvre:

  • Flexion and abduction of the maternal hips (positioning the maternal thighs on her abdomen). There is no rotation of the fetus in this manoeuver.
  • The pelvic rotation which occurs due to the straightening of the sacrum tends to free the impacted anterior shoulder of the baby.
  • Suprapubic pressure may be used simultaneously.
  • The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh is the most common nerve to get injured during this manoeuvre.

If the first line of management fails, proceed with internal rotational manoeuvres such as Rubin's and Wood corkscrew in McRoberts position.

Rubin's manoeuvre:

  • Internal rotational manoeuver used to deliver the baby in case of shoulder dystocia.
  • It involves dislodging the easily accessible shoulder towards the anterior aspect of the chest from under the pubic symphysis by 30-45° while staying in the McRoberts' position.
  • Pressure is applied on the scapular aspect (posteriorly) of the shoulder.

Wood corkscrew manoeuvre:

  • Internal rotational manoeuver used to deliver the baby in case of shoulder dystocia.
  • It involves dislodging the posterior shoulder by 180° in a corkscrew fashion to lie beneath the pubic symphysis while staying in McRobert's position.
  • Pressure is applied on the clavicular aspect (anteriorly) of the shoulder.

explanationHtml:
Applying a gentle suprapubic pressure is the first step in the management of shoulder dystocia along with McRoberts manoeuvre. Fundal pressure is not a method of delivery in such cases.

Hernandez and Wendel suggested the use of a shoulder dystocia drill to better organize emergency management:

  • Call for help and mobilize labour assistants, anaesthesia and pediatric doctors.
  • An attempt at traction is tried followed by episiotomy to afford room posteriorly.
  • Apply pressure suprapubically, not fundally, with the palm or fist, directing the pressure on the anterior shoulder.
  • This should be both downward (below the pubic bone) and laterally (toward the baby's face or sternum) in conjunction with the McRoberts manoeuvre.

These manoeuvres will resolve most cases of shoulder dystocia. If the above-listed steps fail, the following steps may be attempted, and any of the manoeuvres may be repeated:

  • Rubin's manoeuvre
  • Woods corkscrew manoeuvre
  • Gaskin (all four's position)
  • Zavanelli manoeuvre
  • Cleidotomy (fracture of the clavicle of baby)
  • Symphysiotomy (divide pubic symphysis of mother).

The presentation depicted in the image is breech presentation. The most common cause of this presentation is prematurity.

The incidence of breech at term is 3%. At 28 weeks of pregnancy, 20% of women have a breech presentation. The fetus undergoes spontaneous version usually between 30 - 34 weeks thereby correcting its position by itself.

Persistent breech occurs when this spontaneous version is prevented by any of the following causes:

  • Intrauterine death of the fetus
  • Anomalies such as trisomy 13, 18, 21
  • Anomalies of uterus (septate/bicornuate)
  • Oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios
  • Twins
  • Short cord
  • Hydrocephalus
  • Placenta previa
  • Contracted pelvis

Recurrent/habitual breech is when breech recurs in 3 or more pregnancies. It is usually due to uterine anomalies and cornufundal attachment of the placenta.

explanationHtml:
Placenta previa is an absolute contraindication for external cephalic version (ECV).

Relative contraindications for ECV:

  • early labor
  • oligohydramnios
  • ruptured membranes
  • known nuchal cord
  • structural uterine abnormalities
  • fetal-growth restriction
  • prior abruption or its risk factors
  • severe pre-eclampsia and hypertension
  • previous LSCS

ECV is contraindicated in multifetal pregnancy except after the delivery of the first twin. An internal podalic version or intrapartum external cephalic version can be attempted for the second non-cephalic twin. However, ECV can lead to an increased incidence of fetal distress when compared with the internal podalic version.

Previous LSCS is a relative contraindication for ECV. However, it is not attempted often and needs to be performed with caution.

The most common cause of transverse lie is prematurity. In term pregnancy, it is commonly seen in patients with placenta previa. Although the most common cause of cord prolapse is transverse lie, hand prolapse is also frequently seen in such conditions. The transverse lie is managed by the caesarean section.

In a twin pregnancy, management of 1st twin with a transverse lie is caesarean section whereas the 2nd twin is managed by internal podalic version.
question: A multiparous woman presents in labour at 38 weeks of gestation.  On examination, the uterus appears asymmetrical and fundal height is less than the period of amenorrhea. explanationHtml:
In a breech presentation, chin to pubis delivery can be done by Prague manoeuvre.

Rarely, the back of the fetus fails to rotate to the anterior. In such cases, rotation of the posteriorly oriented back of the fetus to the anterior may be achieved by using stronger traction on the fetal legs or bony pelvis.

If this still does not succeed, the fetus still may be delivered using the modified Prague manoeuvre. This consists of two fingers of one hand grasping the shoulders of the back-down fetus from below while the other hand draws the feet up and over the maternal abdomen.

If the back is oriented anteriorly, extraction may be accomplished using the Mauriceau manoeuvre and delivering the fetus back down.
question: An obstetrician is performing a breech delivery. Which of the following manoeuvres can be used for chin to pubis delivery?

explanationHtml:
Delivery of the aftercoming head in breech is not done with the help of Keilland's forceps. These forceps are used for the rotation of the fetal head. It is not used anymore.

The methods used for delivery of the aftercoming head include the following:

Burns-Marshall manoeuvre: When the occiput is seen under the pubic symphysis, steady traction is given on the feet. The baby is swung in an arc towards the mother's abdomen. Simultaneous suprapubic pressure is given and the head is born by flexion.

Malar flexion and shoulder traction (modified Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit technique):

The baby is placed on the supinated left forearm (preferred) with the limbs hanging on either side. The middle and the index fingers of the left hand are placed over the malar bones. The ring and little fingers of the pronated right hand are placed on the child’s right shoulder. The index finger is placed on the left shoulder and the middle finger is placed on the suboccipital region.

Traction is now given in a downward and backward direction till the nape of the neck is visible under the pubic arch. The assistant gives suprapubic pressure during the period to maintain flexion. The fetus is carried in an upward and forward direction toward the mother’s abdomen releasing the face and brow. Lastly, the trunk is depressed to release the occiput and vertex.

The image below shows Piper's forceps, identified by its distinct perineal curve.
question: Which of the following methods is not used for delivery of the aftercoming head in breech?

explanationHtml:
The management of entrapment of aftercoming head does not involve Kristellar manoeuvre.

Kristeller manoeuvre is the application of uterine fundal pressure during the second stage of labour to shorten the second stage of labour. This should be used sparingly used as it leads to avulsion of the levator ani.

An incompletely dilated cervix will constrict around the neck and impede the delivery of the aftercoming head in breech.

Management options:

With gentle traction on the fetal body, the cervix may be manually slipped over the occiput.

If this is not successful, then Dührssen incisions may be necessary. These are a set of three incisions in the cervix:

  • Can be made at the 2 and 10 o'clock position on the cervix. An additional incision at the 6 o’clock position is sometimes needed.
  • Done for delivery of aftercoming head in breech or delivery of head through an incompletely dilated cervix.
  • There is a significant risk of haemorrhage; the cervical incision may extend upwards within the broad ligament causing broad ligament haematoma.

Other alternatives include intravenous nitroglycerin, typically 100 μg, to provide cervical relaxation. General anaesthesia with halogenated agents is another option.

As a last resort, the following methods are used:

  • Zavanelli manoeuvre: It involves the replacement of the fetal head into the pelvis followed by cesarean delivery. This is performed for the protruding head and intractable shoulder dystocia.
  • Symphysiotomy: The intervening symphyseal cartilage and ligamentous supports are cut to widen the symphysis pubis. It is also used to aid the delivery of an entrapped aftercoming head.

explanationHtml:

Vaginal breech delivery is considered when:

  • Fetal weight is between 1.5 kg and 3.5 kg
  • There is an adequate pelvis
  • The presentation is frank breech
  • The fetal head is flexed

  • Facilities for continuous labor monitoring are available (option C)
  • A skilled obstetrician is present (option D)
  • Detailed informed consent has been obtained, explaining the risks of vaginal breech delivery

Cesarean delivery for breech presentation is considered in the following cases:

  • Lack of operator experience
  • Patient's request for cesarean delivery
  • Prior perinatal death or neonatal birth trauma
  • Large fetus: > 3800 to 4000 g
  • Severe IUGR, term weight <2.5kg to 2.8kg

  • Oligohydramnios
  • Fetal anomaly incompatible with vaginal delivery

  • Contracted pelvis
  • Prior cesarean delivery
  • Preterm breech
  • Twins, with the first baby in the breech position

question: A multiparous woman was admitted to the labour room at term with complaints of draining per vaginum.  On examination, the uterus corresponds to term size, presentation is cephalic and the presenting part is face.  Which diameter is engaged in this type of presentation?

explanationHtml:
Occipitoposterior position (OP) is the most common cause of a mobile head at term.

It is the most common fetal malposition. It is an abnormal position seen in the vertex presentation, not an abnormal presentation.

  • Occipitoposterior position is commonly seen in android pelvis/deflexed head.
  • The engaging diameter of this position is sub-occipitofrontal/occipitofrontal.
  • The most common type in occipitoposterior position is right OP.
  • A persistent occipitoposterior position results from a failure of internal rotation prior to birth.

Cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) occurs due to a difference in the size of the fetus and the maternal pelvis. This can lead to a prolonged labour requiring the need of operative interference.

CPD can occur due to the following causes:

  • Fetal malpositions like occipitoposterior position, transverse position or asynclitism.
  • Malpresentations like face or brow presentations.
  • Large fetal anomalies like teratomas or conjoined twins
  • Small or deformed maternal pelvis (due to pelvic trauma)
question: A G2P1 woman presented to the clinic at 40 weeks of gestation. On examination, the uterus corresponds to term size and the fetal head is mobile. What is the most common cause to be suspected here?

correctAnswer: B. Wait and watch for progress of labour
explanationHtml:
The most appropriate management for pregnant women in labour whose fetus is in occipitoposterior position is to wait and watch for progress of labour. In a majority of cases, the occiput rotates through 3/8th of the circle and the baby is born as occipitoanterior.

Hence, when the diagnosis of occipitoposterior is made, labour is allowed to proceed normally when there are good uterine contractions and favourable pelvis.

Indications of caesarean section in occipitoposterior position:

  • Arrest of labour
  • Inadequate uterine contraction
  • Fetal distress
  • Other obstetrical indications.
