question: What is the given device used for?

correctAnswer: A. Minor scalp abrasions and subgaleal hematomas in newborns are frequently seen
explanationHtml:
Minor scalp abrasions and subgaleal hematomas in newborns are more frequently seen with ventouse delivery than with forceps delivery.

Maternal morbidity is seen more with forceps deliveries, and perinatal morbidity is seen more with vacuum deliveries.

Maternal morbidity seen in operative vaginal deliveries includes:

  • Increased third and fourth-degree vaginal lacerations
  • Pelvic floor disorders
  • Postpartum hemorrhage

Perinatal morbidity seen in operative vaginal deliveries includes:

  • Vacuum-assisted perinatal injuries: Cephalohematoma, subgaleal hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhage, neonatal jaundice secondary to these hemorrhages, shoulder dystocia, clavicular fracture, intracranial hemorrhage, and scalp lacerations.
  • Forceps-assisted perinatal injuries: Increased incidence of nerve injury to the brachial plexus and facial nerve; depressed skull fracture, and corneal abrasions.

In cardiac patients, vaginal delivery is preferred. It is conducted with the laboring woman in an upright or left decubitus position. Prophylactic use of a vacuum is done to cut short the second stage of labor. This is to minimize aortocaval compression. Caesarean section is not preferred since it is associated with more blood loss and higher thromboembolic and infection risk.

In ventouse delivery technique, suction is created within a cup placed on the fetal scalp such that traction on the cup aids fetal expulsion. The important step in ventouse extraction is proper cup placement over the flexion point.

The vacuum is gradually created by increasing the suction in increments of 0.2 kg/cm2 every 2 minutes until a total negative pressure of 0.8 kg/cm2 is reached. Progressive descent should accompany each traction attempt.

  • Minimum cup detachment
  • Twisting of fetal head is avoided
  • Smallest head diameter is delivered through the pelvic outlet
  • Success rate is improved
  • Fetal scalp injury rates are lowered
  • Perineal trauma is reduced because the smallest fetal head diameter distends the vulva

Gradual vacuum creation is recommended. This is generated by increasing the suction in increments of 0.2 kg/cm2 every 2 minutes. This is done until a total negative pressure of 0.8 kg/cm2 is reached.

This slow incremental approach would allow for a more firm attachment of the vacuum cup to the fetal head and thereby a lower failure rate.

explanationHtml:
According to ACOG guidelines, the ideal time to administer antibiotics is within a time period of 60 mins prior to the planned caesarean section.

Antimicrobial administration before surgical incision has been shown to lower postoperative infection rates without adverse neonatal effects, as compared with drug administration after umbilical cord clamping. A 1 g dose of cefazolin is an efficacious and cost-effective choice.

For emergency delivery, antibiotic prophylaxis should be given as soon as possible.

The above partogram is suggestive of obstructed labour and the definitive management in this case is caesarean section. Cefazolin is an efficacious and cost-effective choice for antibiotic prophylaxis before caesarean section.

According to the partogram, there is a secondary arrest of dilatation for >2 hours and arrest of descent for >1 hour. The amniotic fluid is stained with meconium and there is fall in fetal heart rate indicating fetal distress. Hence, the management plan is to perform a caesarean section.

The recommended prophylactic drug is a single intravenous dose of a β-lactam antimicrobial. This could either be a cephalosporin or an extended-spectrum penicillin derivative. A 1 g dose of cefazolin is usually given. For obese women, a 2 g dose is better to provide an adequate coverage.

question: The partogram of a 26-year-old G2P1 woman is shown below. What is the prophylactic antibiotic of choice for this patient before definitive management is done?

explanationHtml:
Patients with prosthetic valves are advised to receive antibiotics prior to surgery as prophylaxis against infective endocarditis.

Pregnant women at the highest risk for endocarditis are those with cyanotic cardiac disease, prosthetic valves, or both. However, endocarditis prophylaxis is not required if the patient is already receiving intrapartum prophylaxis with broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent endometritis.

Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for atrial septal defect (ASD). The risk of endocarditis with ASD is negligible. Bacterial endocarditis is associated with unrepaired ventricular septal defects where antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended. Similarly, prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis is indicated at delivery for unrepaired patent ductus arteriosus.

explanationHtml:

In women with significant penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, a single 600 mg intravenous dose of clindamycin combined with a weight-based dose of aminoglycoside is recommended. For obese women, a 900 mg dose is preferred.

Spinal anesthesia is not preferred when the operation is expected to result in blood loss or in a previously haemorrhaging patient. It is because in such cases the development of severe hypovolemia is likely which is a contraindication for this type of anaesthesia.

explanationHtml:
The recti muscles are transected in the Maylard incision for caesarean delivery which is marked as '2' in the given image.

It is a variation of the Pfannenstiel incision in which the rectus abdominis muscles are sectioned transversely to permit wider access to the pelvis. It is also known as the Mackenrodt incision.

The various incisions mentioned in the image are:

Incision '1' - Midline vertical incision is made in the middle extending from just below the umbilicus to just above the symphysis pubis. This is used less commonly compared to the transverse abdominal incision.

Incision '3' - Joel Cohen is a straight incision higher than the Pfannenstiel incision. The fascia was incised transversely in the midline then extended laterally with blunt finger dissection; finger dissection was used to separate the rectus muscles vertically and laterally.

Incision '4' - Pfannenstiel incision is the most common incision made in caesarean delivery. It follows Langer lines of skin tension. A transverse and slightly curvilinear incision is made in the skin and subcutaneous tissue 3 cm above the superior border of the pubic symphysis.

This is stretched laterally for 12-15 cm to accommodate the delivery of the fetus. Following this, the rectus sheath is incised transversely and rectus muscles are separated in the middle to gain entry to the peritoneum.

explanationHtml:
Adnexal exposure is high and hence tubal sterilization is easy.

After delivery of the placenta, the uterus is lifted through the incision onto the draped abdominal wall. The fundus is covered with a moistened laparotomy sponge and this is known as exteriorisation of uterus.

Benefits of exteriorization:

  • Relaxed, atonic uterus can be recognized quickly and massage applied.
  • The incision and bleeding points are more easily visualized and repaired.
  • Adnexal exposure is superior, and thus, tubal sterilization is easier.

Drawbacks of exteriorization:

  • Intraoperative nausea and vomiting
  • Need for additional uterotonics
  • Longer time duration to the first recognized bowel movement

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Sheehan's syndrome.

Sheehan's syndrome (SS) is postpartum hypopituitarism secondary to the necrosis of the pituitary gland. It usually results from severe hypotension or shock caused by massive hemorrhage during or after delivery. Patients with SS have varying degrees of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency. The hyperplastic enlargement of the pituitary, which occurs normally during pregnancy, increases the risk of infarction.

Affected women may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to a deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to a deficiency of gonadotropins). Because deficiencies of some or all pituitary-responsive hormones may develop after the initial insult, Sheehan syndrome can be heterogeneous and may not be identified for years.

It can present acutely as pituitary apoplexy, an endocrine emergency, characterized by a sudden onset of headache, nausea, visual deficits, and in severe cases, severe hypoglycemia, hypotension and shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death.

Also, it can present late with the following features:

  • Loss of pubic and axillary hair
  • Hypothyroidism due to decreased TSH secretion
  • Adrenal insufficiency due to low ACTH

Treatment is by hormone replacement - first glucocorticoids, later - thyroid hormone, sex steroids, vasopressin and growth hormones are given. If there is evidence of progressive visual loss, cranial nerve involvement or loss of consciousness, immediate surgical decompression must be carried out. Fertility can be achieved in these women with hMG and hCG. Clomiphene is ineffective.

The best time to identify the type of twin pregnancy on ultrasound is 11-14 weeks.

Twin pregnancies should ideally be dated when the crown–rump length (CRL) measurement is between 45 and 84 mm (i.e. 11 + 0 to 13 + 6 weeks of gestation).

Chorionicity should be ideally determined between 11 + 0 and 13 + 6 weeks of gestation (the earliest time to identify chorionicity is 7 weeks). This is done using the membrane thickness at the site of insertion of the amniotic membrane into the placenta. The T‐sign (in monochorionic twins) or lambda sign (in dichorionic twins) can be seen here. As the determination of chorionicity is most accurate when the amnion and chorion have not yet been fused, the first‐trimester scan in twin pregnancy is highly important.

Markers of dichorionicity include 4 layers of membranes between the twins, membrane thickness >2mm, different sex of twins, 2 different placentas, and positive twin peak sign.

Women with an uncomplicated dichorionic twin pregnancy should have a first‐trimester scan, a detailed second‐trimester scan, and scans every 4 weeks thereafter.

Women with uncomplicated monochorionic twins should have a first‐trimester scan and then scans every 2 weeks from 16 weeks onwards. This is done in order to detect TTTS and TAPS in a timely manner.

question: In a woman receiving artificial reproductive therapy, the inner cell mass divides on the 7th day. Which of the following complications is not seen in the resulting multifetal pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Artery-vein anastomoses are most commonly seen in monochorionic pregnancies.

All monochorionic placentas have anastomoses that can be:

  • Superficial artery-vein
  • Deep artery-vein
  • Artery-artery
  • Vein-vein
  • One vessel with connections to multiple arteries and veins

These anastomoses are not functional as long as the fetuses are hemodynamically balanced. When a pressure gradient develops between the fetuses, complications can occur like:

  • TTTS - Twin-twin transfusion syndrome
  • TAPS - Twin anemia polycythemia sequence
  • TRAP - Twin reversed arterial perfusion

The most common complication in monochorionic twins is twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). Deep artery-vein anastomosis is the pathology seen in this condition.
question: What is the most common type of placental vascular anastomoses seen in monochorionic twin pregnancies?

explanationHtml:
Congestive heart failure is seen in the recipient twin.

Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is a deep arteriovenous anastomotic complication seen in monochorionic diamniotic twins. Deoxygenated blood from the donor enters through the anastomosis into a shared cotyledon for oxygen exchange. Oxygenated blood is taken up by the recipient twin causing imbalance in the blood volumes.

Donor twin characteristics Recipient twin characteristics
Oliguria Polyuria
Oligohydramnios Polyhydramnios
Hypotension Hypertension
Anaemia Polycythemia
Activation of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) Activation of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
Renal failure, growth restriction, pulmonary hypoplasia, contractures Congestive cardiac failure, premature rupture of membranes

Diagnosis of TTTS depends on 2 USG criteria:

  • Monochorionic diamniotic gestation
  • Hydramnios (DVP>8cm) in one twin and oligohydramnios (DVP<2cm) in the other twin

Treatment modalities for TTTS:

  • Serial amnioreduction
  • Laser ablation of vascular placental anastomoses
  • Selective fetal termination

Note: Donor twin is called the stuck twin as the oligohydramnios limits fetal movement.

options.text: It is called the stuck twin

question: A 26-year-old woman, pregnant with twins, is diagnosed to have twin-twin transfusion syndrome. Which of the following statements is true regarding the recipient twin in this condition?

explanationHtml:
In poly - oli or polyhydramnios - oligohydramnios syndrome, the basic pathology is the presence of a deep artery-vein anastomosis.

TTTS can present as poly-oli syndrome or twin oligohydramnios polyhydramnios syndrome (TOPS). This is usually seen in mid-pregnancy. In this syndrome, there is decreased donor renal perfusion, causing oliguria and oligohydramnios. Because of the anastomosis, the recipient twin has increased renal perfusion and increased urine production causing polyhydramnios.

Donor twin characteristics Recipient twin characteristics
Oliguria Polyuria
Oligohydramnios Polyhydramnios
Hypotension Hypertension
Anemia Polycythemia
Renal failure Congestive cardiac failure
Growth restriction Premature rupture of membranes
Pulmonary hypoplasia Hyperbilirubinemia
Contractures
question: The ultrasound findings in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy are indicative of poly-oli syndrome. What is the pathology seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given USG findings are indicative of twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) with twin A being the recipient and twin B being the donor twin. Oligohydramnios (AFI<5cm), absent urine and abnormal Doppler flow findings in the donor twin indicate stage III of twin-twin transfusion syndrome according to Quintero staging.

Quintero staging system for TTTS classification:

Stage USG findings
I Discordant amniotic fluid volumes + urine visible in donor's bladder
II Discordant amniotic fluid volumes + urine not visible in donor's bladder
III Stage II + abnormal Doppler studies of umbilical artery/vein or ductus venosus
IV Ascites or frank hydrops in either twin
V Death of either twin
question:
Ultrasound findings in a twin pregnancy are given below:

  • AFI of twin A is 26 cm
  • AFI of twin B is 4 cm
  • Urine visible in bladder of twin A
  • Urine not visible in bladder of twin B
  • Abnormal Doppler flow in twin B

What is Quintero staging in this case?

explanationHtml:
In twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), the fetal outcome depends on the cardiac function of the recipient twin. Tei index or myocardial performance index (MPI) is used to assess the ventricular function using doppler.

Option A: Deepest vertical pocket on USG is used to diagnose polyhydramnios-oligohydramnios in TTTS.

Options B and D: Fetal haemoglobin and MCA peak systolic velocity are used to diagnose TAPS (Twin anaemia polycythemia syndrome).
question: An anxious mother pregnant with twins was recently diagnosed with twin-twin transfusion syndrome. She wants to know the possible fetal outcome of the pregnancy. Which of the following investigations can be used to predict this?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows an acardius acephalus fetus. This refers to the acardiac twin seen in twin reversed arterial perfusion (TRAP). Both artery-artery and vein-vein anastomosis can be seen in TRAP.

TRAP is a placental vascular anastomotic complication seen in monochorionic twins where anastamosis between the twins transfer deoxygenated blood from the donor twin to the lower half of the recipient twin through the anastomosis thus depriving the heart and upper body of the recipient causing poorly developed heart and lower body of the recipient twin.

The below image depicts the circulation pattern seen in TRAP.

Based on the supply of deoxygenated blood, the recipient twin might have the following fates:

Fate Type
Lower body is perfused with failed head growth Acardius acephalus
Partially developed head with identifiable limbs Acardius myelecephalus
No recognizable structure Acardius amorphous

The donor twin develops high output cardiac failure.

The treatment for this condition is radiofrequency ablation of the acardiac or recipient twin.

explanationHtml:
The second twin being in transverse lie is the only indication for internal version in modern obstetrics.

In a twin pregnancy, if the first twin has vertex presentation, vaginal delivery can be performed. Following the vaginal delivery of the first twin, if the second twin is in transverse lie, it is corrected by external version (preferably cephalic) into a longitudinal lie. If external version fails and the membranes are intact, internal version is done under general anaesthesia, followed by breech extraction.

If the membranes are ruptured, caesarean section is done immediately.

Mode of delivery depends on the presentation of the 1st twin:

Presentation of the 1st twin Mode of delivery
Vertex Vaginal
Breech Caesarean section
Transverse Caesarean section
question: A 25-year-old woman, pregnant with twins, goes into labour. Following the vaginal delivery of the first twin, she was taken to the OT for internal version. What could have been the possible indication for this procedure?

explanationHtml:
The given specimen depicts a monochorionic monoamniotic pregnancy as:

  • 2 umbilical cords are arising from 1 placenta (monochorionic)
  • No intervening amniotic membrane is attached to the placenta. This means that both fetuses must have been inside a single amniotic cavity (monoamniotic).

Option B: In Monochorionic diamniotic pregnancy, on gross examination, there will be 1 placenta and intervening 2 layers of amnion attached to the placenta. In this type of pregnancy, each fetus will have its own amniotic cavity (diamniotic) with a shared placenta (monochorionic). This is seen if the fertilized zygote divides into 2 between 4-8 days.

The below given gross image of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancy shows two umbilical cords arising separately from the placenta with the intervening amniotic membrane held by the forceps.

Option D: In dichorionic diamniotic pregnancy each fetus has it’s own amnion & chorion. The placentas here may be fused or separate. This is seen in dizygotic twins as well as monozygotic twins that divide within 0-4 days.

Option A: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) most commonly complicates monochorionic (single placenta) twin pregnancy. In TTTS blood is transfused from the donor twin to the recipient twin through the abnormal vascular connections within the placenta leaving the donor anemic while the recipient becomes polycythemic.

The box below describes the type of amnion and chorion seen in different types of twins depending on the time of division.

Monozygotic twins- division occurs within Dizygotic twins - Dichorionic diamniotic

explanationHtml:
Selective fetal reduction is done between 10-13 weeks via intracardiac injection of KCl.

In multi-chorionic multifetal gestations, selective reduction of the smallest or anomalous fetus/fetuses is done to increase the chance of survival of the other fetuses.

Laser ablation or bipolar coagulation of the umbilical cord of the targeted fetus is done. This protects the surviving fetuses from the adverse effects of the drug.
question: A pregnant woman was diagnosed with triplets on ultrasound. The obstetrician has planned to do a selective fetal reduction of one of the fetuses to improve the outcome of the pregnancy. What is the ideal timing and the method for the procedure?

explanationHtml:
Immediate cesarean section is done as the first twin is in breech presentation. Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies are terminated at 38 weeks of gestation.

Timing of delivery depends on the type of twin pregnancy:

Type of twin pregnancy Timing of delivery
Dichorionic diamniotic 38 weeks
Monochorionic diamniotic 34 - 37 weeks + 6 days
Monochorionic monoamniotic 32 - 34 weeks by Caesarean section

The mode of delivery depends on the 1st twin:

1st twin presentation Mode of delivery
Vertex Vaginal
Breech Cesarean section
Transverse Cesarean section

After delivery of 1st twin, if the 2nd twin is in breech, assisted breech delivery is done. If the 2nd twin is in a transverse lie, the internal podalic version is done under GA in the OT followed by breech extraction.

Complications in attempting vaginal delivery in non-vertex presentation (i.e) transverse and breech:

  • Interlocking of twins
  • Fetal head trapping above the cervix
  • Umbilical cord prolapse

According to ACOG criteria (2019), preeclampsia requires proteinuria of grade 2+ or more. In the case of pre-eclampsia, termination of pregnancy must be done at 37 weeks. According to the updated criteria, this patient does not have pre-eclampsia. Hence, a Caesarean section can be done at 38 weeks as for any uncomplicated DCDA twin pregnancy.

options.text: Monitor BP and terminate pregnancy if BP rises
Terminate pregnancy at 40 weeks of gestation

question: A 35-year-old primigravida who conceived after in-vitro fertilization therapy came for an antenatal checkup at 38 weeks of gestation. Her obstetric history revealed that she was pregnant with DCDA twins. On examination, the first twin was found to be in a breech position and the maternal blood pressure was found to be greater than 140/90 mm Hg on two occasions with grade 1+ proteinuria. What should be done next?

explanationHtml:

The complications seen with internal podalic version are as follows:

The order of the most common site to the least common site in the fallopian tube for ectopic pregnancy is ampulla>isthmus>fimbriae>interstitium.

An ectopic pregnancy is any pregnancy implanted outside of the endometrial cavity.

Extrauterine sites: The most common site of ectopic pregnancy is the extrauterine fallopian tube.

  • Tubal - 97% (most common)
    • Ampulla - 55%
    • Isthmus
    • Infundibulum

Intrauterine ectopic sites:

Arrange the following sites of ectopic pregnancy from the most common to the least common.

  2. Isthmus

Prior tubal surgery for ectopic pregnancy has the highest risk of tubal pregnancy among the given options.

Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy:

  • Previous history of ectopic pregnancy
  • Previous tubal surgery for ectopic pregnancy
  • Recanalization of tube after sterilization
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease - most common cause for ectopic pregnancy

  • Artificial reproductive techniques like IVF

question: Which of the following factors maximally increases the risk of tubal pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Endometrial sloughing in ectopic gestation is due to the fall in the levels of progesterone and hCG.

During normal pregnancy, endometrium is maintained by the high levels of hCG and progesterone. In ectopic pregnancy, a fall in the levels of these hormones will cause endometrial sloughing and uterine bleeding. If the decidua is expelled as a single piece through the cervix, it is called a decidual cast.
question: The fall in which of the following hormone/s leads to endometrial sloughing in ectopic gestation?

explanationHtml:
Interstitial tubal pregnancy ruptures at a later stage i.e. at 12-16 weeks. This is because pregnancy at this site is closer to the uterine myometrium which provides support as pregnancy progresses.

Isthmic, ampullary, and interstitial pregnancies terminate by tubal rupture. However, isthmic and ampullary pregnancies rupture earlier. Ampullary and infundibular pregnancy can terminate by tubal abortion as well.
question: Which type of tubal pregnancy ruptures at a later stage?

explanationHtml:
A shock index of >0.85 is seen in a case of ruptured ectopic pregnancy. There is massive blood loss (SBP<110 mmHg) sometimes leading to shock.

The shock index is calculated as HR/systolic BP.

Condition Range of shock index
Normal value of shock index (non-pregnant) 0.5 - 0.7
Normal value of shock index in pregnancy (i.e) obstetrical shock index 0.7 - 0.8
Significant or massive blood loss 0.9 - 1.1

Option A: Sub-diaphragmatic blood irritates the phrenic nerve. This causes a referred pain at the shoulder tip. This is called as Danforth sign.

Option B: The expulsion of decidua in a single piece through the cervix is called a decidual cast. This is due to the fall in the levels of β hCG and progesterone.

Option C: Vertigo and syncope are due to reflex vasomotor disturbances due to peritoneal irritation from hemoperitoneum.
question: Which of the following clinical features is not seen in a patient with ruptured ectopic pregnancy?

correctAnswer: A. Low levels with prolonged doubling time
explanationHtml:
Low levels of β hCG and prolonged doubling time increase the suspicion of ectopic pregnancy.

Urine pregnancy test is very sensitive and found positive in most ectopic pregnancies. Hence, serial serum β hCG levels are estimated to detect ectopic pregnancy. In early normal pregnancy, the doubling time of β hCG concentrations in plasma is 1.4 to 2 days.

options.text: Low levels with prolonged doubling time
High levels with decreased doubling time

question: A woman presented with complaints of amenorrhoea for 6 weeks and a history of prior ectopic pregnancy. Serial serum beta hCG levels were estimated in her. Which of the following findings will increase the suspicion of ectopic gestation in her?

explanationHtml:
Ring of fire pattern is seen on color doppler in a tubal ectopic pregnancy. This is due to placental blood flow in the tubal pregnancy.

This finding may also be seen in corpus luteum cysts but the wall is less echogenic compared to tubal ectopic.

Option A: There is an enhanced blood flow pattern outside the uterine cavity in case of ectopic pregnancy.

Option B: Arias-Stella reaction/phenomenon is a histological finding. It is an atypical endometrial change due to the action of progesterone on the endometrial tissue seen in normal, ectopic, and molar pregnancies.

On histology, there are:

  • large cells with abundant eosinophilic or vacuolated cytoplasm
  • nuclear enlargement
  • hyperchromasia

Option D: Whirlpool sign refers to the twisted ovarian pedicle seen on USG of ovarian torsion.

options.text: Enhanced blood flow pattern in the uterine artery

question: A patient presented with 6 weeks of amenorrhoea and a positive UPT. TVS revealed a tubal ectopic pregnancy. Which of the following findings can be usually picked up on colour Doppler?

explanationHtml:
Central location is a feature of the pseudogestational sac seen in ectopic pregnancies.

Pseudogestational sac is a collection of fluid between the endometrial layers, surrounded by a thick decidua. Its presence increases the suspicion of ectopic pregnancy.

Differences between pseudogestational sac and true gestational sac:

Feature Pseudogestational sac True gestational sac
Location within the endometrial cavity Central Eccentric
Shape Usually ovoid Usually round
Fetal and yolk sac poles Absent Present
Double ring sign Absent Seen
Intradecidual sign Absent Seen
question: A pregnant woman came for routine antenatal USG. Which of the following features is suggestive of a pseudogestational sac?

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, the next step would be to confirm the tubal ectopic by measuring serum β hCG. This can be used to differentiate tubal ectopic pregnancy from missed abortion and early intrauterine pregnancy.

If the level is ≥2000 IU/L, ectopic pregnancy is suspected. If the level is <1500 IU/L, a repeat serum β hCG is taken after 48 hours. If the levels are:

  • Doubled - early intrauterine pregnancy
  • Decreased - abortion
  • Increased but less than doubled value - ectopic pregnancy

Investigations for ectopic pregnancy:

  • Serum β hCG - lower levels compared to normal pregnancy, prolonged doubling time
  • Transvaginal ultrasound - empty uterine cavity, fluid in pouch of Douglas, adnexal mass
  • Colour Doppler - ring of fire pattern
  • Laparoscopy
  • Dilatation and curettage - decidua identified without villi
  • Serum progesterone
  • Culdocentesis

Diagnostic laparoscopy may be done when the diagnosis is still uncertain after serial β-hCG monitoring and repeat ultrasonography. In high-risk situations, such as a history of previous ectopic pregnancy, earlier diagnostic laparoscopy is considered.
question: A patient with suspected tubal pregnancy underwent transvaginal ultrasound which was inconclusive. What is the next step of management?

correctAnswer: B. Gestational sac size of 5 cm
explanationHtml:
A gestational sac size of <4 cm is an indication of expectant management.

Expectant management is done only in the case of unruptured tubal pregnancy. In this, observation is done till there is spontaneous resolution. It can be done but is not preferred due to prolonged follow-up and uncertainty in resolution.

The indications are:

  • Initial serum β hCG <1000 IU/L
  • Falling serum β hCG levels
  • Gestational sac size <4 cm
  • No fetal cardiac activity on TVS
  • No evidence of rupture or bleeding on TVS

options.text: Initial serum beta hCG level of 200 mIU/mL

question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with unruptured ectopic gestation. Which of the following is not an indication for expectant management in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical vignette most likely suggests an unruptured ectopic pregnancy. Oxytocin is not used in the management of this condition.

A history of sexually transmitted disease (STD) or pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) leads to peritubal adhesions causing kinking of the fallopian tubes and increasing the risk of tubal implantation of the zygote leading to an ectopic pregnancy.

Indications for medical management of unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy:

  • Hemodynamically stable patient
  • Serum β hCG <5000 IU/L
  • Tubal diameter <4 cm
  • No fetal cardiac activity
  • No intra-abdominal haemorrhage

Medical management of unruptured tubal ectopic:

  • Direct local therapy (laparoscopy or USG guidance) -
    • Methotrexate
    • Potassium chloride
    • Actinomycin
    • Hyperosmolar glucose
    • PGF2α
  • Systemic therapy - single dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM

Follow-up after medical management is done by measuring the decline in serial serum β hCG.
question: A primigravida in her first trimester with a previous history of sexually transmitted disease came for a routine ANC. USG findings revealed an empty uterine cavity. Serum beta hCG was measured and was found to be 1700 IU/mL. All of the following drugs can be used in managing this patient except:

explanationHtml:
In the multi-dose protocol, methotrexate is given at a dose of 1 mg/kg as an IM injection on alternate days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

This regimen is continued on alternating days until the hCG level drops by 15% over two days. Up to 4 doses may be given. Along with this, leucovorin rescue (folinic acid) is given at 0.1 mg/kg after 24 hrs (on days 2, 4, 6, and 8) to buffer the side effects of methotrexate.

MTX Protocol Multi-dose regimen Single-dose regimen
Dose

1 mg/kg
(+ 0.1 mg/kg LEU)

50 mg/m2
(Body surface area)
Regimen Alternate daily doses Day 0
hCG measurement Days 0, 1, 3, 5, 7 Days 0, 4, 7
Treatment success hCG declines >15% from the previous value hCG declines >15% between Day 4 and 7
When to administer additional dose 2nd, 3rd or 4th dose to be given if hCG does not decline 15% from the previous value. Maximum 4 doses Second dose on Day 7 if hCG does not decline 15%

Note: If the decline is ≥15%, the patient is followed up weekly till the levels fall to <10 IU/L.
question: A patient with unruptured ectopic pregnancy is planned for medical management with methotrexate. What is the multi-dose protocol for this drug?

explanationHtml:
Sunlight exposure, sexual intercourse and NSAIDs must be avoided when patients are on methotrexate therapy.

The following should be avoided when methotrexate therapy has been initiated for the treatment of ectopic gestation:

  • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs - can cause reduced renal blood flow and delay drug excretion
  • Alcohol - can predispose to concurrent hepatic enzyme elevation
  • Sunlight - may provoke methotrexate-related dermatitis
  • Sexual intercourse - can rupture the ectopic pregnancy
  • Phenytoin, tetracyclines, salicylates, and sulfonamides - can increase serum methotrexate levels
question:
Which of the following must be avoided by a patient with tubal pregnancy on methotrexate?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of ruptured ectopic pregnancy which must be immediately managed with simultaneous resuscitation and laparotomy. On laparotomy, salpingectomy is the definitive surgery.

Diagnosis of ruptured ectopic pregnancy is made based on clinical features:

  • Amenorrhoea for 6-8 weeks followed by bleeding PV
  • Abdominal pain
  • Hemodynamically unstable
  • Urine pregnancy test - positive

Surgical treatment of ectopic pregnancy includes salpingectomy or salpingostomy, performed either through laparoscopy or laparotomy.

Management of suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy consists of initial resuscitation and stabilization, followed by point-of-care ultrasound (FAST) to identify intraperitoneal free fluid and surgical exploration.

Laparotomy is done for hemodynamically unstable patients with ruptured ectopic pregnancies. Salpingectomy is the treatment of choice and is done with preservation of the ipsilateral ovary and its vascular supply.

For patients wishing to preserve future fertility, if the contralateral fallopian tube is damaged, salpingostomy is preferred. However, salpingostomy may result in inadequate evacuation of the products of conception and a recurrence of symptoms. Therefore, after a patient undergoes salpingostomy, it is important check the β-hCG level on a weekly basis to ensure that it reaches zero.

question: A 30-year-old woman was brought to the casualty in a drowsy state with complaints of bleeding PV  associated with abdominal pain and a history of amenorrhoea for 8 weeks. On examination, BP was 90/60 mmHg, PR was 140 bpm, and UPT was positive. What is the next step of management?

explanationHtml:
Ectopic pregnancy Criteria
Abdominal Studdiford
Cervical Rubin
Ovarian Spiegelberg

Spiegelberg’s criteria used for the diagnosis of ovarian pregnancy include intact ipsilateral tube, pregnancy occupying ovary connected by the utero-ovarian ligament.

Studdiford’s criteria used for the diagnosis of primary abdominal pregnancy include the presence of normal bilateral tubes and pregnancy related to the peritoneal surface.

Rubin's criteria used for the diagnosis of cervical pregnancy includes presence of soft, enlarged cervix and closed internal os and partially opened external os.

Ectopic pregnancy Criteria

According to the 2022 FOGSI guidelines, Anti-D is given at a dose of 150 μg intramuscularly for alloimmunization after surgical management of ectopic pregnancy.

The dose of anti-D in a surgically treated case of ectopic is 150 μg if gestation <20 weeks. If the gestation is ≥20 weeks, 300 μg of anti-D is given intramuscularly.

Anti-D is not given when the ectopic is treated with medical methods.
question: An O-ve primigravida underwent surgery for ectopic pregnancy at 13 weeks of gestation. What will be the dose of anti-D immunoglobulin to be given to her?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of heterotopic pregnancy. Surgery is the ideal treatment in heterotopic pregnancy.

A normal uterine pregnancy co-existing with an extrauterine (ectopic) pregnancy is termed a heterotopic pregnancy. Although heterotopic pregnancy can occur spontaneously, it is more likely after ART and ovulation induction.

Tubal ring sign also referred to as bagel sign is one of the ultrasound signs of a tubal ectopic. It comprises an echogenic ring that surrounds an unruptured ectopic pregnancy.

USG image showing bagel sign or tubal ring sign:

Methotrexate is not to be given as it harms even the normal intrauterine fetus. Although potassium chloride may be injected into the sac of the ectopic, the safer method would be surgery to remove the ectopic.
question: A 30-year-old female patient (G2P0A1) with a history of FSH therapy and in vitro fertilization presented with lower abdominal pain, vomiting, and vaginal discharge. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy of 8 weeks associated with a heterogeneous right adnexal mass showing a positive bagel sign. What is the most appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Methotrexate is most effective when given at β hCG levels are <5000 IU/L.

Methotrexate is given at a dose of 50 mg/m2 of body surface area. Monitoring is done by measuring β hCG levels on days 4 and 7. If the decline is ≥15% of the initial value, the patient is followed up weekly till the levels fall to <10 IU/L. A second dose of methotrexate is required on day 7 if the observed decline is <15%.
question: Methotrexate was administered to a patient with unruptured ectopic pregnancy. At what serum beta hCG levels will this drug be most effective?

explanationHtml:
Studdiford’s criteria is used for the diagnosis of primary abdominal pregnancy.

Primary abdominal pregnancy is the rarest type of ectopic gestation. The conceptus implants on the peritoneal surface of the abdomen.

Studdiford’s criteria:

  1. The presence of normal bilateral tubes and ovaries with no evidence of recent or past pregnancy.
  2. No evidence of a uteroperitoneal fistula.
  3. The presence of pregnancy, related exclusively to the peritoneal surface, early enough to eliminate the possibility of secondary implantation

Criteria used in the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy are:

  • Cervical pregnancy: Paalman and McElin (clinical criteria); Rubin's criteria (histological criteria)
  • Ovarian pregnancy: Spiegelberg’s criteria
question: Studdiford’s criteria is used for the diagnosis of _____________

explanationHtml:
According to WHO, abortion is defined as pregnancy termination or loss before 20 weeks of gestation or with a fetus weighing <500 g.

Some common causes of spontaneous abortion are:

  • Chromosomal abnormalities
  • Luteal phase defects
  • Diabetes mellitus and thyroid disorders
  • Cervical incompetence
  • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

  • Alcohol and cigarette smoking

question: Abortion is the expulsion of fetus weighing _____.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of first-trimester abortion which is most commonly caused by chromosomal abnormalities.

Aneuploidy accounts for 50-70% of first-trimester pregnancy losses, with autosomal trisomies being the most common subtype (approximately 50% of genetic causes). Among these, the most common trisomy involved in abortions is trisomy 16. Turner syndrome (monosomy X) is the single most common chromosomal abnormality in miscarriages.

Causes of spontaneous abortion are:

  • Genetic -
    • Numerical chromosomal abnormalities
    • Chromosomal rearrangements
    • Mendelian etiology
  • Endocrine -
    • Luteal phase defects
    • Thyroid abnormalities
    • Diabetes mellitus
  • Anatomical -
    • Cervical incompetence
    • Congenital uterine malformations
    • Uterine fibroid
    • Uterine synechiae
  • Infectious (TORCH infections)
  • Immunological -
    • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
    • Autoimmunity
  • Maternal illness -
    • Cyanotic heart diseases
    • Hemoglobinopathies
  • Environmental -
    • Radiation exposure
    • Alcohol
    • Cigarette smoking

question: A patient presented with vaginal bleeding following 6 weeks of amenorrhoea. Her UPT was positive. What is the most common cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The least likely chromosomal abnormality involved in first-trimester abortions is trisomy 1.

The most common chromosomal abnormality in first trimester abortions is trisomy. The common trisomies are:

  • Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18)
  • Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
  • Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13)
  • Trisomies 16 and 22

Turner syndrome (Monosomy X) is the single most frequent chromosomal abnormality. It usually results in abortion.

question: A patient presented with a spontaneous abortion at 7 weeks of gestation. Which of the following is the least likely chromosomal abnormality that can lead to this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given USG image shows an empty gestational sac which is seen in missed abortion before 12 weeks. At this gestational age, the entire ovum is covered by the chorionic villi giving rise to the empty gestational sac.

If this condition occurs beyond 12 weeks of gestation, a dead fetus is seen on USG. This is not preceded by any warning signs and the fetus is not expelled outside spontaneously.

question: You are examining a primigravida with complete abortion. Which of the following findings would you not expect?

explanationHtml:
According to the 2026 American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) guidelines, recurrent miscarriage is defined as ≥ 2 consecutive pregnancy losses at ≤ 20 weeks. This excludes confirmed molar or ectopic pregnancies. Pregnancy can be confirmed by blood or urinary HCG, histopathology or ultrasonography.

This definition is also supported by the ACOG.

Recurrent pregnancy losses can be of 2 types:

  • Primary recurrent miscarriage where there are multiple losses in a woman who has never delivered a liveborn
  • Secondary recurrent miscarriage where multiple pregnancy losses occur in a patient who has had a prior live birth

question:
According to the ASRM, recurrent miscarriage is the loss of:

ASRM - American Society for Reproductive Medicine.

explanationHtml:
Infections do not usually cause recurrent miscarriages.

Common causes of recurrent miscarriage:

  • Parental chromosomal abnormalities
  • Anatomical factors -
    • Uterine synechiae or Asherman syndrome
    • Uterine leiomyomas
    • Congenital genital tract anomalies
  • Immunological factors -
    • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
  • Endocrine factors -
    • Luteal phase defect
    • Polycystic ovarian syndrome

question: Which of the following conditions does not usually cause recurrent miscarriages?

explanationHtml:
The given lab findings are suggestive of anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome(APLS).

Criteria for diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome:

Clinical criteria -

  • Obstetric
    • Three or more unexplained consecutive pre-fetal losses(<10 weeks) or early fetal deaths (10w 0d-15w 6d)
    • Fetal death (16w 0d-33w 6d) in the absence of pre-eclampsia with severe features or placental insufficiency with severe features
    • Placental insufficiency with severe features or pre-eclampsia with severe features at <34 weeks
    • Placental insufficiency with severe features and pre-eclampsia with severe features at <34 weeks
  • Vascular
    • One or more episodes of arterial, venous, or small vessel thrombosis in any tissue or organ

Laboratory criteria -

  • Presence of lupus anticoagulant
  • Presence of IgG or IgM anti-cardiolipin antibodies
  • Presence of IgG or IgM anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies

At least one clinical and one laboratory criteria is needed for the diagnosis.

Non-specific tests for lupus anticoagulant are increased aPTT, Kaolin clotting time, and dilute Russell viper venom time.

question:
A primigravida had a spontaneous abortion at 18 weeks. On examination, the fetus was morphologically normal. Further investigations were performed upon the patient's insistence and the results are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:

question: A woman comes to the casualty at 18 weeks of gestation with complaints of vaginal bleeding. She has a history of two early pregnancy losses. USG reveals the absence of fetal cardiac activity. Which of the following investigations need not be done in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The best mode of treatment for a pregnant woman with antiphospholipid syndrome(APS) is aspirin and heparin.

APS is a prothrombotic disorder (autoantibody-mediated thrombophilia) affecting both arterial and venous systems.

Patients present with recurrent pregnancy loss due to thrombosis of uteroplacental vessels, poor placental perfusion, and prevention of normal decidual changes after zygote implantation. They may also present with preterm delivery, pre-eclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and fetal death.

2023 ACR/EULAR criteria (Obstetric domain) for APS:

  1. ≥ 3 consecutive losses upto 15 weeks + 6 days
    1. Pre fetal loss : before 10 weeks 0 days of gestation.
    2. Early fetal loss : between 10 weeks and 15 weeks 6 days
  2. ≥ 1 fetal loss between 16 weeks 0 days and 33 weeks 6 days gestation in absence of Pre-eclampsia (PEC) with severe features or placental insufficiency (PI) with severe features.
  3. PEC with severe features (<34w 0d) or PI with severe features (<34w 0d) with/without fetal death
  4. PEC with severe features (<34w 0d) and PI with severe features (<34w 0d) with/without fetal death

Aspirin (60-80mg daily) with heparin (5000-10,000 U subcutaneously every 12h) is the most effective therapy for APS. Treating APS with only aspirin (option A) is not recommended as heparin is crucial in preventing thrombus formation at the decidual-thrombotic interface, Corticosteroids (option C, D) should not be used in primary APS (without an associated connective tissue disorder) but are indicated in patients with pre-existing systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and APS (secondary APS).

question: A pregnant lady with a history of recurrent abortions is now diagnosed to have antiphospholipid syndrome. What would be the best mode of treatment for her?

correctAnswer: B. At least 2 organ systems should be involved to make a diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (CAPS) is a complication of APLA syndrome, in which ≥3 organ systems are involved. It is also known as Asherson syndrome.

It is seen in both primary and secondary APLA syndrome. Triggering factors include infections, trauma, and obstetric causes. IVIG can be used in CAPS when the first-line therapies with aspirin and heparin have failed.

Note: Asherman syndrome is an acquired condition characterised by formation of intrauterine adhesions or synechiae.

question: A G3A3 patient was admitted to the hospital with catastrophic APLS following a spontaneous abortion. Which of the following is false about this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Repeated mid-trimester painless cervical dilatation
explanationHtml:
Cervical incompetence or insufficiency is characterized by repeated mid-trimester painless cervical dilatation. Escape of amniotic fluid followed by painless expulsion of products of conception can also be seen.

Risk factors for cervical incompetence:

  • Congenital uterine anomalies
  • Acquired -
    • Dilatation and currettage
    • Dilatation and evacuation
    • Vaginal operative delivery through an undilated cervix
    • Amputation of cervix
  • Multiple gestations
  • Prior preterm birth

options.text: Repeated third trimester painless cervical dilatation
Bleeding per vaginum in the first trimester

question: Which of the following features can be seen in a patient with cervical incompetence?

explanationHtml:
In-utero exposure to DES, twin pregnancy, and bicornuate uterus increase the risk of cervical incompetence.

Offsprings born to pregnant mothers who were treated with diethylstilbestrol may develop cervical hypoplasia and malformation. They may also present with cervical incompetence during their 2nd trimester.

Cervical incompetence can be seen following MTP with surgical methods and not with medical methods.

The retentive power of the internal os may be compromised by anatomical abnormalities like bicornuate uterus and overdistended uterus due to twin gestations.

Risk factors for cervical incompetence:

  • Congenital uterine anomalies
  • Acquired -
    • Dilatation and currettage
    • Induced abortion by dilatation and evacuation
    • Vaginal operative delivery through an undilated cervix
    • Amputation of cervix
  • Multiple gestations
  • Prior preterm birth

question:
Which of the following increase the risk of developing cervical incompetence?

  1. In-utero exposure to DES
  2. Twin pregnancy
  3. History of MTP with Mifepristone
  4. Genital tract infections
  5. Bicornuate uterus

explanationHtml: In the given image, the parameter marked A is funnelling of the internal os and the parameter marked B is cervical length. Funnelling of internal os >1cm and cervical length <25 mm are diagnostic of cervical incompetence on transvaginal ultrasound.

question: The transvaginal ultrasound of a pregnant woman is given below. What are the cutoff values of the parameters marked A and B for a diagnosis of cervical incompetence?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cervical incompetence. It can be managed with prophylactic cervical cerclage done between 12 and 14 weeks of gestation.

Rescue or emergency cerclage is done anytime within 24 weeks of gestation. It should only be done when there is bulging of membranes through the dilated cervix.

Investigations for cervical incompetence:

  • In interconceptional period -
    • Passage of number 6 - 8 Hegar's dilator beyond the internal os without resistance or pain
    • Funnel-shaped shadow in premenstrual hysterocervicography
  • During pregnancy -
    • Per speculum examination showing cervical dilatation with herniation of membranes
    • USG revealing cervical length <2.5 cm and funnelling of internal os >1 cm

question: A 26-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive UPT. Her past obstetric history was significant for 2 mid-trimester abortions. On USG, cervical length was 20 mm and no bulging membranes were seen.  What is the next step in her management?

explanationHtml:
McDonald's procedure is a type of cervical cerclage. It can be done up to 24 weeks of gestation.

Contraindications to cervical cerclage are:

  • Absolute
    • >24 weeks of gestation
    • Active labour
    • Active vaginal bleeding
    • Abruptio placenta
    • Premature rupture of membranes
    • Chorioamnionitis
    • Severe uterine irritability
    • Fetal death or defect
  • Relative
    • Prolapsed membranes
    • Vaginal spotting

question: A patient with cervical insufficiency is posted for McDonald's procedure.  Which of the following is not a contraindication for this surgery?

correctAnswer: B. A mersilene tape is tied around the cervix
explanationHtml:
In McDonald's cerclage, a nonabsorbable suture, such as Mersilene, is placed as a purse-string suture as high as possible at the level of the internal os, positioned at the junction where the rugose vaginal epithelium transitions to the smooth vaginal portion of the cervix, below the bladder.

Another cerclage procedure is Modified Shirodker's technique. In this, a non-absorbable (mersilene) tape is passed subcutaneously through a transverse anterior incision and is tied posteriorly.

Removal of cerclage should be done by 37 weeks of gestation. It can be removed earlier in case of preterm labour.

Complications of cervical cerclage:

  • Slipping of suture
  • Chorioamnionitis
  • Rupture of membranes
  • Abortion or preterm labour
  • Cervical laceration or scarring

question: A woman with cervical incompetence is posted for prophylactic McDonald's cerclage. Which of the following statements is false about this procedure?

explanationHtml:
Only the patient's consent is required for medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) and her male partner's consent is not required.

Consent of parent/guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 yrs or if the patient is mentally ill.

question: A 20-year-old female patient came for medical termination of pregnancy. From whom will you obtain consent for the procedure?

explanationHtml:
Chronic diabetes mellitus is not a contraindication to medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) with medical methods.

Contraindications to medical methods of abortion are:

  • Women with in situ intrauterine device
  • Severe anemia, coagulopathy, or anticoagulant use
  • Long term corticosteroid therapy
  • Severe liver, renal, pulmonary, or cardiovascular disease
  • Inherited porphyria
  • Uncontrolled hypertension

Contraindications to surgical methods of abortion are:

  • Suction and evacuation - uterine size >10 weeks
  • Intrauterine instillation of hypertonic solution - cardiovascular or renal lesion and severe anaemia

explanationHtml:
Suction and evacuation can be done up to 12 weeks of gestation. It is a method of termination of pregnancy in the first-trimester.

question: A 23-year-old pregnant rape victim was posted for a suction and evacuation procedure. This procedure can be done up to _____ of gestation.

explanationHtml:
Doxycycline is the preferred drug for post-abortal antibiotic prophylaxis in this case. The dosage is 100 mg of oral doxycycline 1 hour prior to surgical evacuation, followed by 200 mg of oral doxycycline after the procedure.

The best method of MTP at 7-12 weeks is by suction and evacuation. Following this procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis is given with doxycycline.

question: You have performed MTP on a multigravida at 10 weeks of gestation.  As a part of post-op advice, you must prescribe her a prophylactic antibiotic. Which of the following drugs would you prefer?

explanationHtml:
Misoprostol is given at a dose of 800 mcg by mucosal route for MTP.

Mucosal misoprostol administration has increased efficacy and minimizes gastrointestinal side effects. Hence, it is preferred over oral administration.

WHO guidelines for medical management in induced abortion for <12 weeks of gestation:

  • Combined regimen (recommended): 200 mg of oral Mifepristone followed 1-2 days later by 800 mcg of buccal, vaginal, or sublingual misoprostol
  • Misoprostol only regimen (alternative): 800 μg misoprostol administered vaginally, sublingually, or buccally

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the methods of MTP?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of toxic shock syndrome (TSS) following septic abortion. Escherichia coli can be detected in septic abortion, but it is not a causative agent for TSS.

Organisms causing toxic shock syndrome in septic abortion:

  • Streptococcus pyogenes
  • Clostridium perfringens
  • Clostridium sordellii

Clinical features of septic abortion:

  • Fever with chills and rigors
  • Abdominal or chest pain
  • Diarrhoea and vomiting
  • Renal angle tenderness
  • Offensive purulent vaginal discharge.

Clinical grading of septic abortion:

  • Grade I - infection localized in the uterus
  • Grade II - infection spreads to parametrium, tubes, ovaries, or pelvic peritoneum
  • Grade III - generalized peritonitis, endotoxic shock, jaundice, or acute renal failure

Empirical antibiotic therapy in septic abortion is started for the broadest microbial coverage. Piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem and clindamycin are given intravenously. Antibiotics can be changed once culture sensitivity reports are available.

question: A 21-year-old woman is brought in a drowsy state from a PHC with complaints of fever, severe lower abdominal pain, and purulent vaginal discharge. Her mother revealed that she had had an unsafe abortion a week ago. On examination, her abdomen was distended, BP was 80/60 mmHg, PR was 140 bpm, and RR was 36 breaths/ minute. Which of the following is not a causative agent of her present condition?

correctAnswer: C. Untreated seizure disorder in pregnancy
explanationHtml:
An untreated seizure disorder in pregnancy is not a risk factor for stillbirth. However, the use of certain anti-epileptic drugs like valproate could lead to the development of neural tube defects in the baby.

Recent studies haven't consistently shown that untreated women with epilepsy face a higher risk, though it's hard to rule out entirely because those who manage without medication usually have milder symptoms. Recent research found that birth defects were more common in children of women who used anticonvulsants.

Risk factors for stillbirth are:

  • Advanced maternal age
  • African-American race
  • Smoking
  • Illicit drug use
  • Maternal medical diseases - overt diabetes or chronic hypertension
  • Assisted reproductive technology
  • Nulliparity
  • Obesity
  • Previous adverse pregnancy outcomes - prior preterm birth or IUGR

Note: Stillbirth rates appear to be slightly increased in pregnancies conceived via assisted reproductive technology.

options.text: Illicit drug abuse by the mother

question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for stillbirth?

explanationHtml:
The development of uterine synechiae is the most likely cause of amenorrhoea in the given clinical scenario.

Certain types of spontaneous abortions such as inevitable, incomplete and missed abortions might require medical assistance for complete removal of products of conception including procedures such as dilatation and curettage.

Vigorous uterine curettage in early pregnancy damages the basal layer of endometrium leading to scarring and adhesions in the uterus that interferes with normal endometrial growth and shedding.This causes the clinical feature of secondary amenorrhea as seen in this patient.

This intrauterine adhesions are known as uterine synechiae or Asherman syndrome.

As there is no defect in the hypothalamo-pituitary-ovarian axis in the asherman syndrome, the levels of FSH remain within the normal range of 4 - 25 IU/L as seen in this patient.

In the case of Pituitary dysfunction (option A) the FSH levels are usually decreased.

In ovarian dysfunction (option B) the negative feedback of ovarian hormones (estrogen) on pitutary and hypothalamus is lost. Hence, the levels of FSH is increased (≥ 25 IU).

Extensive uterine destruction and scarring can give rise to a condition called uterine synchae or Asherman syndrome. Uterine curettage or uterine surgeries can lead to thin uterine adhesions, dense bands or a completely obliterated uterine cavity which are all features of the syndrome. Damage may also occur from other uterine surgeries such as myomectomy or cesarean delivery or from an infection related to an intrauterine device.

Depending on the degree of scarring, patients may present with amenorrhea, hypomenorrhea or recurrent pregnancy loss due to inadequate placentation.

Asherman syndrome shows multiple filling defects on hysterosalpingography (HSG) or saline-infusion sonography. Definitive diagnosis requires hysteroscopy. Hysteroscopic lysis of adhesions is the preferred surgical treatment for the syndrome.
lessonTitle: Abortion And Medical Termination Of Pregnancy
question: A young female has history of a spontaneous abortion. She has had amenorrhea since then. Her FSH now is 6 mIU/ml. Which of the following can be a cause for her amenorrhea?

explanationHtml:
Abruptio placenta is the most common cause of antepartum haemorrhage (APH).

Placental abruption or abruptio placenta is the premature separation of a normally situated placenta. The bleeding can be revealed, concealed or mixed type.

Causes of APH:

  • Placental causes:
    • Abruptio placenta (most common)
    • Placenta previa (2nd most common)
    • Circumvallate placenta
    • Circummarginate placenta
  • Fetal causes:
    • Vasa previa
  • Extraplacental causes (local cervicovaginal lesions):
    • Local trauma
    • Varicose veins
    • Cervical polyp
    • Carcinoma cervix.
question: What is the most common cause of antepartum haemorrhage?

correctAnswer: A. Placental edge within 2 cm from the internal os
explanationHtml:
In low lying placenta, the edge of the placenta lies within 2 cm from the internal os but does not cover the internal os.

Placenta previa is a condition where the placenta is implanted over the lower uterine segment (partially or completely).

ACOG classification of placenta previa:

  • True placenta previa - placenta covers the internal os partially or completely
  • Low lying placenta - placenta does not cover the internal os but the edge is within 2 cm of the internal os

Major degree of placenta previa includes posterior marginal, partial and complete central.

    • Type II anterior or anterior marginal

    • Type III or partial central
    • Type IV or complete

Which of the following types are included in the major degrees of placenta previa?

  1. Lateral
  2. Anterior marginal

  4. Partial central
  5. Complete

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of placenta previa. Pre-eclampsia is a risk factor for abruptio placenta, not placenta previa.

Painless bleeding PV, fundal height proportional to gestational age and presence of FHS are the differentiating features of placenta previa from abruptio placenta.

Risk factors for placenta previa are:

  • Demographic factors
    • Maternal age >35 years
    • Multiparity
    • Cigarette smoking
  • Clinical factors
    • Prior caesarean section
    • Past history of placenta previa
    • Artificial reproductive technology
    • Multifetal pregnancy
    • Succenturiate lobe.
question: A 30-year-old multiparous woman presented at 32 weeks of gestation with complaints of recurrent painless vaginal bleeding. On examination, fundal height corresponded to gestational age and fetal heart rate was 140 bpm. Which of the following is not a risk factor for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Placenta protruding through the internal os on per speculum examination indicates complete placenta previa or type IV placenta previa.

Cervical digital examination must only be done in suspected cases of placenta previa in an operation theater with provisions for cesarean section kept ready.
question: Per speculum examination findings in a pregnant woman with vaginal bleeding showed placenta protruding through the cervical os. What is the type of placenta previa in this case?

correctAnswer: A. Painful recurrent vaginal bleeding is seen
explanationHtml:
Painless recurrent vaginal bleeding is seen in placenta previa.

Clinical features of placenta previa:

  • Bleeding per vaginum - sudden onset, painless, recurrent, bright red in colour, sometimes a history of warning haemorrhage is present
  • Uterus - relaxed, soft, no tenderness, size proportional to the period of gestation
  • Floating head i.e., persistent displacement of fetal head as it cannot be pushed down into the pelvis
  • Fetal heart sound - present
  • Stallworthy sign - seen in low lying placenta, especially the posterior type. Slowing of fetal heart rate (FHR) on pressing the head down into the pelvis, which recovers promptly as pressure is relieved, is called Stallworthy sign.

options.text: Painful recurrent vaginal bleeding is seen
The size of the uterus corresponds to gestational age

question: A patient at 34 weeks of gestation presented with placenta previa. Which of the following is false about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Stallworthy sign is observed in posterior placenta previa.

The slowing of fetal heart rate on pressing the head down into the pelvis, which recovers promptly when the pressure is relieved, is called Stallworthy sign.

Note: This sign is not always significant as this could also occur in normal pregnancies due to fetal head compression.
question: Abdominal examination during a routine antenatal checkup gave a positive Stallworthy sign. What could be the most probable cause?

correctAnswer: A. Transvaginal ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of antepartum haemorrhage (APH) due to placenta previa (painless bleeding PV). The next step in the management is to confirm the diagnosis with transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) as the patient is stable.

Transabdominal ultrasound (TAS) is used to detect the cause of APH.

If the placenta is in the lower uterine segment on TAS, confirmation of placenta previa is done by TVS. TVS provides a clearer image of the relationship between the edge of the placenta and the internal cervical os than TAS.

Approach to placenta previa after confirmation with TVS:

  • Minor placenta previa - repeat USG at 36 weeks
  • Major placenta previa or accreta - USG at 32 weeks followed by elective caesarean delivery
  • Bleeding present - individual management

On TAS, if the placenta is in the upper uterine segment with evidence of retroplacental blood clot, abruptio placenta is suspected.

Per vaginal examination in placenta previa must not be done as it may further separate the placenta and cause excessive bleeding. However, transvaginal ultrasound is safe as long as the probe is 2-3 cm away from the cervix.

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis

question: A G2P1 woman presents to the casualty at 30 weeks with a history of self-limiting painless bleeding PV 3 hours ago. On examination, BP - 110/70 mmHg and PR - 80 bpm. What is the next best step in management?

explanationHtml:
Then given clinical scenario is suggestive of placenta previa and precipitate labour is not a complication. Precipitate labour is seen in abruptio placenta and uterine tachysystole.

Vaginal bleeding in placenta previa is sudden in onset, recurrent, painless, unrelated to activity, and often occurs during sleep.

Fetal complications:

  • Low birth weight
  • Asphyxia
  • Intrauterine death
  • Birth injuries
  • Congenital malformations.
question: A G2P1L1 woman at 30 weeks of gestation was rushed to the casualty with complaints of painless vaginal bleeding. She had woken up to find herself in a pool of blood. On examination, her vitals were unstable. Active bleeding per vaginum was present. Which of the following complications would not be anticipated in her?

correctAnswer: C. Manage as per McAfee and Johnson method
explanationHtml:
In the given clinical scenario, the next best step of management is conservative management till 37 weeks i.e., McAfee and Johnson's regimen.

The aim of conservative management is to continue the pregnancy for fetal maturity without compromising maternal health.

Prerequisites:

  • Blood for transfusion
  • Facilities for cesarean section

Selection of cases for expectant management for placenta previa:

  1. Mother is hemodynamically stable (Hb >10 g% and/or hematocrit > 30%)
  2. Duration of pregnancy <37 weeks
  3. No active vaginal bleeding
  4. Fetus reactive on cardiotocography and no congenital anomalies on USG

Conduct of expectant treatment:

  • Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity
  • Bed rest or pelvic rest
  • Periodic monitoring of mother for bleeding PV
  • Fetal surveillance with USG
  • Tocolytics if contractions are present
  • Anti-D to all Rh-negative unsensitized women

Option A: Immediate caesarean section after resuscitation is done if the patient is unstable.

question: A 23-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation presents to the labour room with lower abdominal pain. Her vitals are BP - 90/60 mmHg and PR - 120 bpm. The doppler findings are suggestive of vasa previa. Maternal mortality is not seen in vasa previa, but fetal mortality is seen.

Vasa previa is a condition where fetal vessels travel within the membranes and overlie the cervical os. Hence, there can be bleeding during cervical dilatation or membrane rupture.

question: Colour doppler studies in a patient with velamentous cord insertion revealed fetal vessels which were overlying the cervical os. Which of the following is false regarding her condition?

Apt test is based on the principle that HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation, while HbA is not. It is done by taking the blood sample in a test tube containing water and adding 1% NaOH. Maternal blood turns yellow-brown, while fetal blood remains pink in the test tube.

Bleeding due to vasa previa must be managed immediately with an emergency caesarean section. Hence, Apt test is not practically done in all cases.

Other options: Bleeding due to cervical polyp, placenta previa, and abruptio placenta is of maternal origin. So, Apt test will be negative in these cases.

Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) in vaginal delivery is defined as a blood loss of more than 500 ml after completion of the third stage of labour.

Uterine atony is the failure of the uterus to contract sufficiently after delivery. Contraction helps to arrest bleeding from vessels at the placental implantation site.

Types of PPH:

As per the latest guidelines, uterine massage is no longer a core component of Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) that is performed for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH).

Uterine massage or fundal massage is not recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH in women who have already received prophylactic uterotonics such as oxytocin (core component of AMTSL). Hence, it is now an optional component of AMTSL that is done in patients with uterine atony as a part of the management of PPH.

AMTSL is recommended by the WHO to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). Uterotonics are the most important components in AMTSL to do so.

The currently recommended components of AMTSL are as follows:

1. Uterotonics should be injected within 1 minute of delivery or immediately after delivery of the anterior shoulder
  • Most important step
  • Oxytocin 10 IU im/iv infusion is the preferred uterotonic.

(Not recommended by WHO- carboprost)
2 Delayed cord clamping
  • Done within 1-3 mins of delivery
  • 80 ml of additional blood goes to the fetus
  • Prevents fetal anemia
3 Delivery of placenta by controlled cord traction: Modified Brandt Andrews technique
  • The uterus is pushed upwards and backward
  • The traction of cord is downwards and forwards
4 Intermittent assessment of uterine tone Done every 15 mins for 2 hours

Note: In the event that uterine atony is diagnosed during the assessment of uterine tone, uterine massage can be performed to control PPH.

explanationHtml:
Using a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment (NASG) is not one of the first measures for the management of atonic PPH. NASG is used to reduce bleeding and stabilize the patient for shifting to tertiary centers.

The image below shows a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment.

First step measures in the management of PPH must be done immediately and simultaneously. This includes:

  • Hysterectomy.

The most probable diagnosis is uterine inversion.

Hydramnios is a risk factor for uterine inversion due to uterine over-distension. Fundal pressure while the uterus is atonic (soft, relaxed, and boggy) causes uterine inversion. question: Which of the following statements is false regarding hydatidiform moles?

question: Which of the following is not associated with the development of a hydatidiform mole?

correctAnswer: C. Theca lutein cysts are rare
explanationHtml:
Theca lutein cysts are rare in partial molar pregnancy, but may be seen in 25-30% of patients with complete molar pregnancy.

Serum β-hCG levels are elevated more than expected for gestational age in a complete mole.

The sensitivity of most hCG tests is set to the pregnancy hCG range. An excessive β-hCG hormone causes an oversaturation of the test assay giving a false negative UPT. This is called the hook effect.

The thyrotropin-like effects of hCG frequently cause serum free-T4 levels to be elevated which normalize after uterine evacuation.

question: A 20-year-old primigravida with bleeding PV was diagnosed to have a complete hydatidiform mole. Which of the following is not true in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and USG showing snowstorm appearance is suggestive of a complete mole.

The snowstorm appearance is due to an echogenic uterine mass that has numerous anechoic cystic spaces. Fetus and amniotic sac are absent.

Investigations for molar pregnancy are:

  • USG - shows snowstorm appearance
  • Serum β hCG - elevated to >2 MoM (multiples of median) for corresponding gestational age
  • Histological examination of products of conception

Snowstorms in radiology:

  • Extracapsular breast implant rupture (ultrasound)

question: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks of gestation presents with spotting PV, hyperemesis, and lower abdominal pain for the past 2 days. USG done is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given USG image shows theca lutein cysts in the ovary. These cysts are usually seen in patients with complete molar pregnancies. They are usually bilateral and are also seen in multiple pregnancies.

Theca lutein cysts result from the overstimulation of lutein elements by massive amounts of β hCG. The cystic fluid is rich in chorionic gonadotropin, estrogen, and progesterone.
question: A primigravida at 12 weeks of gestation presented with complaints of the expulsion of grape-like vesicles PV for the past day. A diagnosis of molar pregnancy was made on USG examination. Incidentally, the following adnexal lesion was also noted. What is the lesion?

explanationHtml:
Untwisting of the cyst is the only management in an asymptomatic patient with a twisted theca lutein cyst.

Laparoscopic oophorectomy is done only when there is associated extensive necrosis or hemorrhage.

Theca-lutein cysts regress within 2 months after pregnancy evacuation, and hence expectant management is preferred in uncomplicated cases. If the cysts are symptomatic, they can be aspirated trans-abdominally under ultrasound guidance.
question: A patient who was treated for molar pregnancy came for follow-up after 4 months. Her USG revealed a large, twisted theca lutein cyst. How will you manage this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of molar pregnancy which is managed by suction and evacuation, regardless of uterine size.

If the cervix is unfavorable, slow dilatation is done with vaginal PGE1. Volume resuscitation with IV fluids and parenteral antibiotics can be given as supportive therapy. Blood transfusion is done if the patient is anaemic.

Intraoperative sonography is recommended to help ensure that the uterine cavity has been emptied.

Indication for hysterectomy in molar pregnancy:

  • Women who have completed their family
  • Age >40 years
  • Uncontrolled hemorrhage
  • Perforation during surgical evacuation.
question: A pregnant woman at 14 weeks of gestation complains of excessive vomiting and mild vaginal bleeding for 2 weeks. On examination, fundal height corresponds to 16 weeks and fetal heart sounds are absent. USG shows a snowstorm appearance and no fetus. What is the best step of management?

correctAnswer: C. Monthly follow-up for 6 months after three consecutive normal values
explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, the patient is followed up with serum β hCG every month for 6 months.

Follow-up after the termination of molar pregnancy is done with serum β hCG levels. During the follow-up period, pregnancy must be avoided as it might interfere with the β hCG levels.

The initial β-hCG level is obtained within 48 hours after evacuation and used as a baseline.

It is measured weekly till it becomes negative, and three consecutive normal values are obtained. This normally happens in 4-8 weeks.

After this, β hCG levels are measured monthly for 6 months. Women who undergo chemotherapy must be followed up for 1 year.

options.text: Twice weekly estimation for a month following evacuation
Monthly follow-up for 6 months after three consecutive normal values
After 6 months of follow-up, regular yearly estimation should be done

question: A 36-year-old woman underwent suction evacuation for a hydatidiform mole. Which of the following statements is true regarding her follow-up with β-hCG estimation?

question: All of the following are non-molar trophoblastic neoplasms except _____.

explanationHtml:
Chorioadenoma destruens or invasive mole is the most common non-metastatic GTN that follows hydatidiform moles. Almost all invasive moles arise from partial or complete moles.

Invasive mole is characterized by extensive tissue invasion by trophoblast and whole villi. They can penetrate deep into the myometrium, peritoneum, parametrium, or vaginal vault. They are locally aggressive and do not usually metastasize.

The most common GTN following term pregnancy or miscarriage is choriocarcinoma.
question: What is the most common non-metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia that develops following hydatidiform mole?

explanationHtml:
Maternal age >40 years, β-hCG levels >100,000 mIU/mL and grand multiparity are risk factors for malignant change in a patient with molar pregnancy.

Risk factors for malignant change are:

  • Patient's age ≥ 40 years or <20 years
  • Increasing parity
  • Uterine size that is large-for-gestational age
  • Previous history of molar pregnancy
  • Complete moles have 15-20% risk of malignant transformation, partial moles have 1-5% risk
  • Serum β hCG >1,00,000 mIU/mL
  • Large theca lutein cysts >6 cm in diameter

Post-evacuation uterine sonographic surveillance can be used as a predictor of subsequent neoplasia. Findings indicative of malignant transformation are:

  • Suburethral nodules
  • Myometrial nodules
  • Hypervascularity.
question:
Which of the following are risk factors for malignant change in a patient with molar pregnancy?

  1. Maternal age >40 years
  2. β-hCG levels > 100,000 mIU/mL
  3. Theca-lutein cysts < 6 cm
  4. Uterine size that is small for gestational age
  5. Grand multiparity

correctAnswer: A. Increased number of theca lutein cysts
explanationHtml:
Increased number of theca lutein cysts is not an indicator of choriocarcinoma. Increased size or persistence of theca lutein cysts indicates choriocarcinoma.

Plateau of high serum β-hCG level for four measurements for ≥3 weeks is an indicator of choriocarcinoma.

Risk factors for malignant change are:

  • Molar pregnancy - complete moles have 15-20% risk, partial moles have 1-5% risk
  • Patient's age ≥ 40 years or <20 years
  • Parity ≥3
  • Serum β hCG >1,00,000 IU/mL
  • Uterine size >20 weeks
  • Previous history of molar pregnancy
  • Large theca lutein cysts >6 cm in diameter

Post-evacuation uterine sonographic surveillance can be used as a predictor of subsequent neoplasia. Findings indicative of malignant transformation are:

  • Suburethral nodules
  • Myometrial nodules
  • Hypervascularity.

explanationHtml:
IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) is contraindicated in this patient as the uterus is friable and can cause further bleeding.

Accepted methods of contraception after suction evacuation in molar pregnancy include:

explanationHtml:
The common sites of metastases of choriocarcinoma are in the following order:

  • Lungs - most common
  • Vagina - second most common
  • Vulva
  • Kidneys
  • Liver
  • Ovaries
  • Brain
