Lung metastases present as cannon-ball or snowstorm appearance on chest X-ray. Vaginal metastases present as purplish sub-urethral nodules.
question: A patient was diagnosed to have choriocarcinoma two years post-evacuation of molar pregnancy. Which of the following is the most common site of metastasis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Metastases in the lungs are considered stage III GTN (gestational trophoblastic neoplasia) in FIGO classification.

International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging for GTN is as follows:

Stage Description
I GTN confined to the uterus

II

GTN extends outside of the uterus but is limited to the genital structures

(adnexa, vagina, broad ligament)
III GTN extends to the lungs, with or without known genital tract involvement
IV All other metastatic sites i.e. kidney, liver, brain, bowel, etc.

The chest X-ray below shows lung metastasis - stage III GTN.

Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) refers to the aggressive invasion of the endometrium and myometrium by trophoblast cells. It includes invasive mole, gestational choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumors, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. GTN is diagnosed based on elevated β-hCG levels. FIGO criteria for diagnosis of GTN:

  • Persistence of β-hCG level plateau in 4 measurements for 3 weeks or longer
  • Rise in β-hCG levels in 3 or more consecutive measurements done weekly, over a period of 2 weeks or longer
  • Elevated β-hCG level for 6 months or more
  • Histologic diagnosis of choriocarcinoma

Treatment for low-risk disease is chemotherapy with methotrexate, while those with high-risk disease are treated with etoposide, methotrexate, and dactinomycin alternating with cyclophosphamide and vincristine (EMA/CO) chemotherapy.
question: A case of gestational trophoblastic neoplasm is detected to have metastasis in the lungs. It is considered as stage _____.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of high-risk (WHO) stage III choriocarcinoma which is treated with EMA-CO regimen. The given X-ray shows numerous, dense, bilateral metastatic nodules, of varying sizes indicative of lung metastases.

The components of EMA-CO are:

  • Etoposide
  • Methotrexate
  • Actinomycin D
  • Cyclophosphamide
  • Oncovin i.e. vincristine

EMA-CO regimen

Option A: PSTT (placental-site trophoblastic tumor) and ETT (epithelioid trophoblastic tumors) are treated by hysterectomy only, as they are resistant to chemotherapy.

Option B: R-CHOP regimen is used for B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Option D: MVAC regimen is used for advanced bladder carcinoma.
question: A 43-year-old woman presents with complaints of hemoptysis, vaginal bleeding, and abdominal pain for 7 days. Chest X-ray is shown below. Transabdominal USG revealed a solid mass occupying the uterus which was found to be choriocarcinoma with a WHO score of 8. How would you manage this patient?

explanationHtml:
Placental-site trophoblastic tumor arises from implantation site intermediate trophoblast. As syncytiotrophoblastic cells are generally absent in this site, it is composed mainly of cytotrophoblastic cells.

Patients with placental site trophoblastic tumors present with vaginal bleeding and modestly elevated serum β-hCG levels. Local invasion into the myometrium and lymphatics occurs. Hysterectomy is the preferred treatment.
question: Placental-site trophoblastic tumor arises from _____.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of placental-site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT). Hysterectomy is the treatment of choice because they are locally invasive tumors and resistant to chemotherapy.

PSTT is a rare tumor arising from intermediate trophoblastic of the placental bed. Patients with placental site trophoblastic tumors present with vaginal bleeding and modestly elevated serum β-hCG levels. They produce variant forms of hCG.
question: A 26-year-old woman with a history of early miscarriage presented with amenorrhoea. Her serum beta hCG levels were persistently low and USG revealed a single solid mass in the uterine fundus. Histopathological examination of the biopsy showed abundant intermediate trophoblastic cells. What is the next step of management?

explanationHtml:
Severe anemia is defined as Hb < 7 g/dL.

Anemia in pregnancy is said to occur when Hb level is <11 g/dL. It is classified as shown below:

question: A pregnant woman presented to the clinic with complaints of dizziness. On examination, pallor was present. She will be considered severely anemic if her hemoglobin is less than _____.

explanationHtml:
Iron deficiency anemia is the most common pathological cause of anemia during pregnancy.

Women with chronic disorders may develop anemia for the first time during pregnancy. Causes include:

  • Chronic renal insufficiency - the most common cause. Recombinant erythropoietin is used for treating anemia due to chronic renal failure.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Connective tissue disorders
  • Granulomatous infections
  • Malignant neoplasms
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Chronic suppurative conditions.
question: Which of the following is the most common pathological cause of anemia in pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Maternal requirement of iron during a singleton gestation averages close to 1000 mg.

Iron requirement during pregnancy
Fetus and placenta 300 mg
Expansion of maternal hemoglobin mass 500 mg
Losses through normal excretion routes 200 mg
Total 1000 mg

The average iron stores in a non-pregnant female is around 300 mg. This falls short of the requirement of iron during pregnancy which is 1000 mg. Hence iron supplementation is necessary to prevent iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy. This also forms the basis for prophylactic iron supplementation during pregnancy.

Note: The Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (FOGSI) states that the iron requirement in pregnancy is 840 mg, as about 160 mg of iron is saved due to amenorrhea during pregnancy.
question: What is the average maternal requirement of iron during a singleton pregnancy?

explanationHtml: The guideline recommends 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 μg of folic acid daily for at least 180 days, starting from the 4th month of pregnancy, and to be continued throughout pregnancy. Ideally, this must be continued until 180 days postpartum.
question: You initiate iron and folic acid supplements for a woman at 13 weeks of gestation. According to the ministry of health & family welfare (MoHFW), what is the minimum duration for which she should take these supplements?

explanationHtml:
The amount of folic acid to be given to pregnant women suffering from sickle cell anemia is 5 mg.

This is to reduce the risk of neural tube defects and to compensate for the increased demand for folate during pregnancy.

Normally in all sickle cell patients (irrespective of age or sex), 1mg of folic acid is given to prevent folate deficiency.

Note: William's Obstetrics 26th Edition mentions folic acid 4 mg daily for pregnant women with sickle cell disease. However various other sources and RCOG guidelines mention it as 5 mg daily. Hence this is the best answer.

options.text: Previous child with neural tube defect - 1 mg

question: Identify the correctly matched dose for folic acid supplementation that should be given in pregnant women with the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, history suggestive of restless leg syndrome and Hb of 10.1g/dL points to a diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia. Serum ferritin is the most sensitive indicator of iron deficiency anemia in pregnant women.

This is because its concentrations are not affected by the recent intake of iron-rich foods. Serum ferritin concentration <15 μg/L indicates iron deficiency anemia.

However, treatment needs to be initiated when the concentration falls <30 μg/L, as this indicates early iron depletion.

Restless leg syndrome also called Willis-Ekbom Disease, causes unpleasant or uncomfortable sensations in the legs along with an irresistible urge to move them. It may be associated with iron deficiency anemia.
question: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks of gestation presented with insomnia due to a compulsive urge to keep moving her legs. Blood tests revealed a Hb value of 10.1 g/dl. Which of the following is the most sensitive indicator for her underlying condition?

explanationHtml:
In the given clinical scenario presence of microcytic hypochromic RBCs indicates iron deficiency anemia, and hyper segmented neutrophils indicate anemia due to folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency. This is also known as dimorphic anemia.

Blood picture in iron deficiency anemia:

  • Microcytic hypochromic RBCs
  • Typical photo pencil cells
  • Presence of poikilocytes (pre-erythrocytes)

Blood picture in folic acid/vitamin B12 deficiency anemia:

  • Hyper segmented neutrophils - earliest change
  • Macrocytic RBCs
question: A pregnant teacher presented with complaints of difficulty concentrating at work. Investigations revealed normal MCV with blood picture as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of pica associated with moderate iron-deficiency anemia. Since the anemia was diagnosed late in pregnancy, the most appropriate treatment is parenteral iron therapy. Ferrous sucrose is a form of parenteral iron given as an IV infusion.

If anemia is diagnosed:

  • In the first trimester - Oral iron therapy is preferred
  • In the second trimester - Oral iron therapy should be switched over to parenteral iron if Hb falls <8g/dl or if serum ferritin is <15ng/ml
  • In the third trimester - Parenteral iron therapy is preferred

Ferrous sucrose is the most commonly used preparation for IV infusion. It is safe and does not require a test dose.

Other iron preparations include:

  • Oral preparations- Ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, ferrous ascorbate
  • IM preparations- Iron sorbitol, Iron polymaltose
  • IV preparations- Ferric carboxymaltose
  • Both IM and IV- Iron dextran.
question: A woman at 36 weeks of gestation was brought to the clinic by her concerned husband. He mentioned that over the last few weeks he noticed her chewing on cardboard pieces and ice cream sticks on multiple occasions. On examination, pallor was present and Hb was 8.6 g/dl. What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

explanationHtml:
Ferric carboxymaltose is considered superior to all other parenteral iron supplementation especially for iron deficiency anemia in postpartum women.

Ferric carboxymaltose is a IV iron preparation which does not contain dextran. It allows rapid administration of high doses of iron (up to 1000 mg iron in 15 min).

It is safe and effective in improving the mean Hb level. It avoids the need for blood transfusions.
question: Which of the following is the most effective parenteral iron preparation prescribed for postpartum women with iron deficiency anemia?

correctAnswer: B. 2.4 × (target Hb-actual Hb) × body weight (kg) + 500 mg
explanationHtml:
The formula for calculating dose of parenteral iron is:

Total dose in mg = 2.4 X (Target Hb - Actual Hb) X Body Wt. + 500 mg

  • 2.4 - conversion factor
  • Target Hb - Hb you want to achieve
  • Actual Hb- level of current Hb
  • 500 mg - additional amount to replenish the iron stores

Iron sucrose must be diluted only using normal saline at a concentration of 1-2 mg of iron/mL of saline. It is given over 20-30 minutes intravenously.
question: You have been asked to start parenteral iron infusion for a woman at 38 weeks of gestation. What formula would you use to calculate the required dosage?

correctAnswer: B. Avoided in chronic liver disease
explanationHtml:
Parenteral iron therapy for iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy is avoided if the patient has a history of chronic liver disease.

It is used as an alternative therapy in people who cannot tolerate oral iron.

Contraindications include:

  • A history of prior anaphylactic reaction to parenteral iron therapy
  • First trimester of pregnancy - there is no evidence on the use of IV iron in the first trimester of pregnancy
  • Chronic liver disease
  • Active infection (acute or chronic)

A sensitivity test prior to the infusion is not mandatory. IV iron should be given with caution even if previous administrations have been well tolerated.

Oral iron should be stopped at least 24 hours prior to therapy to avoid iron toxicity.

options.text: Can be given in first trimester
Sensitivity test is mandatory before administration
Can be given alongside oral iron therapy

question: Which of the following is true regarding parenteral iron therapy for iron deficiency anemia in pregnant women?

explanationHtml:
The treatment of choice for severe anemia (< 7g/dL) in the third trimester is packed cell transfusion. It is preferred over whole blood as it avoids volume overload.

Indications of blood transfusion in pregnancy include:

  • Pregnancy <34 weeks
    • Hb <5 g/dL with or without signs of cardiac failure or hypoxia
    • Hb 5-7 g/dL – in presence of impending heart failure
  • Pregnancy >34 weeks - Hb <7 g/dL.
question: A G3P2 female patient who is an agricultural laborer presents with complaints of fatigue at 36 weeks of gestation. On examination, pallor and mild pedal edema are present. Her hemoglobin is 6.7 g/dl. How will you manage this patient?

correctAnswer: B. 1000 μg of IM cyanocobalamin + folic acid
explanationHtml:
The given scenario points to vitamin B12 deficiency. It is treated by vitamin B12 injections with folic acid supplementation. 1000 μg of IM cyanocobalamin should be given initially every week for 6 weeks, following which it should be given once every month.

Megaloblastic anemia caused by Vit B12 deficiency should be identified and treated accordingly because folic acid supplementation alone will not help.

Causes of Vit B12 deficiency leading to anemia in pregnancy:

  • Gastric resection
  • Addisonian pernicious anemia
  • Crohn’s disease
  • Ileal resection
  • Bacterial overgrowth in the small bowel.

options.text: 1000 μg of IM cyanocobalamin + folic acid

question: A pregnant woman was brought by her husband after fainting at home. He gave a history of her being clumsy and forgetful over the last few weeks. Investigations revealed high MCV with hypersegmented neutrophils. How will you manage this patient?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, patients with sickle cell trait are at a higher risk of developing urinary tract infections.

Sickle cell disease, on the other hand, is associated with increased risk of :

  • Miscarriages
  • Fetal growth restriction
  • Preterm labor
  • Venous thromboembolism
  • Pre-eclampsia
  • Placental abruption
  • Fetal distress in labor

Note: Sickle cell trait is a benign condition in which the affected person has only one abnormal hemoglobin beta gene allele whereas, in sickle cell disease, the affected person has two abnormal hemoglobin beta gene alleles and is hence severely symptomatic. Unlike individuals with sickle cell disease, those with sickle cell trait do not have symptoms related to sickling and mostly lead a normal life.
question:
An anxious primigravida with sickle cell trait comes to you for her first antenatal checkup. Which of the following is she at a higher risk of developing during the course of this pregnancy?

  1. Pre-eclampsia
  2. Abortions
  3. Urinary tract infections
  4. Placental abruptions
  5. Preterm labor

explanationHtml:
Low-dose oral progestins or progesterone injections or implants are ideal contraceptives in a patient with sickle cell anemia. Progesterone has been known to prevent painful sickle cell crises.

It is considered very safe in pregnancy. It is rated level 1 indicating that there is no restriction in their use.

Contraceptive methods and their safety profile in sickle cell anemia:

Level 1 contraceptives (no restriction):

  • Progestogen-only injection (DMPA)
  • Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena)
  • Emergency contraception containing progestins

Level 2 contraceptives (advantages outweigh disadvantages):

  • Combined oral contraceptive
  • Copper intrauterine device.
question: A sexually active woman with sickle cell anemia comes to the clinic for advice regarding contraception. Which of the following is the ideal contraceptive for this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Parenteral iron therapy is the treatment of choice
explanationHtml:
In thalassemia major, both oral and parenteral iron preparations are avoided. This is because these patients are already in a state of iron overload due to multiple blood transfusions.

Pregnancy in patients with thalassemia major is very rare. In case pregnancy occurs the following strategies are adopted:

  • Iron chelating agents should be stopped
  • 5mg folic acid supplementation should be given daily
  • Pneumococcal vaccination and boosters are advised prior to pregnancy
  • Repeated blood transfusions are given to maintain Hb levels above 10 g/dL
  • Breastfeeding is safe and iron chelation therapy can be resumed post-delivery.

options.text: Parenteral iron therapy is the treatment of choice
Breast feeding is safe after delivery
Repeated transfusions are necessary to maintain Hb levels above 10 g/dl

question: A pregnant woman with thalassemia major presents to the clinic at 24 weeks of gestation with fatigue and shortness of breath. Which of the following is not true regarding the management of this condition?

correctAnswer: D. BP > 140/90 after 20 weeks of gestation
explanationHtml:
Gestational hypertension is defined as BP >140/90 after 20 weeks of gestation.

Hypertension in pregnancy is defined as BP of >140/90 mmHg measured 2 times with at least a 4-hour interval.

Gestational hypertension

Pre-eclampsia

Proteinuria is not an essential criterion to define pre-eclampsia.

Pre-eclampsia is hypertension with any of the following features:

  • Proteinuria
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Renal insufficiency
  • Liver involvement
  • Cerebral symptoms
  • Pulmonary edema.

Note: A normotensive pregnant woman may have an acute increase in BP from baseline levels and develop eclamptic seizures/HELLP syndrome, despite being normotensive. This condition is known as delta hypertension.
question: Gestational hypertension is defined as:

explanationHtml:
The cut-off for defining proteinuria in pre-eclampsia is ≥30 mg/dl (0.3 g/L) in a random urine sample.

Proteinuria in preeclampsia is also defined by:

  • ≥0.3 g protein in a 24-hour urine specimen.
  • Random urine protein: creatinine ratio (PCR) ≥0.3 mg protein/mg creatinine
  • Protein ≥2+ on urine dipstick as per the latest NICE guidelines.

A urine dipstick is used only if the above quantitative methods are not available. It has a high false positive rate which increases with lower dipstick values. Hence, it is better to use 2+ as the discriminant value, especially when urine dipstick is the only test available.

Note: Proteinuria is not an essential criterion to define pre-eclampsia.
question: What is the minimum cut-off for defining proteinuria in pre-eclampsia in a random urine sample?

explanationHtml:
In a normal pregnancy, the second wave of spiral artery remodeling begins at 12 weeks.

Remodeling of arteries includes invasion of arteries by trophoblasts that lowers the resistance and increases the rate of blood flow through the vessels.. These modified vessels are more capable of meeting the demands of the developing fetus.

Uteroplacental vessel development takes place in two stages:

The first stage occurs before 12 weeks post-fertilization. During this stage, trophoblasts invade the spiral arteries up to their intradecidual segments.

The second stage occurs between 12-16 weeks. It involves invasion of the endovascular trophoblasts into the intramyometrial segments of spiral arteries. Interstitial trophoblasts surround the arteries.

Incomplete trophoblastic invasion leads to pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) where the vessels remain in a state of high resistance, causing low blood flow to the placenta, leading to its ischemia and bringing about the release of inflammatory mediators and vasoactive substances, which ultimately results in endothelial injury.

As the second stage of invasion occurs by 18 weeks, PIH develops after 20 weeks of pregnancy.
question: In a normal pregnancy, when does the second wave of spiral artery remodeling begin?

explanationHtml:
In the above scenario of hypertension in a patient with gestational age <20 weeks, the diagnosis is chronic hypertension.

Chronic hypertension is diagnosed when the patient is a known hypertensive (or) BP > 140/90 mmHg before 20 weeks of gestation.

Gestational hypertension and preeclampsia are only diagnosed after 20 weeks of gestation.
question: A 28-year-old G2P1 patient at 17 weeks of gestation comes for a routine antenatal visit. Her blood pressure is 142/94 mm of Hg. A repeat blood pressure after 4 hours is measured to be 148/92 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Smoking is not a risk factor for pre-eclampsia rather it is protective.

Although smoking during pregnancy causes various adverse pregnancy outcomes, it is associated with a reduced risk for hypertension in pregnancy.

Risk factors for pre-eclampsia are:

  • Previous history of pre-eclampsia
  • Primigravida: young or elderly
  • Family history: Hypertension, pre-eclampsia.
  • Placental abnormalities:
    • Hyperplacentosis: excessive exposure to chorionic villi (molar pregnancy, twins, diabetes)
    • Placental ischemia
  • Thrombophilias: APLA, Protein C, Protein S deficiency, Factor V laden mutation, homocysteinemia
  • Twin pregnancy
  • Molar pregnancy
  • Rh-negative pregnancy
  • New paternity - A new partner for subsequent pregnancies
question: Which of the following does not put a patient at an increased risk for preeclampsia?

correctAnswer: D. Increased placental perfusion due to inflammation
explanationHtml:
Placental perfusion is reduced in patients developing pre-eclampsia.

The development of pre-eclampsia may be explained by:

  • Abnormal trophoblastic invasion of uterine vessels, leading to decreased placental perfusion.
  • Maternal inflammatory response directed against foreign fetal antigens leading to immunological maladaptation.
  • Maternal maladaptation to cardiovascular and inflammatory changes of normal pregnancy.
  • Genetic factors and epigenetic influences.

options.text: Abnormal trophoblastic invasion of uterine vessels
Maladaptive immunological tolerance to fetal antigens
Maladaptation to cardiovascular changes of normal pregnancy
Increased placental perfusion due to inflammation

question: Which of the following does not occur in patients developing pre-eclampsia?

correctAnswer: B. Calcium supplementation above RDA reduces the incidence
explanationHtml:
Calcium supplementation above the RDA does not reduce the incidence of pre-eclampsia.

However, women who have a calcium-deficient state may benefit from calcium supplementation to reduce their risk of preeclampsia.

Prophylactic measures for the prevention of pre-eclampsia include low-dose aspirin administration (50–150 mg/day). It is started after the 1st trimester, continued throughout pregnancy, and is to be stopped 7 days before labor.

Magnesium administration may be beneficial as it lowers endothelin-1 concentrates.

There is no role of a low salt diet, anti-oxidants, or vitamin C.

options.text: Low dose aspirin may reduce severity of disease
Calcium supplementation above RDA reduces the incidence
Treatment with magnesium lowers endothelin-1 concentrates
Megadoses of vitamin C has no proven benefit

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the management of patients with an increased risk of pre-eclampsia?

correctAnswer: D. A decrease in the level of soluble endoglin is seen
explanationHtml:
In pre-eclampsia, there is an increase in the level of soluble endoglin.

Excessive amounts of antiangiogenic factors, increased sensitivity to angiotensin, and lowered angiotensinase levels worsen hypoxia at the uteroplacental interface.

Trophoblast of women who develop preeclampsia overproduces at least two antiangiogenic peptides that enter the maternal circulation. They increase months before clinical preeclampsia develops.

  • Soluble endoglin (sEng) is derived from the placenta and blocks endothelial nitric oxide-dependent vasodilatation. It also inhibits various TGFβ isoforms from binding to endothelial receptors.
  • Soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) is a variant of the Flt-1 receptor for placental growth factor (PlGF) and for VEGF. Elevated maternal sFlt-1 acts as a trap for PlGF and VEGF. By deactivating and decreasing these growth factors, sFlt-1 causes widespread dysfunction of the endothelial cells.

options.text: Vascular sensitivity to angiotensin 2 is increased
There is an increase in sFlt -1 levels
A decrease in the level of soluble endoglin is seen

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of pre-eclampsia and low fibronectin is not a feature of pre-eclampsia.

Features associated with pre-eclampsia:

  • Fibronectin is a glycoprotein associated with vascular endothelial cell basement membrane and is elevated in women with preeclampsia.
  • Thrombocytopenia (HELLP syndrome)
  • Hemolysis (HELLP syndrome)
  • Increased hemoglobin, caused by a decrease in plasma volume.

Hemoconcentration is a hallmark of eclampsia. In preeclampsia, hemoconcentration is present but usually not marked.
question: A 24-year-old primigravida at 22 weeks of gestation came for a regular antenatal checkup. Her BP is 152/96mmHg. Urine analysis shows proteinuria of 3+. All of the following would be consistent with her probable diagnosis, except:

explanationHtml:
Decreased GFR is seen in pre-eclampsia.

During normal pregnancy, renal blood flow and GFR are increased. However, in pre-eclampsia, renal blood flow and GFR decrease due to increased renal afferent arteriolar resistance. The hallmark renal lesion is glomerular endotheliosis. Diminished filtration causes serum creatinine levels and plasma uric acid concentration levels to rise. The elevation is also due to enhanced tubular reabsorption.

The most common system involved in pre-eclampsia is the renal system.

Several studies have demonstrated that pre-eclampsia is associated with low urinary calcium. This is often used as a predictive test.
question: Which finding is most likely to be seen in a patient with pre-eclampsia?

correctAnswer: D. Permanent blindness due to serous retinal detachment
explanationHtml:
Serous retinal detachment does not cause permanent visual loss.

The most common visual symptom of preeclampsia is scotoma.

Blindness can be due to occipital cortex edema, Purtscher’s retinopathy (retinal ischemia), or retinal detachment. The blindness is mostly reversible and corrects automatically after delivery.

Retinal artery occlusion sometimes causes permanent vision loss.

options.text: Central vision loss due to temporary scotoma
Permanent visual loss due to retinal artery occlusion
Permanent blindness due to serous retinal detachment

question: Ophthalmic manifestations in patients with  preeclampsia syndrome include all, except:

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario and radiological image are suggestive of posterior reversible leukoencephalopathy syndrome (PRES). This condition is usually reversible.

Endothelial dysfunction and cerebral autoregulation failure are implicated as etiologies of PRES. PRES lesions are almost universal in women with eclampsia but less frequent in pre-eclampsia.

PRES is characterized by the following:

  • Severe headaches
  • Altered sensorium
  • Seizures
  • Visual disturbances.

Radiological findings in PRES:

  • Hyperintense T2 lesions in the subcortical and cortical regions of the parietal and occipital lobes.
  • The basal ganglia, brainstem, and cerebellum are commonly involved.
  • Posterior circulation is commonly involved, and anterior circulation involvement is seen in severe cases.

Neurological manifestations of preeclampsia include:

  • Headaches
  • Convulsions
  • Cerebral edema
  • Blindness
  • Cerebral hemorrhage.

options.text: Anterior circulation is most commonly involved
This lesions may be seen in most pre-eclampsia patients

question: A patient, diagnosed with preeclampsia was brought to the emergency room with three episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, urinary incontinence, and altered sensorium for 3 hours. After stabilization, an MRI revealed the following findings. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Among the given statements, the presence of pulmonary edema, scotoma, or epigastric pain is indicative of severe pre-eclampsia.

Criteria for diagnosing severe preeclampsia include:

Systolic BP Diastolic BP Proteinuria Signs of end-organ damage
≥160 mmHg ≥110 mmHg + +/-
≥140 mmHg ≥90 mmHg +/- +

Signs and symptoms of significant end-organ dysfunction are:

  • New-onset cerebral or visual disturbance, i.e., photopsia, scotoma, altered mental status, and severe headache
  • Moderate to severe pain in the right hypochondrium or epigastric tenderness (OR) Raised liver enzymes (AST, ALT)
  • Thrombocytopenia with platelets <100,000/microL.
  • Progressive renal insufficiency (serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL)
  • Pulmonary edema.
question:
Which of the following are indicators of severe disease in a patient with preeclampsia?

  1. Pulmonary edema
  2. Systolic BP >130 mmHg
  3. Mild headache
  4. Scotoma
  5. Epigastric pain

explanationHtml:
Decreased deep tendon reflex is not a symptom of impending eclampsia. There will be increased deep tendon reflex i.e., hyperreflexia.

Symptoms and signs of impending eclampsia include:

  • Severe occipital or frontal headache
  • Oliguria - diminished urine output <400 ml/day
  • Epigastric pain
  • Visual symptoms - blurring, scotomas, blindness
  • Disturbed sleep
  • Ankle clonus
  • Severe elevation in blood pressure
  • Pulmonary edema.
question: A patient at 32 weeks of gestation with pre-eclampsia is admitted to your ward. All of the following symptoms would warn you of impending eclampsia, except:

correctAnswer: A. Absence of diastolic notch on Doppler
explanationHtml:
In this above scenario, the absence of a diastolic notch at 24 weeks on Doppler is not a predictor of pre-eclampsia.

In normal pregnant women, a diastolic notch in the uterine artery disappears by 24 weeks. Thus, a persistent diastolic notch present in uterine artery flow between 22-24 weeks is predictive of preeclampsia.

Predictors of preeclampsia:

  • Imbalance in angiogenic and anti-angiogenic factors: ↑sFLT-1, ↑ S. Endoglin, ↓ VEGF, ↓Placental growth factor.
  • Diastolic notch present in uterine artery flow between 22-24 weeks (high resistance index in the second trimester)
  • Average MAP ≥105 mmHg

Predictors no longer used include:

  • Hemoconcentration
  • Elevated fibronectin
  • Increase in uric acid levels
  • Hypocalciuria - calcium in urine <12mg/dl in 24 h
  • Increased homocysteine levels
  • Roll-over test - screening test is done between 28-32 weeks
  • Angiotensin II infusion test

options.text: Absence of diastolic notch on Doppler
High resistance index in uterine artery Doppler in the second trimester

question: A G2P1 woman with a history of pre-eclampsia presents at 24 weeks of gestation for an antenatal check-up. You decide to evaluate her risk of developing pre-eclampsia in the present pregnancy. Which of the following results is not an indicator?

  • Limb contracture
  • Pulmonary hypoplasia.

Anti-hypertensives to be avoided in pregnancy include:

  • ACE inhibitors
  • Angiotensin receptor blockers
  • Diuretics (contraindicated as anti-hypertensive but can be given in CCF)
  • Reserpine
  • Sodium nitroprusside (used only as a drug of last resort in refractory severe hypertension)
  • Diazoxide.

question: A G3P1A1, preeclamptic patient at 33 weeks of gestation came for a regular antenatal check-up.  At present, her BP is 130/90 and an NST is reactive. What is the plan of management for this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Corticosteroids aid in increasing platelet count
explanationHtml:
Corticosteroid treatment for thrombocytopenia is not recommended in patients with HELLP syndrome.

HELLP syndrome is a serious complication in pregnancy characterized by HEmolysis, ELevated liver enzymes, and Low Platelet count. It occurs in 0.5-0.9% of all pregnancies and in 10–20% of patients with severe preeclampsia.

Management of HELLP syndrome is supportive, including:
- Antiseizure prophylaxis with MgSO4
- Platelet tansfusion if platelet count <50,000/mm3 , FFP transfusion
- Plasmapheresis
- Immediate termination of pregnancy in the interest of the mother.

The most common cause of maternal death in HELLP syndrome is abruptio placenta and DIC.

question: A 33-week-pregnant lady with pre-eclampsia presents with features suggestive of HELLP syndrome. Which of the following is false about her condition?

explanationHtml:

HELLP syndrome occurs at 27-37 weeks. PT, PTT, and fibrinogen levels are normal. This differs from DIC where PT and PTT are elevated while the plasma fibrinogen level is decreased.

In mild pre-eclampsia, steroids are given and the patient is delivered at 37 weeks.

In severe pre-eclampsia:

Blindness due to eclampsia can be due to a central or peripheral cause. It is irreversible only if the etiology is a combination of retinal infarction and bilateral lateral geniculate nuclei lesions.

correctAnswer: D. It blocks neuronal sodium influx
explanationHtml:
MgSO4 blocks calcium influx, not sodium.

Mechanism of action of MgSO4:

  • It is a membrane stabilizer and acts as a neuroprotector by reducing motor endplate sensitivity to Ach.
  • It blocks neuronal calcium influx.
  • It reduces the presynaptic release of the neurotransmitter glutamate.
  • It blocks glutaminergic NMDA receptors and potentiates adenosine action.

question: The mechanism of action of MgSo4 includes all, except:

explanationHtml:
Repeat injections of MgSO4 are given only if knee jerks are present.

The next dose of MgSO4 is only given when all signs of magnesium toxicity are absent.

Identification of magnesium toxicity:

  • Loss of deep tendon reflexes
  • Decreased respiratory rate (<12 per min)
  • Urine output <30 ml/hr
  • Chest pain, heart block

Management of magnesium toxicity:

  • Stop magnesium therapy
  • Estimation of serum magnesium and creatinine levels
  • Injection of calcium gluconate 10 ml (10% solution) IV

Side effects of MgSO4:

  • Anuria
  • Pulmonary edema.
question: Which of the following is an indication to skip the next dose in a patient with severe pre-eclampsia taking MgSO4 prophylactically?

explanationHtml:
Patellar reflexes disappear when plasma magnesium concentration reaches 10 mEq/L. As there is no respiratory depression, the plasma concentration is likely to be 10-12 mEq/L.

The earliest warning sign of impending magnesium toxicity is the loss of the patellar reflex. MgSO4 is prophylactically used in impending eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, and HELLP syndrome.

question: A pregnant woman with pre-eclampsia is started on prophylactic MgSO4 in view of signs of impending eclampsia. An hour later, examination reveals RR - 16 breaths/minute and absent patellar reflexes. What is her plasma concentration of MgSO4 most likely to be?

correctAnswer: C. Prevention of RDS in premature baby
explanationHtml:
Magnesium sulfate has no role in the prevention of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in a premature baby, where there is a deficit of surfactant (which results in alveolar collapse).

Magnesium in the MgSO4 competes with calcium on voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby altering its uptake and release. Functions of MgSO4 include :

  • Membrane protector and neuro stabilizer. It is used in the prevention of cerebral palsy in very low birth weight neonates.
  • Reduction of motor endplate sensitivity to acetylcholine, and thus is used as an adjunct in the management of acute severe asthma in children and adults
  • Blocking of neuronal calcium influx, and is thus used in the conservative management of pre-term labor (tocolytic, option D)
  • Inducing cerebral vasodilatation, dilating the uterine arteries, increasing the production of endothelial prostacyclin, and inhibiting platelet activation. Hence it is used in the management of pre-eclampsia (option A) and to prevent progression to eclampsia (option A).

options.text: Prevention of seizures in severe pre-eclampsia
Prevention of recurrent seizures in eclampsia
Prevention of RDS in premature baby

question: Magnesium sulphate has no role in:

correctAnswer: C. Treatment may be based on recommendations from the Magpie trial
explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of eclampsia and management may be based on recommendations from the Magpie trial.

The advantage of the prophylactic use of magnesium sulfate in lowering the risk of eclampsia was given by the Magpie trial. Based on this recommendation, MgSO4 is administered to women having eclampsia to control the seizures and prevent further convulsions.

The following are the steps taken in the management of eclampsia:

  • The first step is maintaining the airway and ensuring oxygen delivery to both mother and fetus.
  • The next step is to administer MgSO4 to control seizures.
  • Antihypertensives are given to lower the blood pressure.
  • Finally, the pregnancy is terminated and the fetus is delivered.

Thiopentone > phenobarbitone may be used to control seizures. No attempt should be made to shorten the convulsion using diazepam as it often leads to thrombophlebitis and respiratory depression.

Maternal acidosis usually occurs and is corrected when present.

explanationHtml:
Supine vena cava syndrome is the complication of the given representation. The image shows compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus which can sometimes lead to supine hypotension.

During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus compresses the great vessels against the hard spine, when the patient is in the supine position. Of the two vessels, the vena cava is compressed, but the aorta, owing to its structure is relatively resistant.

Normally, the vena cava compression results in opening up collateral circulation by means of paravertebral and azygous veins but in some cases, when the collateral circulation fails to open up, the venous return of the heart may be seriously curtailed resulting in hypotension, tachycardia, and syncope and is called supine vena cava syndrome.

The normal blood pressure is quickly restored by turning the patient to the lateral position.
question: A pregnant lady with PIH was being monitored with bed rest in supine position. Which of the following is a complication of the below representation?

explanationHtml:
Obesity in first-degree relatives is not a high-risk factor for gestational diabetes mellitus. However, severe obesity is a risk factor for developing gestational diabetes.

Gestational diabetes mellitus is defined as carbohydrate intolerance of variable severity with onset or first recognition during the present pregnancy.

It usually presents in the second or third trimester. More than 50% of women with GDM ultimately develop overt diabetes within 20 years.

It is recommended to screen for gestational diabetes mellitus in the presence of the following high-risk factors:

  • Severe obesity
  • Strong family history of type-2 diabetes
  • Previous history of gestational diabetes mellitus
  • Impaired glucose metabolism or glucosuria.
question: Which of the following are not risk factors for developing gestational diabetes?

explanationHtml:
Overt diabetes is when fasting blood sugar is ≥ 126 mg/dl. Overt diabetics are women who are known to have diabetes before pregnancy.

A patient is said to have overt diabetes if:

  • Fasting blood sugar ≥ 126 mg/dL
  • A random blood sugar of ≥ 200 mg/dL
  • HbA1c of ≥ 6.5%

The maternal complication of diabetes:

  • increased Miscarriage and preterm labor.
  • increased incidence of preeclampsia
  • polyhydramnios
  • prolongation of labor due to shoulder dystocia, operative interference, and cephalo-pelvic disproportion.

Fetal and Neonatal complications of diabetes:

  • fetal macrosomia (birth weight > 4kg)
  • congenital malformations - Musculoskeletal, urogenital, and CNS anomalies.
question: You discover that there is evidence of cardiac malformation in a fetus during a routine USG scan at 16 weeks. What is the minimum level of fasting blood sugar at which you can suspect overt diabetes?

correctAnswer: B. 100 grams of glucose is given after overnight fast
explanationHtml:
In one-step procedure, the patient is given 75g of glucose after an overnight fast, and blood glucose is measured hourly for 2 hours.

Diagnostic criteria with one-step procedure is as follows:

  • Fasting ≥ 92 mg/dL
  • 1-hour ≥ 180 mg/dL
  • 2-hour ≥ 153 mg/dL

In two-step approach patient is given glucose and subsequent values measured in two separate steps.

  • Step 1 - the patient is given 50 grams of glucose and blood glucose is measured after one hour. If it is ≥140 mg/dl then the screen is positive and step 2 is done.
  • Step 2 - the patient is given 100g of glucose and values measured hourly, for 3 hours. A diagnosis is made if at least two values are high using one of two methods.

DIPSI (Diabetes In Pregnancy Societies of India) recommends a one-step procedure without regard to the time of the last meal. Here the patient is given 75 grams of oral glucose. A blood glucose value of ≥140 mg/dL after 2-hours is diagnostic.

100 grams of glucose is given after overnight fast

According to the American college of obstetricians (ACOG), macrosomia is defined as the fetal birth weight of ≥ 4.5 kg.

Macrosomia refers to growth of a fetus, irrespective of gestational age, such that its weight exceeds a specific threshold, which is above 4.5 kg in developed nations; however, a weight above 4 kg is also frequently used.

The WHO defines the cut-off at 4.0 kg for fetal macrosomia in its guidelines for the management of common maternal conditions. This is followed in India.
question: According to the American college of obstetricians, macrosomia is defined as the fetal birth weight of______.

explanationHtml:
BMI (body mass index) and HbA1c are both independent and substantial risk factors for macrosomia in gestational diabetes.
BMI levels are associated with increased birth weight, regardless of glucose levels. Gestational diabetes prevalence increases by approximately 1 percent for every 1 kg/m2 increase in BMI.

BMI in pregnancy:

  • Underweight - < 18 kg/m2
  • Normal - 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2
  • Overweight - 25 to 29.9 kg/m2
  • Obese - >30 kg/m2

Weight distribution also seems to play a role because the risk of gestational diabetes is increased with truncal obesity.

HbA1c levels, reflecting average glycemic control, independently correlate with fetal macrosomia. Higher maternal HbA1c increases fetal exposure to glucose, driving fetal hyperinsulinemia and excess growth. Elevated HbA1c in pre-gestational diabetes is additionally associated with fetal malformations.

question: On screening, a primigravida is found to have fasting blood glucose of 110mg/dl. What is the likelihood that she will develop overt diabetes within the next 20 years?

explanationHtml:
Tetrology of Fallot is the least likely anomaly seen in infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs).

Ventricular septal defect and transposition of great arteries are the most common cardiac anomalies in infants of diabetic mothers.

Other associated anomalies include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), transposition of the great vessels (TGA), and tricuspid atresia.

The most common cardiac anomaly in an infant of a diabetic mother is a controversial topic. Most resources mention that VSD and TGA are the most common, but do not specify which is more common.
question: A 29-year-old woman with overt diabetes comes to you for pre-conception counseling. Which of the following congenital heart defects are least likely to occur if she were to have a child?

explanationHtml:
Hypocalcemia in a term newborn is defined as serum calcium < 8 mg/dl.

Hypocalcemia is one of the potential metabolic derangements in neonates of diabetic mothers.

There is hypomagnesemia in the mother and the infant due to increased maternal urinary excretion of magnesium due to diabetes. There is maternal hyperparathyroidism due to hypomagnesemia, which leads to increased maternal calcium.

This maternal calcium passes to the infant through the placenta and suppresses fetal PTH synthesis and impairs PTH response to postpartum hypocalcemia. PTH suppression, in this case, can be severe and lead to convulsions in the early neonatal period and may persist for months.
question: Hypocalcemia in a term newborn is defined as serum calcium _____ mg/dl.

explanationHtml:
A diagnosis of neonatal hypoglycemia is considered when plasma glucose levels fall below 45 mg/dL. This value is widely accepted in clinical practice and supported by the WHO guidelines.

However, variations in diagnostic thresholds exist. This is due to the lack of a universally established blood glucose level definitively proven to cause brain injury. Ideal glucose levels can differ based on a newborn's age and presenting clinical symptoms.
question: You are performing plasma glucose charting for newborns in the postnatal ward. According to the WHO, below what level is it considered hypoglycemia?

explanationHtml:
The image showing a poorly developed lower limb suggests the diagnosis of caudal regression sequence/sacral agenesis seen in pregestational diabetes. It is the most specific anomaly seen in diabetes.

Caudal regression sequence is an uncommon birth defect that involves genitourinary and structural malformations in the caudal region, from an underdeveloped sacrum to incomplete lumbar vertebrae. This condition is frequently associated with maternal pre-gestational diabetes.

Overt diabetes (pregestational diabetes) is associated with higher malformation rates than the general population. Elevated maternal HbA1c levels correlate with fetal malformations. Neural tube defects (encephalocele, meningomyelocele, anencephaly), transposition of great vessels, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis and coarctation of the aorta are commonly seen.

Small left colon syndrome is a rare anomaly that develops in the second and third trimesters.

Option B: Malformations are not associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Malformations occur due to the disruption of organogenesis, usually occurring in the first trimester. The abnormal glycemic status in GDM manifests only in the second trimester.

Option C: Valproate leads to neural tube defects and not sacral agenesis.

Option D: ACE inhibitors can cause oligohydramnios.

Even though the barrier method will not lead to complications in such patients, the failure rate is high due to incorrect use and non-compliance. Hence it is not preferred.

question: What is the commonest congenital valvular lesion observed in pregnancy?

Cardiac failure in pregnancy is least likely to occur during 24 weeks, considering the given options.

The order of risk of cardiac failure in pregnancy is immediate postpartum > 2nd stage of labor > 30 weeks > 22 weeks.

Maternal cardiac risk predictors according to AHA are as follows:

  • NYHA class >2 or cyanosis during first antenatal visit
  • Obstructive lesions of left heart (Area of mitral valve <2 cm2 , Area of aortic valve <1.5 cm2, LV outflow tract peak gradient >30 mmHg)
  • Previous cardiac events prior to pregnancy
  • Prior arrhythmia
  • Myocardial dysfunction (Ejection fraction<40%, cardiomyopathy)

Scoring systems used to calculate risk are Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy (CARPREG) and ZAHARA scores.
question: A 24-year-old lady with rheumatic mitral stenosis becomes pregnant. At what point during her pregnancy would you be least concerned about her developing cardiac failure?

question: An intern posted in the antenatal OPD auscultates a patient who came for her routine checkup. Presence of which of the following features would not suggest a physiological change of pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Prosthetic valve replacement is not an indication for therapeutic termination as it comes under the WHO category risk 3. Only conditions included under WHO category risk 4 are considered as indications for termination of pregnancy.

WHO class 4 comprises of diseases with very high risk of maternal mortality or severe morbidity, such as:

  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension
  • Severe systemic ventricular dysfunction (NYHA III-IV or LVEF 30-40%)
  • Previous peripartum cardiomyopathy with any residual impairment of left ventricular function
  • Severe left heart obstruction
  • Marfan syndrome with aorta dilated >40 mm

Termination of pregnancy is also advised in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome.
question: Which of the following is not an absolute indication for therapeutic termination of pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Primary pulmonary hypertension is not a cardiac indication for cesarean delivery.

Pulmonary hypertension is a WHO Class IV cardiac condition in pregnancy. Pregnancy is contraindicated, and termination is suggested if already conceived due to high maternal mortality and morbidity risk. In very rare cases if the patient still desires to continue pregnancy vaginal delivery is preferred to avoid surgical and anesthetic risks, provided there is adequate epidural analgesia and cardiac monitoring.

Cardiac indications for cesarean delivery:

  • Aortic root dilation > 4 cm
  • Acute severe congestive heart failure

  • Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis

question: A pregnant lady with heart failure planned for valve replacement surgery is posted for cesarean section. Which of the following is not a cardiac indication for cesarean delivery?

explanationHtml:
Perimortem cesarean delivery should be considered if there is no return of spontaneous circulation in 5 minutes, according to the AHA 2020 Guidelines.

The goal of perimortem cesarean section (PMCS) should be primarily aimed at saving the life of the mother. PMCS improves maternal survival by decreasing compression of the IVC by the gravid uterus. This improves venous return and diaphragmatic displacement, which in turn improves respiratory dynamics.
question: You are performing CPR on a woman who is 38-weeks pregnant. She was admitted to the emergency after a massive pulmonary embolism led to cardio-pulmonary arrest. Despite the initial management of airway, oxygenation and vasopressor support, there is no improvement. What is the cut off time  for perimortem cesarean delivery in this patient?

correctAnswer: D. Trendelenburg position during first stage of labor
explanationHtml:
Lateral recumbent position is advised during the first stage of labor in this patient.

Management of labor in patients with heart disease:

First stage:

  • Lateral recumbent or propped-up position
  • Oxygen administration (5 to 6 L/min)
  • Analgesia by epidural
  • Fluids should not be infused at more than 75 ml/h
  • Central venous pressure monitoring

Second stage:

  • No maternal pushing
  • Cut short second stage by forceps or ventouse under pudendal and/or perineal block anaesthesia
  • The benefit of avoiding haemodynamic fluctuations resulting from pushing must be weighed against an increased risk of perineal trauma, haemorrhage, and fetal head injury with forceps or vacuum delivery.

Third stage:

  • Oxytocin by infusion
  • IV frusemide if needed

Note: As per the current ACC/AHA guidelines, antibiotic prophylaxis for bacterial endocarditis is no longer recommended during labour in patients with mitral valve prolapse.

The final switch to heparin in a pregnant women is advised at 36 weeks of pregnancy and is continued till 7 days postpartum.

This switch is made from warfarin to heparin at 36 weeks, as warfarin is a strong anticoagulant which can cause post partum hemorrhage in the mother at the time of labour and can also cross the placenta into the fetal blood and can increase the risk of intracranial hemorrhage in the fetus

question: A pregnant woman with cardiac disease is on warfarin therapy. When will the final switch to heparin be advised?

explanationHtml:
The best technique for managing the second stage of labor in a patient with heart disease is using ventouse.

For most cardiac patients, vaginal delivery is preferred and cesarean section is reserved for obstetric indications since the cesarean section is associated with more blood loss and higher thromboembolic and infection risk. If vaginal delivery is selected as the mode of choice, it will be conducted with the laboring woman in an upright position, or in the left decubitus position. This minimizes aortocaval compression.

Active pushing during the second stage may also be limited, depending on the degree of cardiac compromise. In moderate to severe cardiac disease, it may be prudent to completely avoid an active second stage. Regional anesthesia can be used to allow the fetal head to descend to the perineum without active pushing. Delivery can be further facilitated by forceps or vacuum extraction.

The benefit of avoiding hemodynamic fluctuations resulting from pushing must be weighed against an increased risk of perineal trauma, hemorrhage, and fetal head injury with forceps or vacuum delivery.

Some journals report that ventouse is preferable to forceps, as it can be applied without putting the patient in lithotomy position (raising the legs increases the cardiac load) however it is controversial.
question: A 28-year-old G2P1 was admitted to the labor room at 38 weeks of gestation. She is a known case of atrioventricular septal defect.  Which of the following is the best for managing the second stage of labor in this patient ?

explanationHtml:
In pregnant ladies with severe aortic stenosis, general anesthesia is the preferable mode of analgesia.

Maternal hypotension is a possible side effect of epidural/spinal analgesia. This is dangerous in women with severe aortic stenosis, as the fixed cardiac output cannot compensate for a drop in systemic vascular resistance, risking critical myocardial ischemia and cardiac arrest. Other possible side effects include reduced preload and arrhythmias. General anaesthesia is preferred in severe cases of aortic stenosis because it maintains systemic vascular resistance and provides tight control over blood pressure, heart rate, and preload.

Other conditions for which general anaesthesia may be indicated:

  • Severe mitral stenosis
  • Right-to-left intracardiac shunts complicated by severe pulmonary hypertension and/or heart failure.
  • Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM)
question: General anesthesia is the preferable mode of analgesia in pregnant women with ______

correctAnswer: D. Warfarin is contraindicated during lactation
explanationHtml:
Warfarin is not contraindicated during lactation.

Warfarin, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), unfractionated heparin (UFH) do not accumulate in breast milk. They do not induce an anticoagulant effect in the infant.

The choice of anticoagulants is the main problem in pregnancy due to the following reasons:

  • Warfarin: Although safe for the mother, can lead to warfarin embryopathy, miscarriage, IUGR, and stillbirths.
  • Heparin: It is safe for the fetus as it does not cross the placenta but less effective than warfarin.
  • LMWH: Inadequate and ACOG does not recommend its use in pregnant women with prosthetic heart valves.

If the patient delivers when the anticoagulant is still effective and bleeds excessively, then protamine sulfate is given intravenously.

question: A pregnant lady with mitral stenosis requires anticoagulation. Which of the following statements is false regarding her management?

correctAnswer: D. The most common cause for death is cardiac failure
explanationHtml:
The most common cause of death in HOCM in pregnant women is ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

Most affected women are asymptomatic, but some patients may develop:

  • Dyspnea
  • Anginal or atypical chest pain
  • Syncope
  • Arrhythmias.

Strenuous exercise is prohibited during pregnancy. Abrupt positional changes are avoided to prevent reflex vasodilation and decrease of preload. Diuretics and vasodilators are generally not used as they decrease preload. If angina develops, beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers are used.

The mode of delivery depends upon obstetric indications and if cesarean section is done, general anesthesia is considered the safest.

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
Left ventricular systolic dysfunction is a feature of peripartum cardiomyopathy (also known as postpartum cardiomyopathy) and not diastolic dysfunction.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a type of dilated cardiomyopathy. It develops during the last month of pregnancy or within the first 5 months following delivery.

The predisposing factors include Cardiac gene mutations involving several genes like TTNC1, TTN, and STAT3, Twin pregnancy/ multifetal gestation, Smoking, and Preeclampsia. Other proposed causes include viral myocarditis, abnormal immune response to pregnancy, malnutrition, inflammation, etc.

PPCM is associated with increased secretion of prolactin by the pituitary and antiangiogenic molecule sFlt-1 (soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase) by the placenta at term gestation.

Pearson’s diagnostic criteria for PPCM:

  • Development of cardiac failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months after delivery
  • Absence of an identifiable cause for the cardiac failure
  • Absence of recognizable heart disease prior to the last month of pregnancy, and
  • Left ventricular systolic dysfunction demonstrated by echocardiographic criteria, such as ejection fraction <45% or fractional shortening <30% along with or without a dilated left ventricle.

Management involves treating the features of heart failure. Bromocriptine has been found useful in this condition. Many women recover within 6 months of delivery, while some continue to have residual effects.

options.text: Development of cardiac failure within 5 months of delivery

question: All are true regarding peripartum cardiomyopathy except _____

explanationHtml:
Prolactin has been proposed to be responsible for peripartum cardiomyopathy.

Oxidative stress during late pregnancy leads to the proteolytic cleavage of prolactin. The resulting 16-kDa prolactin fragment has been found to be cardiotoxic and can impair the metabolism and contractility of cardiomyocytes.

The etiology of peripartum cardiomyopathy remains unknown. Many potential causes have been proposed but are not proven.

  • Viral myocarditis
  • Abnormal immune response to pregnancy
  • Abnormal response to the increased hemodynamic burden of pregnancy
  • Malnutrition
  • Inflammation
  • Apoptosis
  • Prolactin

The resulting 16-kDa prolactin fragment has been found to be cardiotoxic and can impair the metabolism and contractility of cardiomyocytes. Based on this proposed mechanism, bromocriptine therapy has been suggested because it inhibits prolactin secretion.

explanationHtml:
Eisenmenger syndrome is the heart disease with the worst prognosis, having a maternal mortality rate of 50%.

The most common cause of death in Eisenmenger’s syndrome is right ventricular failure with cardiogenic shock. If antenatal diagnosis of Eisenmenger syndrome is made in the first trimester, termination of pregnancy is advised. Eisenmenger syndrome has the highest risk of maternal mortality. However, since mitral stenosis is the most common cardiac condition in pregnancy, it is the most common cause of maternal mortality overall.

Mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse and pulmonary stenosis are well tolerated during pregnancy. Severe aortic stenosis can be life-threatening. However, women with mild to moderate aortic valve stenosis may have a relatively low-risk pregnancy.
question: Which of the following is associated with the highest risk of maternal mortality during pregnancy?

question: The Rhesus blood group antigen complex is located on which chromosome?

explanationHtml:
The Lewis antigens do not cause alloimmunization or hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

Alloimmunization/isoimmunisation is defined as an immune response to foreign antigens after exposure to genetically different cells or tissues.

The Kell blood group system is complex and contains many antigens that are highly immunogenic. These antigens are the third most potent, after those of the ABO and Rh blood groups, at triggering an immune reaction. Anti-Kell causes severe fetal anemia by suppressing fetal RBC synthesis.

MNS and Kidd blood types cause alloimmunization. Hemolytic disease of newborn is mild with Kidd whereas MNS causes potentially severe anemia.
question: Antigens of which of the following blood group systems do not cause alloimmunization in a newborn/fetus?

explanationHtml:
In a non-immunized Rh-negative primigravida, Anti D is given at 28 weeks of gestation. It is also given within 72 hours of delivery.

Routine postpartum administration of anti-D immune globulin to at-risk pregnancies within 72 hours of delivery decreases the alloimmunization rate by 90 percent.

Additionally, the provision of Anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks of gestation reduces the third-trimester alloimmunization rate from approximately 2 percent to 0.1 percent.
question: A pregnant Rh-negative woman presents for her regular antenatal visit. Her Indirect Coombs test is negative. When would you give her prophylactic  Anti-D?

explanationHtml:
Postpartum hemorrhage is not an indication of Anti-D prophylaxis.

Anti-D prophylaxis is administered to Rh-negative patients in the following circumstances:

  • Pregnancy loss due to:
    • Ectopic pregnancy
    • Spontaneous abortion/hydatiform mole
    • Elective abortion
    • Fetal death (any trimester)
  • Procedures:
    • Amniocentesis
    • Chorionic villus sampling
    • Fetal blood sampling
    • External cephalic version
  • Delivery
  • Trauma
  • Placental abruption
  • Unexplained vaginal bleeding during pregnancy
question: Which of the following events in Rh-negative patients does not require Anti-D prophylaxis?

explanationHtml:
According to the 2022 FOGSI guidelines, the dose of Anti-D immunoglobulin to be given is 150 μg.

All Rh-negative unsensitized women should receive 150 μg of Rh-immune globulin IM before 20 weeks of gestation in the following conditions:

  • Within 72 hours of induced or spontaneous abortion
  • Ectopic/molar pregnancy
  • Chorionic villus sampling
  • Amniocentesis

Women with a pregnancy beyond 20 weeks should receive a full dose of 300 μg. Generally, a 300 μg (1500 IU) dose will protect a woman from fetal hemorrhage of up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood.
question: Chorionic villus sampling was performed on a G2P1 Rh-negative woman at 10 weeks of gestation. What is the dose of Anti-D immunoglobulin that should be administered?

correctAnswer: C. The reagent used is citric acid
explanationHtml:
The reagent used for the Kleihauer-Betke test is citric acid.

Kleihauer-Betke test is the most commonly used quantitative test used to detect fetomaternal hemorrhage i.e., the approximate volume of fetal blood entering the maternal circulation. It is also known as the acid elution test.

The principle behind it is that fetal erythrocytes contain hemoglobin F, which is more resistant to acid elution than hemoglobin A.

After exposure to acid, only fetal hemoglobin remains, such that after staining, the fetal erythrocytes appear red and adult cells appear as “ghosts.” Fetal cells are counted and expressed as a percentage of adult cells.

Flow cytometry is the best test for the quantification of fetomaternal hemorrhage. It is more sensitive and accurate as compared to the Kleihauer-Betke test.

Flow cytometry can analyze a larger number of cells and is not influenced by maternal levels of fetal hemoglobin and fetal levels of maternal hemoglobin. It utilizes monoclonal antibodies to HbF or to the D antigen followed by quantification by fluorescence.

The reagent used is citric acid

  • 50 micrograms of Anti-D can neutralize 2.5 ml of fetal RBCs.

question: A 25-year-old Rh-negative primigravida presents to the antenatal clinic at 12 weeks of pregnancy. Her husband is found to be Rh-positive. An Indirect Coombs test is also positive. At what critical titer of the test, would the fetus require monitoring for signs of anemia?

correctAnswer: D. MCA doppler peak systolic velocity
explanationHtml:
MCA Doppler peak systolic velocity (PSV) is used for the monitoring of fetuses in Rh-negative sensitized mothers.

The middle cerebral artery is used as other fetal vessels require a larger insonating angle and confers significant measurement error.

MCA PSV is enhanced due to increased cardiac output and decreased viscosity of fetal blood, which permits the reliable, noninvasive detection of fetal anemia in cases of blood-group alloimmunization.

If the MCA PSV exceeds 1.5 MoM (multiples of the median) and the gestational age is less than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling should be considered. MCA Doppler PSV has replaced amniocentesis as the preferred test for the detection of anemia.
question: In modern obstetrics, which of the following investigations is used for monitoring the fetus of an Rh-negative sensitized mother?

explanationHtml:
A severely affected fetus is represented by zone 3.

Liley developed a chart of changing amniotic fluid bilirubin levels (delta OD450) and weeks of gestation. Amnionic fluid bilirubin is measured by a spectrophotometer and is demonstrable as a change in optical density absorbance at 450 nm (ΔOD450).

However, middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA PCV) is non-invasive and more accurate than optical density at 450 nm, hence Liley’s chart is no longer used in practice.

Liley’s chart has three zones as shown below, delineating the severity of rhesus disease.

  • Liley’s zone I (low zone) - mild disease.
  • Liley’s zone II (mid zone) - fetal anemia.
  • Liley’s zone III (high zone) - severely affected fetus and fetal death is imminent.
question: In Liley's chart, which zone represents a severely affected fetus?

explanationHtml:
Threshold (critical value) of middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity is 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM).

If the MCA peak systolic velocity exceeds 1.5 MoM, further evaluation by fetal blood sampling is necessary to assess the need for fetal transfusion.

The anemic fetus shunts blood preferentially to the brain to maintain adequate oxygenation. The velocity increases because of increased cardiac output and decreased blood viscosity.

In many centers, serial measurement of the peak systolic velocity of the fetal middle cerebral artery has replaced amniocentesis for the detection of fetal anemia. This method provided 100 percent sensitivity.
question: You are performing a Doppler assessment of a fetal middle cerebral artery.  What is the threshold value of its peak systolic velocity that would prompt you to consider fetal blood sampling?

explanationHtml:
Intrauterine transfusion is done if fetal haematocrit is <30%.

The blood for transfusion is usually O negative and cross-matched with the mother's blood. It is highly packed to achieve a hematocrit of 75 -80%.

Intrauterine transfusions may be done intraperitoneally where blood is absorbed through diaphragmatic lymphatics. It may also be done intravascularly through the umbilical vein. The segments of the umbilical vein used are the intrahepatic portion or at its insertion into the placenta.

Complications of intrauterine transfusion include:

  • Fetal demise
  • Chorioamnionitis
  • Placental abruption
  • Pre-term labor
  • Bradycardia/tachyarrhythmia

question: A 32-year-old G4P3 Rh-negative patient with an antibody titer of 1:32 presents to the clinic at 30 weeks. A USG reveals features of fetal edema, ascites, and polyhydramnios. Cordocentesis was done for fetal blood sampling. At what hematocrit value is intrauterine blood transfusion indicated?

correctAnswer: D. It is a not a form of pre-eclampsia
explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of maternal mirror syndrome/Ballantyne syndrome. It may be considered a form of severe pre-eclampsia.

Maternal mirror syndrome is the association between fetal hydrops and the development of maternal edema. The syndrome is named as such because the mother mirrors the fetus. It is characterized by triple edema i.e., the fetus, mother, and placenta become edematous.

The pathogenesis of mirror syndrome, although not well established, mimics trophoblastic damage and maternal vascular endothelial dysfunction, as is also seen in pre-eclampsia. Hence, these two conditions may have a similar clinical presentation, with common features such as:

  • Edema
  • Hypertension
  • Proteinuria
  • Liver enzyme elevation
  • Headache and visual disturbances.

However, in contrast to mirror syndrome, preeclampsia shows hemoconcentration whereas mirror syndrome shows hemodilution. Also, preeclampsia is associated with low uteroplacental perfusion and fetal growth restriction.

The etiology of fetal hydrops is not related to the development of mirror syndrome. Hydrops could be due to rhesus isoimmunization, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, congenital infections, fetal cystic hygroma, Ebstein anomaly, sacrococcygeal teratoma, vein of Galen aneurysms, etc.

In most cases with mirror syndrome, prompt delivery is indicated, because women with severe features of preeclampsia can deteriorate rapidly. In few cases, identification and treatment of the cause of fetal hydrops resulted in the resolution of symptoms for both the mother and baby for the remainder of the pregnancy.

The pale, oedematous fetus in the image is suggestive of fetal hydrops. Fetal hydrops is associated with polyhydramnios, not oligohydramnios.

It often occurs as an effect of iso-immunization in an Rh-negative pregnancy. Other complications that may occur are fetal anemia and hyperbilirubinemia.

Fetal anemia occurs in the initial stage of iso-immunization. It is associated with polyhydramnios and increased placental thickening (hyper-placentosis). An increase in the right atrium size of the fetus is seen.

Fetal hydrops is usually accompanied by severe anemia. It results in stillbirth or fetal demise soon after birth. It is also associated with:

Obstetric cholestasis is a condition in which cholestasis occurs in pregnancy. Serum bilirubin increases very late in the disease and total plasma concentrations rarely exceed 5 mg/dL.

Hyperbilirubinemia results from the retention of conjugated pigment. Serum transaminase levels may be normal or moderately elevated, usually up to 200 IU/L. In rare cases, levels of upto 1000 IU/L may be seen.

It is also referred to as recurrent jaundice of pregnancy, cholestatic hepatosis, and icterus gravidarum. There is a significant genetic influence. It may be more common in multifetal pregnancies.

Patients present with pruritus that develops usually during the third trimester, typically involving the palms and soles. It is worse at night. Icterus may also be present.

question: Which of the following is not true regarding obstetric cholestasis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of cholestasis in pregnancy. Serum bile acid is the earliest and most consistent parameter to increase in obstetric cholestasis.

Serum cholic acid is preferred compared to serum chenodeoxycholic acid.

Although serum bile acid increases after meals it is still considered an important investigation among women with obstetric cholestasis. This is because serum bile acid levels remain significantly elevated in women with obstetric cholestasis in comparison to pregnant women without it.

question: A woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents with severe itching over her palms and soles for 2 weeks. She gives a history of similar complaints in her last pregnancy. On examination, she is icteric. Which of the following is the preferred investigation to diagnose this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of obstetric cholestasis. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the drug of choice in obstetric cholestasis.

It relieves pruritus, lowers bile acid and serum enzyme levels (like SGOT, ALP). It may also reduce certain neonatal complications such as preterm birth, fetal distress, and respiratory distress syndrome.

Antihistamines and topical emollients may provide some relief.

Cholestyramine causes decreased absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, which leads to vitamin K deficiency. Fetal coagulopathy may develop, which may lead to intracranial hemorrhage and stillbirth, and therefore it is not preferred.

Bilirubin= 3.5mg/dl

explanationHtml:
Hyperglycemia, hypercholesterolemia, and thrombocytosis are not likely to be seen in acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP).

Clinical features of AFLP include:

  • Persistent nausea and vomiting
  • Progressive jaundice
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Hypertension
  • Proteinuria
  • Edema
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Moderate to severe liver dysfunction - manifested by:
    • Hypofibrinogenemia
    • Hypoalbuminemia
    • Hypocholesterolemia
    • Prolonged clotting time.

question:
Which of the following features are not likely to be seen in a patient with acute fatty liver of pregnancy?

  1. Hyperglycemia
  2. Coagulopathy
  3. Hypercholesterolemia
  4. Thrombocytosis
  5. Hypofibrinogenemia

explanationHtml:
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is more commonly associated with male fetuses and not female fetuses.

AFLP is a rare, potentially fatal complication also known as acute fatty metamorphosis or acute yellow atrophy. It is more common in the third trimester. It is due to a defect in the long-chain-3-hydroxy acyl-CoA-dehydrogenase (LCHAD) pathway with the fetus being homozygous and the mother heterozygous for the deficiency.

It is also associated with:

  • First pregnancy - uncommon in subsequent pregnancies
  • Maternal obesity
  • Multiple pregnancies

Investigations:

  • Liver function tests such as AST, ALT, and serum bilirubin levels are raised.
  • Hemolysis with coagulopathy:
    • Decreased platelets and fibrinogen
    • Elevated d-dimers and prothrombin time
  • Biopsy reveals a characteristic microvesicular fatty infiltration.

The definitive management of AFLP is rapid delivery of the fetus and supportive care. Hepatic dysfunction usually normalizes within a week of delivery.

question: Which of the following will not increase the risk for urinary tract infection in pregnant women?

correctAnswer: C. Antibiotic therapy is required only if symptoms develop
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of asymptomatic bacteriuria. Antibiotic therapy should be given regardless of the symptoms.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria refers to persistent, actively multiplying bacteria within the urinary tract in asymptomatic women.

Organisms that cause urinary infections are those from the normal perineal flora. The most common causative agent is E.coli. Others include Klebsiella, and Proteus.

Incidence is similar to that in non-pregnant women. Prevalence depends on parity (more in higher parity), race, socioeconomic status (more in low SES).

It is more common in patients with sickle cell anemia/trait, diabetes. There is a high risk of developing chronic renal lesions in later life.

It is also associated with:

  • Hypertension
  • Anemia
  • Premature labor
  • Intrauterine growth retardation
  • Urinary tract abnormalities in recurrent cases.

Diagnostic criteria:

  • A positive bacterial count of the same species - over 1,00,000/mL
  • Organisms in midstream clean-catch specimen of urine on two occasions
  • No symptoms of urinary infection

Treatment:

  • Single-dose therapy - Amoxicillin 3g, Nitrofurantoin 200mg
  • Regular 10-14 days therapy - Amoxicillin, Nitrofurantoin, Cephalexin, or Amoxiclav
  • Recurrent cases need to be treated until delivery with prophylactic doses.

Antibiotics unsafe in pregnancy include:

question: A woman presented to the clinic with severe lower abdominal pain and dysuria at 28 weeks of gestation.  Suprapubic tenderness was noted on palpation. Urine examination revealed pyuria with microscopic hematuria.  All of the following can be used to treat this condition except?

explanationHtml:
Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy most often complicates 2nd trimester of pregnancy.

Acute pyelonephritis occurs more commonly in those with preexisting renal disease. It is caused by E. coli >> Streptococcus sp., S.aureus > Enterobacter, Klebsiella sp.

Clinical features include:

  • Fever with chills
  • Loin pain
  • Vomiting
  • Right-sided renal angle tenderness

Patients may develop acute respiratory distress syndrome due to endotoxin-mediated alveolar injury. Hemolysis can also occur due to endotoxins, leading to anemia.

Treatment includes intravenous fluids with antibiotics.

question: Which of the following statements is true about toxoplasmosis in pregnancy?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario points to a diagnosis of maternal toxoplasmosis. It is treated using spiramycin.

Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide is used when fetal infections are confirmed. It should be avoided in the first trimester.

Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii. Cats are definitive hosts. It can be transmitted to humans either by ingestion of raw or inadequately cooked infected meat or by ingestion of oocysts via exposure to cat litter or soil.

Acute infection is diagnosed either by the presence of IgG and IgM antibodies or by a four-fold increase in paired specimens 4 weeks apart.

question: A woman presents for a regular antenatal check-up at 12 weeks of gestation. She works at a rescue center that held an adoption drive for cats a few weeks ago. On examination, mild cervical lymphadenopathy is noted. Sabin-Feldman dye test is positive. Which of the following will be used to treat this condition?

explanationHtml:
Painful genital ulcers and painful inguinal lymphadenopathy are suggestive of herpes virus infection. The cytological image showing multinucleate giant cells and Tzanck cells confirms the diagnosis of HSV. The best step in the management of delivery in this patient is a cesarean section.

Herpes infection in the newborn may occur during birth, particularly if the mother has genital lesions due to HSV-2. In such cases, a cesarean section may prevent neonatal infection.
