explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hirsutism. The Ferriman-Gallwey score is used to clinically assess and quantify the degree of hirsutism.

Within this system, abnormal hair distribution is assessed at nine body areas and each of them scored from 0-4. Increasing numeric scores correspond to greater hair density within a given area. The maximum score is 36. The degree of hirsutism is mild if the score is ≥8. Moderate to severe hirsutism is present if the score is ≥15.

Note: Ferriman Gallwey score originally had 11 sites which were modified later to exclude 2 sites, viz., forearm, and legs.
question: A mother brought her 15-year-old daughter to the OPD with concerns of excessive growth of coarse hair over her face and chest. Which scoring system is used to clinically grade this condition?

explanationHtml:
The Rotterdam criteria is used to diagnose Stein-Levinthal syndrome or PCOS.

ESHRE/ASRM or Rotterdam criteria (2003):

Any two out of these three must be present-

  • Clinical/ Biochemical hyperandrogenism
  • Oligo/anovulation
  • Polycystic ovaries

Other criteria used for diagnosing PCOS:

  • National Institute of Health (NIH) criteria (1990)
    • To include both
      • Clinical/Biochemicalhyperandrogenism
      • Oligo/anovulation
  • Androgen excess and PCOS society(AE-PCOS) criteria:
    • To include both:
      • Clinical/Biochemicalhyperandrogenism
      • Oligo/anovulation/polycystic ovaries

Option A: Meig's syndrome refers to ascites and pleural effusions that accompany a benign ovarian tumor.

Option B: Asherman's syndrome refers to the formation of intrauterine synechiae, usually following endometrial destructive procedures like curettage or ablation.

Option C: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome is characterised by congenital absence of vagina, primary amenorrhoea, rudimentary cornua uteri and morphologically normal ovaries and Fallopian tubes situated on the pelvic sidewall.
question: Which of the following conditions is the Rotterdam criteria used to diagnose?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history and the necklace appearance on ultrasound are suggestive of polycystic ovarian disease.

The original Rotterdam consensus defined polycystic ovaries when ≥12 follicles were seen per ovary on USG. Each follicle should measure between 2 and 9 mm, and/or an ovarian volume should be >10 ml. Due to improvement in imaging modalities since that time, the threshold for follicle number has now been raised to 25 per ovary.
question: An adolescent girl was brought by her mother to the clinic with complaints of irregular periods and acne. A USG scan was performed which showed the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
PCOS is characterised by multiple small ovarian follicles, each less than 1 cm in size.

Sonographic findings seen in PCOS are:

  • ≥ 12 small follicles of 2 to 9 mm in diameter.
  • Increased ovarian volume (> 10 mL) or both.

A single ovary with these findings is sufficient to define PCOS. However, this criteria does not apply to women taking combined oral contraceptive pills.

Note: In settings with improved sonographic imaging resolution, a follicle number ≥ 20 cysts per ovary can be considered significant for PCOS.
question: A 26-year-old woman who presented with complaints of irregular cycles and weight gain was diagnosed with PCOS. This condition is characterised by multiple ovarian follicles that are less than _____ in size.

explanationHtml:
The hyperpigmented areas in the given image are acanthosis nigricans and this is associated with hyperinsulinemia. This skin condition is thought to be a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance.

Acanthosis nigricans is a velvety, darkening of the skin that usually occurs in the intertriginous areas. It has poorly defined borders, usually occurs in skin fold areas, such as the back of the neck, axilla, and groin, and may include thickening of the skin.

The pathogenesis of acanthosis nigricans is linked to growth factor levels and insulin-mediated activation of insulin-like growth factor (IGF) on keratinocytes and increased growth factor levels.

Acanthosis nigricans is usually seen in people younger than 40 years of age and is associated with the following disorders:

  • Obesity
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Acromegaly
  • Polycystic ovary disease
  • Insulin-resistant diabetes
  • Cushing’s disease
  • Addison’s disease
  • Gastrointestinal malignancies such as adenocarcinoma of the stomach or pancreas.

The treatment for acanthosis nigricans is directed towards the management of the underlying cause.
question: A 29-year-old lady presented to your clinics with lesions as shown in the below images. Which of the following is a false statement regarding her condition?

explanationHtml:
HAIR-AN syndrome is not characterized by mild hyperandrogenism but marked hyperandrogenism (HA). It also includes insulin resistance (IR) and acanthosis nigricans (AN).

HAIR-AN syndrome and ovarian hyperthecosis are exaggerated phenotypes of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Women affected by HAIR-AN syndrome often present with symptoms of severe hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne) and may occasionally display signs of virilization like clitoromegaly, temporal balding and voice deepening.

Ovarian hyperthecosis is a rare condition characterized by nests of luteinized theca cells distributed throughout the ovarian stroma.
question: A 25-year-old female patient presented with hirsutism. After further evaluation, a diagnosis of HAIR-AN syndrome was made. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
A depressed HDL level and elevated total cholesterol:HDL ratios are seen in patients with PCOS.

The following are associated with PCOS:

  • Insulin resistance
  • Impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Dyslipidemia: Increased LDL and triglyceride levels, elevated total cholesterol levels:HDL ratios.
  • Infertility/subfertility
  • A three-fold increased risk of endometrial cancer
  • Mild elevations in testosterone levels <200 ng/dL

Normal range of testosterone in women is 20-70 ng/dL. A mild elevation in testosterone is consistent with the diagnosis of PCOS. However, values > 200 ng/dL may suggest an ovarian tumour and warrant pelvic sonography.
question: A young lady being evaluated for infertility is diagnosed to have PCOS. Which of the following lab findings would you not expect to see in her?

explanationHtml:
The lesions shown in the image are acne. The drugs used to treat acne and hirsutism in a patient with PCOS are OCPs with cyproterone acetate.

The first step in the management of PCOS is weight reduction. OCPs are the drugs of choice for regularisation of cycles. They are also the drugs of choice for hirsutism and acne. OCPs used for PCOS should contain a 3rd/4th generation progestagen like cyproterone acetate. OCPs induce regular menstrual cycles, lower androgen levels and causes thinning of the endometrium.

Insulin sensitizers like metformin have been found to improve metabolic and gynecologic issues. It acts by reducing the insulin level and reducing hepatic production of glucose (liver neoglycolysis). Other benefits of metformin include improvement in fertility rate and reduction of the total and free testosterone levels. It also increases levels of sex hormone-binding globulin. Metformin is contraindicated in hepatic and renal disease.

Treatment of infertility associated with PCOS is done using ovulation-inducing drugs like letrozole and clomiphene citrate. If medical management fails, surgical options like laparoscopic ovarian drilling can be considered.

Note:

FOGSI, in 2024, has replaced Letrozole as the first-line drug for induction of ovulation in patients with PCOS. However, the FDA approval for the same is still pending.
question: A teenage girl who recently got diagnosed with PCOS presented with skin lesions on her forehead as shown in the image below. On examination, hirsutism was also noted. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe to this patient?

explanationHtml:
Clomiphene is an FDA approved drug used for the treatment of infertility associated with PCOS.

Clomiphene induces ovulation in 80% of the cases and 40–50% patients conceive. However, abortions are common due to luteal phase defects. Ovarian hyperstimulation occurs in <1% cases. Co-administration with dexamethasone leads to better outcomes. In resistant case, tamoxifen 20–40 mg daily for 5 days should be tried.

Currently, letrozole has proven to be more effective in ovarian infertility in obese women but its use in such cases is pending FDA approval.
question: A 31-year-old lady has been unable to conceive for the past 2 years in spite of regular intercourse. She has recently been diagnosed with PCOS. Which of the following is the FDA approved medication that you could recommend to her?

explanationHtml:
Surgical management is indicated in all the above conditions except for morbid obesity.

Indications of surgery in PCOS include:

  • Failed medical therapy
  • Ovarian hyperstimulation
  • Infertility
  • Previous pregnancy losses

Surgery comprises of laparoscopic drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. It is done using a laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores the endocrine milieu and improves fertility for a year or so. Thereafter, pelvic adhesions caused by surgery may again reduce the fertility rate. The formation of adhesions can be reduced by hydrofloatation.

The advantages of surgery are as follows:

  • Tubal testing with chromotubation can be performed simultaneously
  • Other causes of infertility like endometriosis can be looked for
  • One-time treatment
  • Intense and prolonged monitoring for side effects is not required
  • Cost-effective compared to IVF
  • Reduces androgen and LH production
  • Following surgery, single ovulation occurs with drugs, and hyperstimulation and multiple pregnancies are avoided
  • Ovulation occurs in 80–90% and pregnancy in 60–70%

The disadvantages of surgery are as follows:

  • It involves giving anaesthesia and performing an invasive procedure like laparoscopy
  • Adhesions may form postoperatively
  • If cautery is used, premature ovarian failure due to destruction of ovarian tissue may be seen
question: In a patient diagnosed with PCOS, which of the following is not an indication for surgical management?

explanationHtml:
The image showing enlarged ovaries with multiple large cysts along with the history of treatment for infertility with human menopausal gonadotropin suggests the diagnosis of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

Human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG) is a medication that is composed of FSH and LH. It is used to stimulate the release of ova in women who do not ovulate spontaneously. It can lead to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is a condition associated with ovarian enlargement due to exogenous gonadotropin therapy. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distention, ascites, gastrointestinal problems, respiratory compromise, oliguria, and thromboembolism. It can occur during ovulation induction or in early pregnancies conceived through exogenous ovarian stimulation.

Predisposing factors for OHSS include multi-follicular ovaries (such as in PCOS), young age, high estradiol levels during ovulation induction, and pregnancy.

Vasoactive substances produced by the corpus luteum, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiotensin II, are believed to contribute to enhanced capillary permeability, resulting in the loss of fluid, protein, and electrolytes into the peritoneal cavity and hemoconcentration.

Sonographic examination reveals enlarged ovaries with numerous follicular cysts and ascites.

Maintaining fluid balance with isotonic fluids like normal saline is crucial. Strategies to prevent OHSS during exogenous ovulation include reducing follicular stimulation (low FSH dose), coasting (withholding FSH administration one or more days prior to the hCG trigger), prophylactic volume expanders, and substituting hCG for FSH towards the end of ovarian stimulation.

Other options:

Option B: Theca lutein cysts are a rare form of follicular cysts characterized by luteinization and hypertrophy of the theca interna layer. Both ovaries are enlarged and cystic. This condition is commonly associated with gestational trophoblastic disease, multifetal gestation, and placentomegaly.

Option C: Polycystic ovarian syndrome shows 12 or more small follicles each 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally (necklace pattern) (shown below). The patient presents with menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, acne, etc.
question: A woman with a history of infertility is on treatment with human menopausal gonadotropin. She presented with the following finding in the USG. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. All patients with hyperprolactinemia present with galactorrhoea
explanationHtml:
All patients with hyperprolactinaemia do not present with galactorrhoea.

Galactorrhoea is the secretion of milky fluid from the nipple which is unrelated to childbirth. Prolactin is the most important hormone involved in the pathophysiology of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Majority of women (80%) with high prolactin levels present with galactorrhoea. However, some hyperprolactinemic women may not have this symptom.

Normal prolactin level is 25 ng/mL and levels more than this can cause galactorrhoea. Levels up to 100 ng/mL occur in hyperprolactinaemia but prolactin level over 100 ng/mL is seen in pituitary tumours.

Galactorrhoea is caused by pituitary adenoma and hyperprolactinemia. The condition is associated with amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea and infertility. The drug of choice for this condition is cabergoline.

options.text: Prolactin is the most important hormone involved in its pathophysiology
Prolactin levels more than 25 ng/ml cause this condition
All patients with hyperprolactinemia present with galactorrhoea
The drug of choice is Cabergoline

question: A 21-year-old nulliparous woman presented with galactorrhoea and breast engorgement. Which of the following is a false statement regarding this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Anencephaly is seen on accidental conception
explanationHtml:
Anencephaly is not seen in the case of accidental conception in a woman using the rhythm method. It occurs due to a deficiency of folic acid in the mother.

The calendar method or the rhythm method is one of the natural methods of contraception by fertility awareness. The couple is advised to avoid sexual intercourse around ovulation. Thus, it is very cost-effective, but it can only be used by educated couples.

According to this method, the safe period in a normal 28-day cycle is from the 1st day of the menstrual period to the 10th day and from the 18th to the 28th day. An alternate method is by calculating the risk period, i.e., 3 days before and 3 days after ovulation. Ovulation can also be estimated by changes in cervical mucus and basal body temperature.

Another method of calculating the safe period is the Knaus-Ogino method. The fertile period is estimated by subtracting 18 days from the shortest cycle and 10 days from the longest cycle. This method has a failure rate of ~25 pregnancies per 100 woman-years due to irregular ovulation or menstrual cycles.

options.text: Anencephaly is seen on accidental conception
It is a cost effective method
Safe period is determined using temperature or mucous method
Abstinence is required for 7-10 days in a month

question: Which of the following statements is false about the rhythm method?

explanationHtml:
Billing’s method of contraception refers to the cervical mucus method. It is also called ovulation method.

The properties of the cervical mucus change during the menstrual cycle. The female partner can predict the fertile period by examining her cervical mucus.

Under the influence of estrogen, the mucus increases in quantity and becomes more slippery and elastic i.e. wet days. This continues till it reaches a peak. After this, under the influence of progesterone, it becomes thicker, scanty i.e. dry days.

Abstinence is advised during the wet days till 4 days after the peak day. The safe period includes the dry days after menses till the appearance of mucus and from the 4th day after the peak day.

question: What does Billing's method of contraception refer to?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a female condom. It consists of a pouch made of polyurethane which is 17 cm in length with a flexible ring at each end. The inner ring at the closed end is smaller than the outer ring.

The inner ring is inserted at the apex of the vagina and the outer ring remains outside. It covers the cervix, the entire vagina, and external genitalia. Hence, it provides protection against HIV and STDs. It has a failure rate of 5–15 per 100 woman-years, which is higher than that of a male condom.

It can be fitted by the patient hours before intercourse, and easily removed soon after. It covers the cervix, vagina, and external genitalia and is protective against sexually transmitted diseases. It can also be worn in the puerperal period, unlike the cervical diaphragm.

The female condom should not be used along with a male condom because if worn together they may slip, tear, or become displaced.

question: Identify the contraceptive shown in the given image.

explanationHtml:
Today sponge contains 1 g of nonoxynol 9. It is a mushroom-shaped polyurethane disposable sponge that is 2 inches wide and 1.25 inches thick.

It is provided with a loop for easy removal. It should be placed high up in the vagina with the concave side covering the cervix. It can remain effective for 24 h. It can be used only once.

It acts as a mechanical barrier preventing the entry of sperms into the cervical canal, absorbs semen, and contains a spermicidal agent. The failure rate is 9-16 per 100 woman-years.
question: A nulliparous woman has been using Today sponge as a contraceptive. What does this contain?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a cervical diaphragm or Dutch cap. It can be used by women having multiple sex partners.

Contraindications of cervical diaphragm usage:

  • Prolapse, cystocele, rectocele - accurate fitting is not possible
  • Recurrent urinary tract infection
  • Allergy to rubber or spermicidal agent

It must be removed following intercourse as it can lead to toxic shock syndrome (TSS) if left in the vagina for a long period. TSS is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus infection.
question: Which of the following is not a contraindication for the use of the contraceptive shown below?

explanationHtml:
Nonoxynol-9 is one of the spermicidal agents which act by disruption of the sperm cell membrane.

Spermicidal agents are chemical contraceptives as they contain surfactants, such as nonoxynol-9, octoxynol, menfegol and enzyme-inhibiting agents. These are available as:

  • Foam tablets
  • Soluble pessaries
  • Creams
  • Jellies
  • Films

The spermicidal agent remains effective for 1–2 hours after the application. They are always used along with other contraceptives such as the diaphragm, cervical cap, and condom. When they are used alone, the failure rate is high i.e., 30 per 100 woman-years.

Chronic use of spermicides can cause vaginal irritation, abrasion, and ulceration. This increases the risk of HIV spread. Hence, spermicidal agents should not be recommended to HIV-positive couples.
question: You are prescribing nonoxynol-9 jelly to a woman using a cervical diaphragm for contraception. What is its mechanism of action?

correctAnswer: A. Lactic acid, Citric Acid, Potassium bitartrate
explanationHtml:
Phexxi is a vaginal gel that contains lactic acid, citric acid, and potassium bitartrate.

Phexxi is a vaginal pH regulator which is a non-hormonal contraceptive. It works by maintaining vaginal pH within the range of 3.5 to 4.5. This acidic environment is inhospitable for sperms.

Phexxi comes in pre-filled vaginal applicators. A single dose must be applied before vaginal intercourse. If more than one act of vaginal intercourse occurs within one hour, an additional dose must be applied.

options.text: Lactic acid, Citric Acid, Potassium bitartrate
Ascorbic acid, Citric acid, Calcium bitartrate
Lactic acid, Ascorbic acid, Potassium bitartrate
Ascorbic acid, Lactic acid, Calcium bitartrate.

question: A young woman who is using a cervical diaphragm asks for an alternative contraceptive. You suggest a recently launched contraceptive Phexxi. What is its composition?

explanationHtml:
Mala-N is a combined oral contraceptive containing 0.15 mg levonorgestrel (LNG) and 0.03 mg ethinyl estradiol. It is supplied free of cost through all PHC's, urban family welfare centers, etc.

All combined oral pills contain a mixture of ethinyl estradiol in a dose of 20-30 mcg and an orally active progestogen. Mala-D has the same composition as Mala-N but is available at a price of Rs 3/- per packet.

Combined oral pill works by suppressing pituitary hormones, FSH, and LH peak which prevents ovulation. At the same time, progestogen causes atrophic changes in the endometrium and prevents implantation.

Progestogen also acts on the cervical mucus making it thick and tenacious and impenetrable by sperms. It also interferes with tubal motility and alters tubal transport.

, so the fertilized egg reaches the uterine cavity before the endometrium is receptive for implantation.

These tablets are taken starting on the first day of the cycle for 21 days. A new course of tablets should be commenced 7 days after the cessation of the previous course. They should be taken at bedtime, preferably after a meal.
question: A newly married woman was prescribed Mala-N at a PHC. What is its composition?

explanationHtml:
Norgestimate is one of the 3rd generation progesterone agents. All OCPs have the disadvantage of increasing the risk of venous thrombosis.

Third-generation progesterone agents are less androgenic and so reduce the occurrence of acne and hirsutism. They also have a lower risk of metabolic and cardiovascular disorders compared to the previous generation progesterone agents.

Benefits of combined pills:

  • Effective contraceptive
  • Useful in menorrhagia and polymenorrhoea
  • Relieves dysmenorrhoea and premenstrual tension
  • Prevents anaemia by reducing the menstrual loss
  • Lower incidence of benign breast neoplasia (fibrocystic disease), functional ovarian cyst, ovarian and uterine malignancy
  • Reduced risk of PID - due to thick cervical mucus caused by progestogen, preventing the organisms from entering into the uterine cavity
  • Reduced incidence of ectopic pregnancy - due to suppression of ovulation and decreased risk of PID
  • Protects against rheumatoid arthritis
  • Reduces the risk of anorectal cancer
  • Useful in acne, PCOD, and endometriosis
question: Which of the following is not an advantage of norgestimate OCPs?

explanationHtml:
Thyroid disorders like hypothyroidism are not a contraindication for OCP usage.

Contraindications of OCPs:

  • Absolute contraindications -
    • Breast and genital cancers
    • Liver disease
    • History of thromboembolism
    • Cardiac abnormalities
    • Congenital hyperlipidemia
    • Undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding
  • Relative contraindications -
    • Age over 40 years, if smoker >35 years
    • Mild hypertension
    • Chronic renal disease
    • Epilepsy
    • Migraine
    • First 6 months of breastfeeding
    • Diabetes mellitus
    • Gallbladder disease
    • History of infrequent bleeding or amenorrhea
question: Which of the following is not a contraindication to the use of OCPs?

explanationHtml:
Sodium valproate is an inhibitor of CYP enzymes that are responsible for OCP metabolism. Thus, it does not lead to OCP failure.

Drugs leading to OCP failure are :

  • Rifampicin
  • Tetracyclines - interferes with enterohepatic circulation of estrogen
  • Phenytoin
  • Phenobarbitone
  • Antifungals
  • Cephalosporin
  • Ritonavir for HIV - interferes with absorption of OCP

Most of the anti-convulsants are enzyme inducers and hence increase the clearance of OCPs. This leads to OCP failure.
question: Which of the following drugs do not lead to failure of OCPs?

correctAnswer: C. Kills the sperms in the cervical canal
explanationHtml:
Minipills or progesterone-only pills (POP) do not kill sperm in the cervical canal. Progesterone-only pills act by thickening the cervical mucus (the main mechanism of all POPs except Cerazette) that inhibits the penetration of sperm, inhibiting tubal motility, and suppressing ovulation.

Other advantages of POPs include a reduction in the incidence of pelvic inflammatory diseases and sexually transmitted diseases (due to thickened cervical mucus).

History of ectopic pregnancy is not a contraindication for Progestogen-Only Pills (POPs) usage

While POPs decrease the absolute risk of all pregnancies, including ectopic pregnancies, by inhibiting tubal motility, the proportion of ectopic pregnancies is higher among the rare pregnancies that do occur while on POPs. This suggests an increased relative risk of ectopic pregnancy.

The action of POPs on clotting, lipid metabolism, or carbohydrate metabolism is minimal and does not affect them. So they can safely be used by women who are obese, breastfeeding, hypertensive, have SLE or a history of thromboembolism, diabetic with vascular disease. Significant adverse effects of POPs are irregular bleeding (mostly scanty) and secondary amenorrhea after long-term usage, as it causes endometrial atrophy.

Contraindications for POPs include undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, pregnancy, known or suspected breast cancer, and benign or malignant liver tumors.

options.text: Kills the sperms in the cervical canal

question: Which of the following is not the mechanism of action of progesterone only pills?

correctAnswer: A. 30 mg on day 1 of cycle
explanationHtml:
Centchroman is a non-hormonal oral contraceptive that is started at a dose of 30 mg on the first day of the menstrual cycle. It can be given to women with a family history of breast cancer where hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated.

Centchroman or ormeloxifene is a synthetic nonsteroidal contraceptive. Following the initial dose of 30 mg on the first day of menses, it is taken twice weekly for 12 weeks and weekly thereafter. It prevents implantation through endometrial changes. The return of fertility occurs within 6 months of stopping the drug.

It can also be used as a postcoital pill, given in 60 mg dose within 24 hours of coitus. It has a failure rate of 1.83 per 100 woman years. It does not provide protection against HIV and other STDs.

Side effects of centchroman:

  • Headache, nausea, vomiting
  • Weight gain
  • Delay in return of fertility (up to 6 months)
  • Atypical endometrial hyperplasia - prolonged use

Contraindications of centchroman:

  • PCOD
  • Hepatic dysfunction
  • Cervical dysplasia
  • Allergy to the drug

This drug has been developed by Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow. It has been released in India under the name of Chhaya (previously called Saheli) under the National Family Planning Programme.
question: A patient has come to your clinic for contraceptive advice. As she has a family history of breast cancer, you suggest a non-hormonal oral contraceptive to her. What is the initial dose of this drug?

explanationHtml:
The most effective reversible method of contraception among the given options is Norplant, which is a subdermal hormonal implant.

The most effective method of contraception overall is sterilization, which is one of the permanent methods. Both methods belong to the first-tier category of contraceptives.

There are 2 types of subdermal implants:

  • Implanon (which has replaced Norplant I)
  • Norplant II

The implants work by inhibition of ovulation, endometrial atrophy, and thickening of cervical mucus. Implanon contains desogestrel and also reduces acne and osteoporosis.

The implants are inserted on the first day of the menstrual cycle, within 5 days of abortion, and 3 weeks after the delivery. The woman needs to use barrier contraception or abstain in the first 7 days of insertion.

The image below shows an implanon:

Advantages of implants:

  • Long-acting with sustained effect
  • Good compliance
  • Coital-independent with no nuisance of daily oral or frequent injections
  • Failure rate - 0.2 and 1.3 per 100 woman-years
  • Implanon reduces acne and osteoporosis.

Disadvantages of implants:

  • Breakthrough bleeding
  • Irregular cycles
  • Amenorrhoea
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Local infection
  • Requires insertion and removal with nonbiodegradable capsules
  • Expensive.
question: Which of the following is the most effective reversible method of contraception?

correctAnswer: D. Formation of cervical mucus plug
explanationHtml:
The given image shows Multiload Cu250, which is one of the copper containing IUCDs. Formation of cervical mucus plug is not one of its mechanisms of action. However, progesterone-containing IUCDs can alter the cervical mucus along with the local effects.

The various mechanisms of action of a copper-containing IUCD are:

  • Interference with the migration of spermatozoa
  • Foreign body reaction releasing prostaglandins - provokes uterine contractility and increases the tubal peristalsis which interferes with implantation
  • Leucocytic infiltration in the endometrium - macrophages engulf the fertilized egg if it enters the endometrial tissue
  • Enzymatic and metabolic changes in the endometrial tissue which interferes with implantation of the fertilized ovum

Some IUCDs like CuT-380A are effective for up to 10 years.

They are a good choice of method of contraception for the following groups of women:

  • Having low risk of STD
  • Multiparous woman
  • Having a monogamous relationship
  • Wanting long-term reversible method of contraception
  • Unreliable users of oral contraception or barrier contraception

IUCDs are avoided in unmarried and nulliparous patients because of the risk of PID and subsequent tubal infertility. Copper IUCDs can also be used as emergency contraception following intercourse.
question: Which of the following is not a mechanism of action of the device given in the image below?

explanationHtml:
IUCDs can be used in HIV-affected women.

Intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUCDs) provide long-term contraception by preventing fertilization.

Contraindications for IUCD insertion:

  • Suspected pregnancy
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
  • Lower genital tract infection
  • Presence of fibroids
  • Severe anaemia
  • Uncontrolled diabetes - due to increased pelvic infection
  • Scarred uterus eg, post caesarean section
  • Septate uterus
  • Menorrhagia and dysmenorrhoea - if Copper T is used
  • Breast cancer - if LNG IUCD is used

Complications of IUCD usage:

  • Immediate -
    • Vasovagal attack
    • Uterine cramps
  • Early -
    • Expulsion of IUCD
    • Perforation of uterus
    • Spotting, menorrhagia
    • Dysmenorrhoea
    • Vaginal infection
    • Actinomycosis
  • Late -
    • PID
    • Ectopic pregnancy
    • Perforation of uterus
    • Menorrhagia
    • Dysmenorrhoea

The failure rate of IUCD is 1–3 per 100 woman-years.

Levonorgestrel IUCD also causes hormonal adverse effects such as headache, acne, breast tenderness, and functional ovarian cysts. Amenorrhoea occurs in 35% of women after 2 years of use.
question: IUCD insertion is being considered in a multiparous woman who wants long-term contraception. This method of contraception is absolutely contraindicated in all of the following except _______.

explanationHtml:
Nova-T contains both copper and silver. The addition of the silver increases its effective lifespan.

In copper-carrying devices, copper wire is wrapped around the vertical stem of a polypropylene frame. Some of them have copper wire wrapped around the arms too. Based on the surface area, they are of various types:

  • Copper T 380 A
  • Multiload copper 250
  • Copper T 200
  • Copper 7
  • Copper T 220
  • Nova-T

They are effective for 3–5 years. It is estimated that about 50 mcg of copper is eluted daily in the uterus. Copper T 380A, known as Paraguard, has a lifespan of 10 years. Nova T has a lifespan of 5 years.
question: You are inserting Nova-T in a patient for spacing of births. This device contains______.

explanationHtml:
Progestasert releases 65 μg of progesterone/day.

Progestasert is a T-shaped device carrying 38 mg of progesterone in a silicon oil reservoir in the vertical stem. The progesterone released causes the formation of a thick plug of mucus at the cervical os. This prevents entry of the sperms in addition to the local contraceptive effect of IUCDs.

There is lesser incidence of menstrual problems like menorrhagia and dysmenorrhoea compared to copper-containing intrauterine devices. However, it is expensive and requires yearly replacement.
question: A nursing mother was prescribed progestasert for contraception. How much progesterone is released by this device?

explanationHtml:
Copper IUCDs increase the risk of PID.

OCPs, Mirena and DMPA injectables contain progesterone which causes thickening of the cervical mucus and decreases the motility of the female genital tract. Thus, they reduce the risk of PID by preventing the ascent of bacteria from the vagina.
question: Which of the following increases the risk of pelvic inflammatory disease?

explanationHtml:
IUCDs are the most effective mode of contraception for women with heart diseases. IUCDs are safe in these patients and come under the first-tier contraceptive methods.

Condoms are not contraindicated in heart disease patients but they are third-tier contraceptives. Hence, they are not as effective as IUCDs.

OCPs and hormonal implants are contraindicated in patients with heart diseases as the constituent hormones can cause thromboembolic disorders.
question: What is the most effective mode of contraception for a woman with heart disease?

explanationHtml:
Essure permanent device is a method of hysteroscopic sterilization. Pomeroy, Parkland, and Irving procedures are methods for tubal ligation via an abdominal approach.

Essure device consists of a micro-inserter with a flexible inner coil made of stainless steel and a dynamic outer coil made of nickel titanium alloy (nitinol).

This device is inserted into the fallopian tube by hysteroscopy. It acts by benign local fibrous tissue growth leading to occlusion of the tube. The failure rate is 3.5%.

Its advantages are that there is no abdominal scar and the procedure can be done under local anaesthesia.

Disadvantages of Essure:

  • Hysteroscopy required for the procedure and to confirm the blockage
  • Expensive procedure
  • Expertise required
  • Irreversible - tuboplasty for reversal not possible
  • 3 months waiting time to ensure sterility - HSG must be done after 3 months to confirm tubal blockage
  • Bilateral insertion difficult due to spasm
  • Can cause perforation of the tube
question: Which of the following techniques of permanent contraception does not require an abdominal incision?

explanationHtml:
Isthmus of the fallopian tube is ligated in Pomeroy technique. It is the most popular technique of tubal ligation.

Midline, paramedian or transverse abdominal incision is made 2 inches above the pubic symphysis (1 inch in puerperal sterilisation). The fallopian tube is identified, made into a loop and tied at the base. The loop is then excised.

The operation is simple and requires a short period of hospitalization. The failure rate is only 0.4% and it is mainly due to spontaneous canalization. It is surgically reversible.

The below image shows Pomeroy’s method of tubal ligation.
question: A woman has come to your clinic for a checkup following tubal ligation by Pomeroy technique. Which portion of the tube is ligated in this technique?

explanationHtml:
Fimbriectomy is also known as Kroener's procedure. This procedure involves ligation of the distal ampulla of the tube with two permanent sutures. Then, resection of the infundibulum of the tube is done.

Some more techniques of permanent sterilization include:

Pomeroy method - The fallopian tube is identified on each side, brought out through the incision. The middle portion is formed into a loop which is tied at the base with catgut and excised. This is the most commonly used technique.

Uchida's method - The tubal serosa is stripped off the muscular layer in the midsegment of the tube. The muscle layer is excised. The proximal end is ligated and buried in the broad ligament. This minimal excision of the tube preserves the potential for tuboplasty.

Irving's procedure - The mid-portion of the tube is ligated and the intervening portion is excised. The proximal end is buried in the myometrium and the distal end is buried in the broad ligament. It is a reliable method but irreversible and may require a laparotomy incision.

Madlener's procedure - A loop of the fallopian tube is crushed and then ligated with a nonabsorbable suture.

This procedure is done under local anaesthesia. A small incision is made in the scrotum. The vas deferens are divided on both sides which disrupts the passage of sperms.

Side effects are headaches and mood changes. It is contraindicated in women with severe hepatic dysfunction and severe asthma.

question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for bacterial vaginosis?

Vaginal itching is not seen in bacterial vaginosis. It is a symptom of Trichomonas vaginitis.

About half of the women having bacterial vaginosis are asymptomatic. Symptomatic women mostly present with a profuse, fishy vaginal discharge. It does not cause pruritus, dysuria, and dyspareunia.

question: A 30-year old woman presents to your OPD with complaints of foul-smelling vaginal discharge for the past 2 weeks. On examination, the discharge is adherent to the vaginal mucosa and has a fishy odour. What is the most likely cause?

An abundance of polymorphs is not a microscopic finding of bacterial vaginosis because it is not an inflammatory condition. It occurs due to an alteration in the normal vaginal flora.

A swab of the discharge is taken from the vaginal wall and a smear is prepared. The microscopic evaluation is done using a gram stained smear. In bacterial vaginosis, this would reveal a clean background with an abundance of gram variable coccobacilli adhering to the epithelial cells. These are called clue cells. A few inflammatory cells, other pathogenic organisms, and a reduced number of Lactobacilli would also be seen.

question: Given below is the image of a smear prepared from the vaginal discharge of a patient. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of bacterial vaginosis which is confirmed by using Amsel’s criteria.

3 out of 4 of the following criteria are needed, to make a positive diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis:

  1. A nonviscous, white discharge that covers the vaginal mucosa
  2. A vaginal pH > 4.5.
  3. A positive whiff test - When 10% KOH is added to vaginal secretions, volatile amines are released which have a fishy odour.
  4. The presence of >20% clue cells on saline wet mount. These are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent coccobacilli at the edge of the cell.

Option A: Boer-Miesel's criteria is used for the prognostic evaluation of pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option B: Light's criteria is used for determining the nature of the pleural fluid i.e., transudate or exudate, in the diagnosis of pleural effusion.

Option D: Nugent's criteria can also be used for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis. However, it is not the best confirmatory method.
question: A woman comes to the clinic with complaints of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. On examination, the discharge was profuse and had a fishy odour. Which of the following is the best criteria to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Nugent's criteria is used to evaluate three types of bacteria in a case of suspected bacterial vaginosis: Mobiluncus, Lactobacillus, and Gardnerella/Bacteroides. Bacteria are graded through gram stain of vaginal samples.

They are each graded on a scale of 1+ to 4+ where:

  • 1+ is < 1 cell per field
  • 2+ is 1-5 cells per field
  • 3+ is 6-30 cells per field
  • 4+ is >30 cells per field

Lactobacillus and Bacteroides/Gardnerella are given scores between 0-4, but Mobiluncus is graded only from 0-2. The total scores are then calculated and interpreted as follows:

  • 0-3 - Normal
  • 4-6 - Intermediate bacterial count
  • 7-10 - Bacterial vaginosis
question: In a patient with suspected bacterial vaginosis, Nugent's criteria is used to quantify the following bacteria except....

HPV causes structural changes in the epithelial cells of the skin called koilocytes, and their presence is characteristic of HPV infection. The koilocytes have large hyperchromatic nuclei and a perinuclear halo, as shown below.

The diagnosis is made by colposcopic studies. The lesions on the vulva are stained by toluidine blue. The abnormal areas of the skin retain the blue dye. These areas are then biopsied for histopathological examination.

It has the following three stages of infection:

Stage of LGV Characteristic features
Primary stage
  • Painless genital ulcer
  • Papules
  • Lymphangitis
Secondary stage
  • Painful unilateral/bilateral lymphadenopathy

Late stage

Chlamydia trachomatis is a gram-negative obligate intracellular bacteria that appears as an intracytoplasmic inclusion body. The gram stain of the cervical smear would show leucocytes but no organisms. Hence, selective culture media like the McCoy cells culture are used to isolate the organism.

Stage of LGV Characteristic features

question: A sexually active man presents with complaints of painful swelling over the inguinal region. He also gives a history of a painless genital ulcer that resolved spontaneously. On examination,  groove sign is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?

question: A 20-year-old female sex worker presents with complaints of constipation and blood in stools for 3 months. On DRE, a circumferential constriction is felt beyond which the finger cannot be advanced. Which of the following is a probable cause for this complication?

explanationHtml:
The causative agent for granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) is Calymmatobacterium granulomatis. It is now called Klebsiella granulomatis and is a gram-negative bacillus causing chronic ulcerative infection of the vulva.

It is highly contagious and transmitted through repeated sexual or non-sexual contact. The incubation period is 1-12 weeks.

Clinical features:

It begins as a painless nodule which later ulcerates to form multiple beefy red painless ulcers that tend to coalesce; the vulva is progressively destroyed, and minimal adenopathy may occur.

Diagnosis:

Microscopic examination of smears from the lesion/ biopsy specimens reveals pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies and clusters of bacteria with a bipolar (safety pin) appearance. Blue-black stained organisms are seen in the cytoplasm of mononuclear cells.

Management:

Azithromycin 1 g orally once per week or 500 mg daily for at least 3 weeks and until all lesions have completely healed.

question: What is the causative agent for granuloma inguinale?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of granuloma inguinale which is caused by a gram-negative bacteria, Klebsiella granulomatis.

Granuloma inguinale begins as a painless nodule that later ulcerates to form multiple beefy red painless ulcers. These ulcers tend to coalesce and bleed easily on contact. If secondarily infected, they may become painful. The ulcers heal by fibrosis, which can result in scarring resembling keloids.

The lymph nodes are usually uninvolved but can become enlarged. New lesions can appear along the lymphatic drainage channels.

The microscopic image below shows the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies. It also shows clusters of gram-negative bacteria with a bipolar/safety-pin appearance.
question: A 19-year-old girl presented with multiple beefy-red ulcers over the labia. Microscopic examination of smear from the lesion showed intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies and gram-negative bacteria having a safety pin appearance. What is your likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The organism seen in the given image of a Pap smear is the Doderlien’s bacillus, also known as Lactobacillus. This is a gram-positive, rod-shaped bacillus that grows in anaerobic conditions.

It is a part of the normal vaginal flora that is responsible for the vaginal defence mechanism.

It is an estrogen-dependent bacillus and appears at puberty and disappears after menopause.

It converts glycogen into lactic acid and maintains the acidic ph in the vagina. This prevents the growth of pathogenic bacteria in the vagina. Its absence causes a condition called bacterial vaginosis where pathogenic organisms replaces the normal flora of the vagina. In this condition, clue cells are visible.

Option B: Gardnerella vaginalis is the most common organism involved in bacterial vaginosis. As the patient in the given question is healthy, this is not the correct option.

Option C: Trichomonas vaginalis is flagellated protozoa that causes trichomonas vaginitis. The organism and the nucleus of epithelial cells appear equal in size on the pap smear. This criterion is used for the identification of trichomonas as flagella are not visible on a pap smear.

Option D: Frisch bacillus is another name for Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It is not seen on Pap smears.

Pregnancy is not a risk factor for PID. Instead, it plays a protective role in this condition.

The risk factors for developing PID are:

  • Having multiple sex partners
  • Previous history of PID

The protective factors for PID are:

question: All of the following are risk factors for PID except______.

explanationHtml:
Cervicitis is not included in pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

Pelvic inflammatory disease is a spectrum of infection and inflammation of the upper genital tract, typically causing:

  • Endometritis
  • Salpingitis
  • Oophoritis
  • Peritonitis

The minimum criteria for diagnosis of PID are:

Pain in the lower abdomen + any one of the following:

  • Uterine tenderness
  • Cervical motion tenderness
  • Adnexal tenderness

Cervicitis and vaginitis are lower genital tract infections.
question: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease. Which of the following is not included in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The most common symptom of acute PID is bilateral lower abdominal pain.

The pain is severe in acute stages and it may or may not be accompanied by a high temperature ( >38.3 degrees C). It may be followed by vomiting.

Some patients with PID can present with pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. This is seen in Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome which is a form of perihepatitis.

If PID occurs due to sexually transmitted organisms, dysuria and vaginal discharge may be seen.

options.text: Pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen

question: What is the most common symptom seen in acute PID?

explanationHtml:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of PID.

PID is an infection of the upper genital tract. It is generally transmitted sexually as an ascending infection along with sperms. It is usually a polymicrobial infection,

Organisms causing PID include:

Sexually transmitted:

  • Chlamydia (most common)
  • Gonococcus
  • Mycoplasma
  • Trichomonas

Pyogenic Aerobes:

Other:

question: A 42-year-old woman presented to the emergency room with abdominal pain and fever for the last 48 hours. She has been using a Cu T 380A for contraception for the past 8 years. On examination, cervical motion tenderness was present. What is the most likely organism to have caused her condition?

explanationHtml:
The mechanism of the spread of gonococci to the tubes in pelvic inflammatory disease is mucosal.

Gonococci ascend to the tubes mainly through mucosal continuity. This is facilitated by sexually transmitted vectors such as sperms and Trichomonas.

The mucous membranes of the fallopian tubes are affected first. They become edematous and are infiltrated with leukocytes and plasma cells. Another route of spread is through the reflux of mucosal blood.

Option A: Hematogenous spread is seen in genital tuberculosis.

Option B: Lymphatics are involved in the spread of secondary organisms and in PID following post-abortal and puerperal infection.

Option C: Parametrium facilitates the spread of Mycoplasma. The gut flora can directly spread to tubes.
question: What is the mechanism of the spread of gonococci to the tubes in pelvic inflammatory disease?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, chlamydial infection causes the most amount of damage to the mucosa and the wall of the fallopian tubes leading to fibrosis and tubal blockage.

Chlamydial infection can remain asymptomatic in the endo-cervix whereas gonococcal infection is more symptomatic and therefore the chlamydial infection usually goes unnoticed and untreated whereas gonococcal infection gets diagnosed early. Thus, chlamydial infections can lead to more damage and complications.

Mycoplasma and Mobiluncus generally cause lower genital tract infections like cervicitis and vaginitis.

question: Which of the following is not a differential diagnosis of acute PID?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario of development of a chronic tubo-ovarian mass following acute PID points towards a diagnosis of chronic PID. A chronic tubo-ovarian mass can manifest as a tubo-ovarian cyst, hydrosalpinx or even a chronic pyosalpinx.

Failure to complete treatment of acute PID or drug resistance can lead to the development of chronic PID. This can lead to the development of chronic tubo-ovarian masses which may manifest as:

  • Hydrosalpinx
  • Chronic pyosalpinx
  • Chronic interstitial salpingitis
  • Tubo-ovarian cyst
  • Tuberculous form

A twisted ovarian cyst and a ruptured endometriotic cyst are differential diagnoses of acute PID.

The above image depicts a hydrosalpinx. Its wall is not opaque but translucent.

explanationHtml:
The image shows the laparoscopic finding of violin string adhesions that are characteristic of Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome. It is a form of perihepatitis that occurs in the setting of PID.

It is characterized by right upper quadrant pain with a pleuritic component, sometimes referred to the right shoulder. It rarely occurs in women with acute PID. The pathological mechanism is as follows:

Gonococcal / Chlamydial infection → transperitoneal/vascular spread → inflammation of the liver capsule and peritoneal surfaces → adhesions and fibrosis in the perihepatic region → Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome

Cholecystitis and ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess are the differential diagnoses of Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome. Violin string adhesions would not be seen in these conditions.
question: In a patient with PID, laparoscopy shows the following appearance. What is true about the syndrome this patient likely has?

correctAnswer: A. Dysmenorrhea is a common presentation
explanationHtml:
Dysmenorrhea rarely occurs in PID. Pain is uncommon and is a result of subacute PID.

Silent PID is thought to follow multiple or continuous low-grade infections in asymptomatic women. It is not a clinical diagnosis. Rather, it is an ultimate diagnosis given to women with tubal-factor infertility who lack a history of upper genital tract infection.

On laparoscopy or laparotomy, these women may have evidence of prior tubal infection such as adhesions, but for the most part, the fallopian tubes are grossly normal. They can have ectopic pregnancies due to tubal dysmotility. Silent PID can occur following infection with M. tuberculosis.

question: Identify the wrong statement with respect to silent PID.

correctAnswer: A. Administration of cefotetan 2 g IV 12 hourly + doxycycline 100 mg IV BD
explanationHtml:
Administration of cefotetan 2 g IV 12hourly + doxycycline 100 mg BD orally/ IV for 48 hours forms the crux of the treatment regimen for PID. This is followed by oral doxycycline 100 mg +/-metronidazole 400 mg for 14 days in all hospitalized patients having PID.

Treatment of PID in hospitalized patients:

  • Cefotetan 2 g IV 12hourly + doxycycline 100 mg BD orally/ IV for 48 hours is given followed by oral doxycycline 100 mg +/- metronidazole 400 mg for 14 days
  • Cefoxitin 2 g IV 6hourly + doxycycline 100 mg IV followed by oral route.
  • Azithromycin 500 mg IV 6 hourly for 2 days, then orally for Chlamydia.

Outpatient treatment of PID (according to the current RCOG guidelines):

  • A single dose of IM ceftriaxone 250 mg followed by oral doxycycline 100 mg BD +/- metronidazole 400 mg BD x 14 days
  • A single dose of IM ceftriaxone 250 mg followed by azithromycin 1 gm per week x 2 weeks.

IUD is not removed in a woman who responds to antibiotics. It is removed only in case of a failed antibiotic response. Barrier contraceptives and OCPs are recommended only in women unresponsive to antibiotics.

The use of Placentrex (aqueous extract of the placenta) is outdated and is not recommended currently.

question: A 30-year-old female presents to the OPD with fever, lower abdominal pain and purulent vaginal discharge. On examination, her vitals are stable and per vaginal examination reveals lower abdominal and cervical motion tenderness. What is the best treatment option for her?

explanationHtml:
Intestinal obstruction would be an indication for surgery in a patient diagnosed with PID.

Criteria for surgery in PID include:

    1. Drainage of pelvic abscess by colpotomy.
    2. Dilatation and evacuation of septic products of conception or for haemorrhage in the postabortal period.
    3. Acute spreading peritonitis resistant to a full course of chemotherapy. Presence of pyoperitoneum mandates laparotomy.
    4. Intestinal obstruction
    5. Suspected intestinal injury as diagnosed in criminal abortion.
    6. Ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess

A tubo-ovarian abscess of 2 cm is not an indication for surgery. Minimally invasive surgery is done in a tubo-ovarian abscess measuring more than 10 cm, that fails to respond to antibiotics in 48-72 hours.

Peritonitis and sepsis are not an indication for surgery. They should be managed medically first. If they do not respond to antibiotic treatment then surgical management should be done.
question: Which of the following would be an indication for surgery in a 30-year-old woman diagnosed with PID?

correctAnswer: C. The abscess fails to respond to antibiotics in 48 - 72 h
explanationHtml:
If the abscess fails to respond to antibiotics in 48–72 h, minimally invasive surgery is indicated.

Criteria for minimally invasive surgery in PID:

  • The size of the abscess is more than 10 cm
  • The abscess fails to respond to antibiotics in 48-72 hours
  • The abscess ruptures
  • Pyoperitoneum

Minimal invasive surgery includes laparoscopic drainage of the tubo ovarian abscess or posterior colpotomy.

explanationHtml:
The treatment of choice for an old multiparous woman with chronic PID is abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A radical hysterectomy involves the removal of the whole uterus, tissue from the sides of the uterus, the cervix, and the upper part of the vagina. It is generally done only in cancer patients.

A supracervical hysterectomy involves the removal of only the body of the uterus and is not done in chronic PID. It is done for the treatment of endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and uterine prolapse.

Boer-Meisel has described the prognostic evaluation for PID. It depends upon the following:

  2. Nature of adhesions such as flimsy or dense.
  3. Size of hydrosalpinx
  4. Macroscopic condition of hydrosalpinx.
  5. The thickness of the tubal wall.

Boer-Meisel system is specifically used for predicting pregnancy outcomes in patients treated for PID.

Stages of PID

question: Who has described the prognostic evaluation for PID?

explanationHtml:
Long-standing pelvic inflammation may lead to pyometra. This refers to the collection of pus in the uterine cavity.

The initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, skene glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. Unilateral pain and swelling over the labia may be caused by the inflammation of the Bartholin glands.

Depending on the extent of tissue involved, PID can be classified into five stages

  • Stage I - Acute salpingitis without peritonitis - No adhesions
  • Stage II - Acute salpingitis with peritonitis - purulent discharge
  • Stage III - Acute salpingitis with superimposed tubal occlusion or tubo ovarian complex
  • Stage IV - Ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess
  • Stage V - Tubercular salpingitis

Long-standing pelvic inflammation may also lead to:

  • Dyspareunia
  • Infertility
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Formation of adhesions like hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess
  • Chronic pelvic pain

Note: Chronic pelvic inflammation leads to dense adhesions between the uterus and the appendages. Thus, it becomes difficult to define the uterus from the pelvic masses. They form a hard mass which is called the frozen pelvis.

The most common cause of the spread of PID: Ascending infection along with sperms
The only PID that does not spread with the sexual route is genital TB. It has a hematogenous spread.

question: Which of the following is the most common site for genital tuberculosis?

explanationHtml:
Endometrial tuberculosis is most commonly acquired by direct spread from the fallopian tubes. Hematogenous spread is thought to be the process by which the tubercle bacilli implant into the mucosa of the fallopian tubes and subsequently affect the endometrium by direct extension.

Female genital tuberculosis is an important cause of significant morbidity, short and long-term sequelae especially infertility. Genital tuberculosis usually occurs secondary to pulmonary (commonest) or extrapulmonary TB like gastrointestinal, renal, skeletal, and miliary TB. However, primary genital TB can rarely occur in women whose male partners have active genitourinary TB (e.g., tuberculosis epididymitis) by transmission through infected semen

Most common site involved in secondary genital TB is fallopian tube (90-100%) >endometrium (50-80%) >ovaries (20-30%) >cervix 5-15%) >vulva. The most common symptom of genital TB is infertility.

Causes of infertility in genital TB:

  • Tubal blockage
  • If tubes are patent, then also infertility occurs due to loss of tubal function.
  • Tubercular endometritis causes uterine scarring resulting in the destruction of the endometrium.
  • Ovarian damage with poor ovarian reserve and volume

A laparoscopy and dye hydrotubation (lap and dye test) is the most reliable tool to diagnose genital TB, especially for tubal, ovarian and peritoneal disease. The test can be combined with hysteroscopy.

Multiple drug therapy ( ATT regimen provided by DOTS) in adequate doses and for sufficient duration is the mainstay in the treatment of TB including genital tuberculosis.
question: What is the most common mode of transmission of tuberculosis to the endometrium?

correctAnswer: D. It commonly presents as a unilateral condition
explanationHtml:
Genital tuberculosis is a bilateral condition.

It can be caused by both Mycobacterium tuberculosis (95% cases) and Mycobacterium bovis (5% cases). It almost always occurs secondary to a primary focus elsewhere in the body. The most common primary focus is lungs > lymph nodes > abdomen > generalised miliary infection.

It mostly spreads hematogenously. Lymphatic spread is also seen sometimes. It can rarely spread by direct contact with the affected intraabdominal organs or peritoneum.

The fallopian tubes are the first to be affected. The disease subsequently spreads to other genital organs and the peritoneum. This is followed by the involvement of bilateral pelvic lymph nodes. Vulvovaginal involvement is usually secondary to uterine involvement.

The most common presentation of genital tuberculosis in the reproductive age group is infertility.

options.text: The causative agent is Mycobacterium bovis
It generally occurs secondary to a primary focus
It commonly presents as a unilateral condition

question: A young woman with fertility issues is diagnosed to have genital tuberculosis. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

explanationHtml:
The most common presentation of genital tuberculosis in the reproductive age group is infertility.

Genital tuberculosis mostly presents in young women in the reproductive age group. It can present as:

  • Infertility is the only complaint in 35-60 % of cases. Of these, 75% of women present with primary infertility.
  • Menstrual abnormalities are seen in 10-40% of cases.
  • Asymptomatic in 10% of cases.
  • Other symptoms like fever and malaise can be seen.

The treatment of infertility in women with genital TB depends on the condition of the endometrium. If the endometrium is receptive and the uterus is normal, then assisted reproductive techniques such as in-vitro fertilisation can be tried. If the endometrium is unfavourable then surrogacy may be considered.
question: What is the most common presenting symptom of genital tuberculosis in the reproductive age group?

correctAnswer: D. The fimbriae are commonly involved in advanced tuberculous salpingitis
explanationHtml:
The fimbriae are often spared even in advanced forms of tubercular salpingitis.

The involvement of fallopian tubes is 100% and bilateral, secondary to hematogenous spread. The ampullary part of the tube appears dilated with the fimbrial end open and pouting. This gives the characteristic tobacco-pouch appearance as seen in the image below.

The external surface of the tubes are enlarged, roughened, and may show the presence of greyish tubercles. The cut section shows yellowish-grey caseous matter in the lumen. Sometimes, serosanguinous fluid can also be seen in the lumen of the fallopian tube. This is called tuberculous hematosalpinx.

On histopathological examination of the tubes, granulomas and chronic inflammatory infiltrate with hyperplasia is seen. This could be mistaken for malignancy as it also produces a similar histological image.

The ampulla of the tube appears dilated with the fimbrial end open and pouting

Genital tuberculosis:

It is caused by M. tuberculosis and almost always occurs secondary to primary infection elsewhere in the extragenital states. The sites and frequency of involvement are as follows:

  • Fallopian tubes (90-100%)
  • Endometrium (50-60%)

  • Cervix (5-15%)

Presentation is variable and it can be asymptomatic in 10-20% of cases, infertility, menstrual irregularities, abdominal pain and mass, vaginal discharge, fistula formation, ectopic pregnancy and ascites. The mass is made up of rolled-up omentum that is adherent to the uterus and adnexa.

Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weakness, anorexia or night sweats may be present.

Investigations:

  • CBC, ESR and Mantoux test
  • Hysterosalpingography shows a lead-pipe appearance of the fallopian tube, calcification of the tube, beading and variation in the filling, cornual block, jagged fluffiness of tubal outline and tobacco pouch appearance of hydrosalpinx and pyosalpinx.
  • Laparoscopy establishes the diagnosis of genital TB. It shows tuberculous lesions and perihepatic adhesions (if present).

Differential diagnosis:

  • Ovarian cyst, broad ligament cyst or encysted fluid
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Carcinoma cervix
  • Elephantiasis of the vulva
  • Pregnancy
  • Puberty menorrhagia and postmenopausal bleeding
  • Fungal infection and sarcoidosis

Management:

It is treated with anti-tubercular therapy for 6 months (DOT strategy):

First 2 months

Next 4 months

  • Rifampicin 450-600 mg
  • Pyrazinamide 30 mg/body weight
  • Ethambutol 30 mg/ kg body weight

3 times a week.

Indications and contraindications for surgery:

Indications Contraindications
  • Unresponsiveness of the disease in spite of adequate antitubercular chemotherapy.
  • Tubercular pyosalpinx, ovarian abscess or pyometra.
  • Persistent menorrhagia and/or chronic pelvic pain causing deteriorating health status
  • Presence of active tuberculosis in extragenital site
  • Favorable response to antimicrobial therapy with the diminishing size of the pelvic mass
  • The accidental discovery of tubercular tubo-ovarian mass on laparotomy in a young patient.

Types of surgery include vulvectomy (if vulval hypertrophy is present), removal of the adnexal mass, drainage of pyometra and fistula repair.

TAH+BSO is rarely required nowadays. Tuboplasty is contraindicated.

Option B: Ovarian tumors usually don't affect menstrual cycles. Though virilizing tumors can cause amenorrhoea, other features of virilization such as hirsutism, flattening of breasts, and enlargement of the clitoris are generally present.

Option C: Though ectopic pregnancy may be suspected here, the tube is likely to rupture with exacerbation of pain, bleeding, and peritonitis before six months of gestation. Additionally, the absence of vaginal bleeding/spotting, and the presence of weight loss makes the diagnosis unlikely.

question: An 18-year-old girl presents with a history of low-grade fever, weight loss, abdominal pain and amenorrhoea for six months. On examination, a pelvic mass is felt on the left side and signs of ascites are positive. What is your diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. The Quantiferon test is positive and indicates latent tuberculosis.
explanationHtml:
The Quantiferon test will be positive in patients having genital TB. It is an indicator of latent tuberculosis. The Quantiferon test measures the release of interferon-gamma by T cells following stimulation by antigens unique to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A differential WBC count shows lymphocytosis at all stages of genital tuberculosis. The ESR is frequently raised and is a non-specific investigation at any stage of the disease. None of these tests can be used for confirmation as these markers are raised in many infections.

The Mantoux test is positive in 90% of cases of genital TB. It is indicative of past exposure to the tubercle bacilli. It is not a confirmatory investigation but a negative result indicates tuberculosis to be unlikely.

The ESR is frequently raised and is specific in early disease.
The Mantoux test is positive and indicative of current exposure to tubercle bacilli.
The Quantiferon test is positive and indicates latent tuberculosis.

question: A gynaecologist suspects tuberculous salpingitis in a young woman and suggests some investigations to confirm the diagnosis. Which of the following statements is true about these investigations?

correctAnswer: A. A wedge shaped defect at the uterine isthmus
explanationHtml:
A wedge-shaped defect is not suggestive of tubercular salpingitis. It is seen at the uterine isthmus in patients with a history of Cesarean section with a uterine scar.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) features of genital tuberculosis are:

  • Lead pipe appearance due to rigid nonperistaltic pipe-like tube
  • Beading and variation in filling defect
  • Calcification of the tube
  • Jagged fluffiness of the tubal outline
  • Tobacco-pouch appearance of hydrosalpinx and pyosalpinx
  • Golf club appearance with slight or moderate dilatation of the ampullary portion of the fallopian tube.
  • Rosette type appearance secondary to multiple small diverticular like outpouching surrounding the ampulla produced by caseous ulceration.

HSG is contraindicated in genital tuberculosis as it causes dissemination of the infection. This further increases the damage to the fallopian tubes.

The investigation of choice in genital tuberculosis is an endometrial biopsy. The tubercle bacilli are present in the deeper layers of the endometrium. They come to the surface just before menstruation. Hence, an endometrial biopsy is done 1 or 2 days before menstruation.

Menstrual blood can also be used for detecting mycobacteria.

An HSG showing the features of tuberculous salpingitis is given below.

Beading and variations in filling defect

question: Hysterosalpingography was done in a young woman with infertility and menstrual abnormalities. Which of the following findings would not point towards a diagnosis of tubercular salpingitis?

correctAnswer: A. It is a thick walled structure on sonography
explanationHtml:
The given image shows bilateral hydrosalpinx. It appears as a thin-walled structure.

A hydrosalpinx is a chronic cystic swelling of the fallopian tube that forms after a distal tubal obstruction. The tubes are enormously distended due to filling with clear serous fluid and become retort-shaped. On histology, the tubal plicae appear flattened. The interstitial end of the tube is open whereas the fimbrial end is indrawn and closed. This permits the dye to enter but not exit the tube during HSG.

It is caused due to:

  • Pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Endometriosis
  • Tuberculosis - tubercular salpingitis may also cause tobacco-pouch appearance, lead pipe appearance and pyosalpinx
  • Fallopian tube neoplasms (rare)

It can be an incidental finding during a pelvic exam or ultrasound. The patient may be asymptomatic, or present with infertility or chronic pelvic pain.

On HSG, it appears as terminal sacculation and occlusion of both fallopian tubes with a normal uterine cavity. Usually, a thin-walled, hypoechoic, cystic structure is seen. However, it may appear as multiple hyperechoic mural nodules around the inner circumference of the tube creating a 'beads on a string' appearance.

Treatment:

  • Treat the underlying cause
  • Laparoscopic salpingostomy - in mild disease
  • IVF recommended for women with infertility and severe hydrosalpinx

options.text: It is a thick walled structure on sonography
Tubal plicae are flattened on histology

Azoospermia is defined as the complete absence of sperm in semen. Other types of sperm disorders are as follows:

question: What does azoospermia refer to?

explanationHtml:
Artificial insemination with donor semen is done in cases of infertility where the husband has azoospermia.

Azoospermia is defined as a complete absence of sperms. Hence artificial insemination with the husband's/partner's semen cannot be performed.

Indications for artificial insemination with husband's/partner's semen are:

  1. Chronic medical disorder
  2. Oligospermia after sperm washout
  3. Impotence
  4. Premature and retrograde ejaculation
  5. Hypospadias
  6. Antisperm antibodies in cervical mucus
  7. Unexplained infertility- direct intraperitoneal insemination (DIPI) is done
  8. HIV-positive male or female
  9. X-Y fractionation of sperms for sex selection in cases of genetic and chromosomal abnormalities

Indications for artificial insemination with donor semen are:

  1. Azoospermia
  2. Uncorrectable immunological factors
  3. Genetic disease in husband/partner
  4. Chronic ill health

Sperms can be frozen and used later for artificial insemination e.g. if the husband requires to undergo radiotherapy or chemotherapy, or if the husband is a frequent traveler and is not available at the time of ovulation.

Artificial insemination techniques include:

  • Intrauterine Insemination (IUI)
  • Intrafallopian-tube Insemination
  • Intracervical Insemination
  • Direct Intraperitoneal Insemination (DIPI)

Steps required to do artificial insemination are:

  1. The semen is washed to remove abnormal sperms, debris, and seminal plasma containing antibodies. It is concentrated, and its quality is improved by the 'swim up technique' or by the use of the Percoll gradient.
  2. Semen with normal sperms and good motility is obtained.
  3. Around the time of ovulation, semen obtained is inseminated into the female genital tract. About 0.5 ml of semen is injected 36 hours after hCG injection when the ovarian follicle reaches 20 mm.

In women with ovulatory disorders, clomifene and metformin increase ovulation and pregnancy rates.

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, the level of follicular stimulating hormone (FSH) is the best indicator of ovarian reserve.

Ovarian reserve is the capacity of the ovary to produce eggs. FSH levels are measured in the early follicular phase on day 2 or 3 of the menstrual cycle.

A high FSH level indicates that the ovarian reserve is getting depleted and fewer oocytes are present in the ovary. FSH is high in ovarian hypofunction and postmenopausal women.

Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) is a better marker than FSH for ovarian reserve. Unlike FSH, its levels can be estimated at any time of the cycle. AMH is produced by the granulosa cells in ovarian follicles.

Note: Studies show that AMH levels decrease under the current use of oral contraceptive pills and tobacco smoking.
question: A 34-year-old woman presented with secondary infertility following radiation therapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma. You plan to test her ovarian reserve. Which of the following is the best indicator of this parameter?

explanationHtml:
In low ovarian reserve, the level of anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) will be <1 ng/ml.

AMH is a glycoprotein secreted by the granulosa cells of the primordial follicle of the ovary. It helps in oocyte maturation and mono-follicular development. AMH is also used in assessing ovarian reserve.

AMH levels in ng/ml Interpretation
2–6.8 Normal
<1 Poor ovarian reserve
>10

PCOD

Hyperstimulation syndrome

In women, AMH is always absent during embryogenesis and is secreted by the granulosa cells after puberty. It helps in follicular development and oocyte maturation. Estimation of serum AMH is used in the study of ovarian reserve in female infertility and secondary amenorrhoea.

In men, AMH starts to be secreted by the Sertoli cells in the testes by the 7th week of intrauterine life. It continues until puberty. It inhibits the development of the Müllerian system. The absence of AMH results in the development of hermaphroditism.

explanationHtml:
The image shows the characteristic ferning pattern of cervical mucus which is seen in the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle.

A specimen of cervical mucus is obtained using a platinum loop or pipette. This is spread on a clean glass slide and allowed to dry. When viewed under the low-power microscope, a palm leaf or fern type pattern is seen in the follicular phase. The ferning is due to the presence of sodium chloride in the mucus secreted under the effect of estrogen.

This pattern disappears after ovulation. If it was previously present, its disappearance is presumptive evidence of corpus luteum activity. Under the influence of progesterone, the cervical mucus becomes thick and tenacious and impenetrable to sperms and bacteria.

explanationHtml:
In the Miller–Kurzrok test, sperm acquiring jerky motility after penetrating cervical mucus is considered abnormal.

The Miller-Kurzrok test is a special test done in semen analysis to diagnose the cause of infertility. It is an in vitro test of sperm–mucus interaction.

It is based on the basic principle that a normal cervical mucus permits invasion by motile sperms. It is done at the time of ovulation. The test consists of placing cervical mucus on a glass slide alongside the specimen of the husband's semen and studying the penetration of sperms under the microscope. The penetration of sperm > 3 cm into the mucus at 30 minutes is considered normal.

Other special tests in semen analysis include:

  • Sperm penetration test
  • Semen–cervical mucus contact test
  • Postcoital test (Sims’ or Huhner’s test)

The post-coital test can not detect a fallopian tube block. It can evaluate the following conditions:

In the post-coital test, the couple is advised to have intercourse early in the morning close to the ovulation phase. The woman is asked to visit the clinic within 2 hours of having intercourse. The mucus is aspirated from the cervical canal and spread over a glass slide. Another smear made from the posterior fornix serves as a control.

On microscopy, 10–50 motile sperms are normally seen per high-power field. The cervical mucus is also examined for its quantity and viscosity. The post-coital test is useless in the presence of cervical infection.

An immunological factor causing infertility is encountered in around 5% of infertile couples.

Asherman syndrome (uterine synechiae) is classified as follows:

  • Minimal: <25% adhesion involves the uterine cavity, flimsy adhesions involving the fundus and tubal ostia.
  • Moderate: 25–70% adhesion of the endometrial surfaces, but no agglutination of the uterine wall.
  • Severe: 75% adhesions with agglutination and thick adhesions.

Asherman syndrome can present in the following ways:

  • Secondary amenorrhea
  • Oligomenorrhoea
  • Dysmenorrhoea
  • Habitual abortions
  • Infertility

The causes of Asherman syndrome are:

  • Dilatation and curettage (D&C)
  • Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP), spontaneous abortions, recurrent abortions
  • Uterine packing in postpartum haemorrhage
  • Uterine infection
  • Tubercular endometritis

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a hysterosalpingogram (HSG). HSG is contraindicated in genital tuberculosis.

Procedure of HSG:

  • It is best performed in the period between the last day of menses to ovulation, usually on the 9th/10th day of the cycle.
  • 10-15ml radioopaque dye is injected into the uterine cavity via Leech-Wilkinson cannula, Rubin's cannula, or Foley's catheter.
  • Fluoroscopy is performed as the dye passes through the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes.
  • If the tubes are patent, the dye will spill out of the tubal ostia into the peritoneum, and smear the adjacent bowel.

It is used for the detection of:

  • Tubal block - It can be due to:
    • Strictures - fibrotic block
    • Inspissated amorphous material
    • Tubal spasm - This can occur in apprehensive patients. It is prevented by premedication with atropine and analgesia.
  • Uterine anomalies
  • Uterine polyps
  • Uterine synechiae
  • The feasibility of tuboplasty, by studying the location and extent of tubal pathology.

Contraindications:

  • Genital tract infections, such as genital tuberculosis. This is due to the risk of spreading infection.
  • Bleeding
  • Suspected pregnancy
  • Allergy to the dye
  • Premenstrual phase:
    • If by chance pregnancy has occurred, it may be dislodged.
    • Thick endometrium might prevent the smooth flow of the dye, at the cornual end.
    • There is a risk of embolism and endometriosis if HSG is done during this phase.
